L67: ## I. Executive Summary
L68: ## 7. Overview
L69: ## 7.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L70: Patients with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) have decreased cortisol synthesis due to an enzymatic defect in the adrenal gland that leads to increases in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and adrenal stimulation, causing excess androgen production. Patients typically require supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages to reduce ACTH and control the excess androgens. The excess glucocorticoid and uncontrolled androgens cause a variety of adverse effects. Crinecerfont inhibits ACTH secretion by the pituitary. The Applicant, Neurocrine Biosciences Inc., submitted this marketing application for crinecerfont (proposed trade name CRENESSITY)(b) (4)
L71: Crinecerfont has fast track, breakthrough therapy, and orphan designations and was granted priority review.
L72: The application contains two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations in classic CAH—one in adults and the other in children 4 years of age and older. These trials clearly met their efficacy objectives, demonstrating androgen control in the setting of reduced glucocorticoid dosing, a clinical benefit given the known adverse effects of excess glucocorticoid use. The review team did not identify any major efficacy issues.
L73: The safety of crinecerfont is adequately characterized in the context of this rare disease. Risks include hypersensitivity reactions, adrenal insufficiency/crisis (if an inadequate dose of glucocorticoid is used, including during times of stress/illness), and tolerability issues (e.g., headache, fatigue). There is also a finding of mild reductions in neutrophil counts, which were not associated with an increased risk of infection, may possibly be related to reductions in glucocorticoid dosages, and are of unclear clinical significance. The trials had 2:1 randomization. Three crinecerfont-treated subjects versus one placebo-treated subject in the adult trial and four crinecerfont-treated subjects versus no placebo-treated subjects in the pediatric trial had an increase in suicidal ideation assessed using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale. An adult on crinecerfont also had a suicide attempt. The relationship of these findings to crinecerfont is unclear given the very low event rates, remote history of suicidality in some of the subjects who had an increase in their Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, lack of neuropsychiatric findings in animals, and no increase in suicidality when crinecerfont was studied in a major depressive disorder trial. All these risks and uncertainties will be mitigated with labeling, and we will continue to monitor these risks in the postmarketing setting.
L74: Existing human data regarding crinecerfont use during pregnancy and lactation are insufficient to inform risks with these uses; therefore, we are requiring further assessment in these settings as postmarketing requirements.
L75: The entire review team and signatory authority agree that the application can be approved. There were no areas of scientific or regulatory disagreement. The overall benefit-risk is favorable as described in the benefit-risk framework below.
L76: ## 7.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L77: Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) was established with two or more adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations.
L78: Substantial evidence of effectiveness was established based on the two pivotal, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled efficacy trials, Trial NBI-74788-CAH3003 (Trial CAH3003, National Clinical Trial [NCT] 04490915) conducted in adults with classic CAH, and NBI-74788-CAH2006 (Trial CAH2006, NCT 04806451) conducted in pediatric subjects aged 4 to 17 years, inclusive, with classic CAH. In both studies, crinecerfont had a statistically significant greater effect than placebo on the primary efficacy endpoint, as described below. In Trial CAH3003, crinecerfont also had a statistically significantly greater effect on the key secondary efficacy endpoints of change from baseline in serum androstenedione level at Week 4 and the proportion of subjects with a reduction to physiologic glucocorticoid dose while maintaining androstenedione control at Week 24. In pediatric Trial CAH2006, crinecerfont was statistically significantly better than placebo for both key secondary efficacy endpoints (i.e., change from baseline in serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone at Week 4 and the percentage change in daily glucocorticoid dose while maintaining androstenedione control at Week 28).
L79: The order of the primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints differed in the two trials. Data are presented as least-squares means with standard error of the mean or 95% confidence interval in parentheses. In the adult trial, CAH3003, crinecerfont resulted in a significantly greater mean percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24 while androstenedione (A4) levels were controlled (i.e., A4 \le 120\% of baseline or \le upper limit of normal (ULN) for age and sex), which was the primary efficacy endpoint. Crinecerfont allowed for lowering of the glucocorticoid daily dose by 27% (2.4) compared to 10% (3.2) in the placebo group at Week 24 while androstenedione levels were controlled. The treatment difference was -17% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -24, -10). Serum androstenedione at Week 4 was a key secondary endpoint and significantly decreased by 299 (37.7) ng/dL compared to an increase of 46 (51.0) ng/dL in the placebo group. The treatment difference was -366 ng/dL (95% CI: -457, -232). In addition, 63% of subjects receiving crinecerfont compared to 18% in the placebo group were able to reduce their daily glucocorticoid dose to the physiologic range (i.e., dose &lt;11 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents) while maintaining androstenedione control at Week 24.
L80: In the pediatric Trial CAH2006, the primary efficacy endpoint was change in serum androstenedione at Week 4. Crinecerfont significantly lowered serum androstenedione levels -197 (39.4) ng/dL, compared to an increase of 71 (56.2) ng/dL for the placebo group at Week 4 while glucocorticoid dosage remained stable. The treatment difference was -268 (95% CI: -403, -132). Key secondary endpoints included percent change in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 28 while androstenedione levels were controlled and change from baseline in serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone at Week 4. In subjects receiving crinecerfont, glucocorticoid daily dose was lowered by 18% (1.8) compared to an increase of 6% (2.6) in the placebo group at Week 28 while androstenedione levels were controlled. The treatment difference was -24% (95% CI: -30, -17). Additionally, crinecerfont lowered 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels at Week 4 by 5865 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 556 ng/dL in the placebo group).
L81: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L82: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L83: In summary, these trials compellingly demonstrated that crinecerfont allowed for adrenal androgen control with decreasing doses of glucocorticoids. In fact, many subjects achieved physiologic glucocorticoid dosing with continued androgen control. The significant decrease in glucocorticoid dose is clinically meaningful because lowering glucocorticoid dose can have a direct impact on the subsequent adverse events associated with glucocorticoid excess.
L84: ## 8. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L85: ## 8.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L86: Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework
L87: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a rare, life-threatening condition most commonly caused by deficiency of the adrenal enzyme 21-hydroxylase.
Newborn screening includes testing for CAH, so affected individuals are usually identified at birth.
Features of CAH include adrenal insufficiency from decreased cortisol synthesis (with or without aldosterone deficiency), loss of negative feedback causing increases in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion, and ACTH-mediated adrenal stimulation, leading to excess adrenal androgens. Androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels are measured clinically as markers of disease control.
Elevated androgen levels cause hirsutism, acne, subfertility (in females), and short adult stature (because of accelerated growth in childhood and premature epiphyseal fusion).
Glucocorticoid deficiency can lead to adrenal insufficiency or adrenal crisis if not adequately treated and also results in elevated ACTH levels, promoting growth of testicular adrenal rest tumors, which may cause subfertility in males.
Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a rare, life-threatening condition that is typically identified at birth and is most commonly caused by deficiency of 21-hydroxylase. This enzyme deficiency causes adrenal insufficiency and excess adrenal androgen production. Adrenal insufficiency can lead to an adrenal crisis. Elevated androgen levels cause hirsutism, acne, subfertility (in females), and short adult stature (because of accelerated growth in childhood and premature epiphyseal fusion). Glucocorticoid deficiency results in elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone levels, promoting growth of testicular adrenal rest tumors, which may cause subfertility in males.

## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L89: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current treatment options	The standard-of-care treatment for the adrenal insufficiency aspect of CAH includes glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone).
Stress dosing of glucocorticoids is needed for acute illness and other situations associated with increased cortisol requirements.
Suppression of excess adrenal androgen is achieved with physiologic glucocorticoid dosages in some patients, but many patients require supraphysiologic dosages of glucocorticoid to achieve androgen control.
Chronic exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid has adverse effects on body weight, metabolic parameters, and bone health.
Standard-of-care therapy includes glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement. Additional glucocorticoid is often needed to suppress elevated adrenal androgen levels, and this supraphysiologic glucocorticoid can have long-term adverse effects on body weight, metabolic parameters, and bone health.
Benefit	By reducing ACTH production via corticotropin-releasing factor-1 receptor antagonism, crinecerfont lowers adrenal androgen levels so that the disease can be managed with lower, more physiologic, total daily glucocorticoid dosages.
In two phase 3 trials, one in adults and one in pediatric subjects (aged 4 to 17 years) with CAH, crinecerfont significantly lowered adrenal androgen levels at Week 4 while glucocorticoid dosage remained stable, and allowed for a significant decrease in glucocorticoid daily dosage at Week 24 (adult trial) or Week 28 (pediatric trial) while androgen levels were controlled.
Crinecerfont lowered androstenedione levels at Week 4 by 299 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 46 ng/dL in the placebo group) in the adult trial and by 197 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 80 ng/dL in the placebo group) in the pediatric trial.
Crinecerfont lowered 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels at Week 4 by 5865 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 556 ng/dL in the placebo group) in the pediatric trial.
In adult and pediatric subjects aged 4 years and older with CAH, crinecerfont allowed for adrenal androgen control at lower glucocorticoid dosages, many at physiologic or near-physiologic replacement dosages. Decreased exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is clinically meaningful because excess glucocorticoid has adverse effects on body weight, metabolic parameters, and bone health. Changes in body weight and metabolic parameters were not improved compared to placebo after 24 weeks of crinecerfont treatment in adults.
L90: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L91: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Crinecerfont allowed for lowering of the glucocorticoid daily dose by 27.3% (compared to 10.3% in the placebo group) at Week 24 in the adult trial and 18% at Week 28 (compared to an increase of 5.6% in the placebo group) in the pediatric trial while androstenedione levels were controlled.
In the crinecerfont group, 62.7% of subjects (versus 17.5% in the placebo group) in the adult study and 29.9% of subjects (versus none in the placebo group) in the pediatric study achieved a glucocorticoid dose in the physiologic range (i.e., \le 11 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents adjusted for body surface area) at Weeks 24 and 28, respectively, while androstenedione levels were controlled.
Change from baseline at Week 24 in HOMA-IR, body weight, and total fat mass in the adult trial were not statistically significantly different from placebo.

Risk and risk management	The crinecerfont safety database was adequate in size and scope in the context of this rare disease. Adverse reactions were generally considered tolerability issues (e.g., headache, fatigue) that can be adequately addressed with labeling.
Decreased neutrophil counts (<2\times 10^3 \text{ cells}/\mu\text{L}, but generally >1\times 10^3 \text{ cells}/\mu\text{L}) occurred more frequently in study subjects treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo during the double-blind treatment periods of both the adult (14.2% versus 5.2%) and pediatric (36.8% versus 15.6%) trials. These mild decreases, which were not associated with an increased risk of infection in the trials, may possibly be related to reductions in glucocorticoid dosages, and are of unclear clinical significance.
Postmarketing requirements for a descriptive pregnancy safety study and a clinical lactation study to determine the extent to which crinecerfont is present in human milk are warranted.
The observations of mildly decreased neutrophil counts and positive findings on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, including the one suicide attempt, in those taking crinecerfont will be described in the Adverse Reactions section of the product label so that prescribers are aware of the findings. We will continue to monitor for these adverse events in the postmarketing setting and require that the Applicant implement enhanced pharmacovigilance for adverse events of suicidality and neutropenia.
Product labeling will include a Warning regarding the need for increased glucocorticoid doses in the setting of concurrent illness or other physiologic stressors.
L92: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L93: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
In the adult trial, 3 (2.5%) of 120 crinecerfont-treated subjects and 1 (1.7%) of the 58 placebo-treated subjects reported suicidal ideation on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale during the 24-week double-blind treatment period. One crinecerfont-treated subject attempted suicide. In the pediatric trial, 4 (6%) of 67 crinecerfont-treated subjects and none of the 31 placebo-treated subjects reported suicidal ideation on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale during the 28-week double-blind treatment period.
The relationship of these findings to study drug is unclear, given the very low event rates, remote history of suicidality in some of the subjects who had an increase on their Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, lack of neuropsychiatric findings in animals, and no increase in suicidality when crinecerfont was studied in a depression trial.
Serious adverse events of acute adrenal insufficiency occurred in both the adult and pediatric trials in subjects receiving crinecerfont. These cases occurred in the setting of physiologic stress (most commonly underlying infection) with insufficient adjustment of corticosteroid dose, and were not caused by crinecerfont itself.
Human data regarding crinecerfont use during pregnancy and lactation are insufficient to inform the risks in labeling.

L95: ## 8.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L96: Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a rare disease most commonly caused by deficiency of the adrenal enzyme 21-hydroxylase. The lack of 21-hydroxylase activity results in deficiencies of cortisol and, in some cases, aldosterone. Because the adrenal gland tries to compensate for the lack of cortisol production, excessive adrenal androgens are produced. Glucocorticoid replacement is necessary for the underlying adrenal insufficiency associated with CAH. Additionally, mineralocorticoid replacement may be needed. Treatment of the excessive adrenal androgen production associated with CAH can be challenging and generally requires glucocorticoid dosing that exceeds the needed physiologic replacement. Therefore, control of adrenal androgens with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosing can be associated with adverse effects on body weight, growth, metabolic parameters, and bone health.
L97: Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of the corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor intended to decrease ACTH stimulation of the adrenal gland's hormone production. This is a novel approach to allow for control of adrenal androgen production as an adjunct to the required physiologic glucocorticoid therapy for treatment of the underlying adrenal insufficiency.
L98: The Applicant conducted two adequate and well-controlled clinical trials in the CAH population: one in adults and one in pediatric subjects aged 4 years and older. These trials demonstrated that crinecerfont allowed for adrenal androgen control with decreasing doses of glucocorticoids. In fact, many subjects achieved physiologic glucocorticoid dosing with continued androgen control. The significant decrease in glucocorticoid dose is clinically meaningful because lowering glucocorticoid dose can have a direct impact on the subsequent adverse events associated with glucocorticoid excess.
L99: The safety profile of crinecerfont was adequately characterized in the context of this rare disease. Based on crinecerfont's mechanism of action, adrenal insufficiency was a clinical concern and was monitored throughout the development program. Cases of adrenal insufficiency, some with fatality, did occur in the setting of stress situations for subjects. The adrenal insufficiency and crisis were not caused by crinecerfont itself but the underlying disease state. Therefore, patients will need to continue physiologic glucocorticoid replacement and to be advised of the need for increased glucocorticoid doses as the time of stress from concurrent illness or other reasons. This will be addressed in product labeling as a Warning and Precaution.
L100: Crinecerfont was previously evaluated as a treatment for depression, and the activity of crinecerfont on the CRF receptors in the pituitary indicate that the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier. Therefore, the clinical development program assessed the risk of suicide with the use of the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). One subject in the adult trial attempted suicide during the conduct of the trial. The assessment of the C-SSRS in the adult trial revealed 3/120 subjects in the crinecerfont group and 1/58 subjects in the placebo group reported suicidal ideation, evident by an increase in their C-SSRS score. In the pediatric trial, 4/67 subjects in the crinecerfont group and 0/31 subjects in the placebo group increased their C-SSRS score. The relationship of these findings to study drug is unclear, given the very low event rates, remote history of suicidality in some of the subjects who had an increase on their Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, lack of neuropsychiatric findings in animals, and no increase in suicidality when crinecerfont was studied in a major depressive disorder trial.
L101: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L102: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L103: Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont for major depressive disorder. In the adult and pediatric CAH studies, decreased neutrophil counts also occurred more frequently in study subjects treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo. The etiology for this is unclear and the findings were not associated with increased risk of infection.
L104: Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema, were reported with crinecerfont treatment. Other noted adverse reactions (e.g., headache, fatigue) may be tolerability issues.
L105: In summary, crinecerfont use as an adjunct to glucocorticoid therapy has been shown to reduce androgen levels in adults and pediatric subjects with CAH and lower glucocorticoid dose requirements, with many subjects able to achieve physiologic or near-physiologic glucocorticoid replacement doses. The decreased exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is clinically beneficial because of the well-known adverse effects of excess glucocorticoid. The safety profile is adequately characterized, and risks (e.g., adverse reactions such as headache and fatigue; contraindication if prior hypersensitivity reaction to crinecerfont; need for adequate glucocorticoid replacement to avoid adrenal insufficiency/crisis) can be adequately addressed through product labeling. Other findings of unclear clinical significance (e.g., minor neutrophil count reductions) and unclear relation to study drug (e.g., suicidality) will be included in labeling for prescriber awareness. These risks and uncertainties are outweighed by the benefits when crinecerfont is used according to the approved labeling.
L106: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L107: ## 9. Introduction
L108: Crinecerfont, a new molecular entity, is a first-in-class selective antagonist of the pituitary corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor. The Applicant submitted two crinecerfont NDAs (for two formulations) for the proposed indication (b) (4)
L109: caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency:
L110: - NDA 218808 for soft gelatin capsules (25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg)
- NDA 218820 for oral solution (50 mg/mL)
L111: The proposed dosing regimen is:
L112: - 100 mg twice daily for adults (aged 18 years and older)
- 100 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing greater than or equal to 55 kg
- 50 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 20 kg to less than 55 kg
- 25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to less than 20 kg
L113: In patients with classic CAH, deficiency of 21-hydroxylase enzymatic activity causes deficiency of adrenal glucocorticoid (cortisol) and mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) production. The glucocorticoid deficiency stimulates excess adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) production from the pituitary gland, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce excess androgens. Levels of androstenedione (A4) and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) are measured clinically as biomarkers of adrenal androgen production and disease control in patients with CAH.
L114: Standard of care treatment of classic CAH consists of glucocorticoid (e.g., hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) replacement. Exogenous glucocorticoids remedy adrenal insufficiency as well as suppress excess adrenal androgen production, while mineralocorticoids are used to correct salt-wasting in the setting of insufficient aldosterone production. While physiologic glucocorticoid doses are required to remedy adrenal insufficiency, supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages are often necessary to suppress the high ACTH levels and control adrenal androgen production.
L115: The use of supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses creates a clinical management challenge of balancing disease control (by lowering adrenal androgen levels) with avoiding iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome due to excess glucocorticoid exposure. Elevated androgen levels cause hirsutism, acne, subfertility (in females), and short adult stature (because of accelerated growth in childhood and premature epiphyseal fusion). Elevated ACTH levels promote growth of testicular adrenal rest tumors, which may cause subfertility in males. Long-term exposure to excess glucocorticoid causes weight gain and adverse effects on metabolism, the cardiovascular system, bone health, and growth (in children) (Merke and Auchus 2020).
L116: The Applicant hypothesizes that by reducing pituitary ACTH production via CRF1 receptor antagonism, crinecerfont lowers adrenal androgen levels so that the disease can be managed with
L117: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L118: lower, more physiologic, total daily glucocorticoid dosages (Table 3). By reducing daily glucocorticoid requirements, crinecerfont treatment as an adjunct to glucocorticoid replacement ultimately minimizes the adverse health consequences of long-term exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid.

L122: The Applicant submitted data from two pivotal phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (with open-label extension periods) supporting the efficacy and safety of crinecerfont in adult (Trial CAH3003) and pediatric (Trial CAH2006) subjects with classic CAH. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled period lasted 24 weeks in the adult study and 28 weeks in the pediatric study. The open-label extension period continued through 12 months (52 weeks in the pediatric study).

L124: - Primary: Percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24 while Week 24 androstenedione levels are controlled (\le 120\% of baseline or \leupper limit of normal [ULN] for age and sex)
- First key secondary: Change from baseline in serum androstenedione level at Week 4 while glucocorticoid dose is stable

- Additional key secondary: Changes from baseline in homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), weight, and fat mass at Week 24
L125: Primary and key secondary endpoints for Trial CAH2006 include:
L126: - Primary: Change from baseline in serum androstenedione level at Week 4 while glucocorticoid dose is stable
- First key secondary: Change from baseline in serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level at Week 4 while glucocorticoid dose is stable
- Second key secondary: Percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 28, while Week 28 androstenedione levels are controlled (\le 120\% of baseline or \leULN for sex and age or, if pubertal, pubertal stage).
L127: Crinecerfont has Orphan (March 15, 2019), Fast Track (June 15, 2021), and Breakthrough Therapy (December 1, 2023) designations. Crinecerfont met breakthrough therapy designation criteria because the Applicant submitted preliminary clinical data showing that the drug may provide a substantial improvement over available therapy based on statistically significant
L128: reductions in total daily glucocorticoid dose requirements (in many cases to physiologic doses) while maintaining control of adrenal androgen levels with crinecerfont compared to placebo.

L138: ## 9.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
L139: Trial CAH3003 in adults with classic CAH and Trial CAH2006 in pediatric subjects aged 4 to 17 years with classic CAH are the pivotal phase 3 trials reviewed as primary evidence of crinecerfont's efficacy and safety (Table 4). Crinecerfont was evaluated in a double-blind, placebo-controlled fashion for 24 weeks (Trial CAH3003) or 28 weeks (Trial CAH2006), followed by an open-label treatment period through 12 months (both trials). These trials are fit for purpose to support this application.
L140: Efficacy results submitted for Trial CAH3003 include analysis of the completed double-blind period (Day 1 to Week 24) and an interim analysis for the ongoing open-label period (Week 24 to Month 12) at the data cutoff (July 19, 2023). Efficacy results submitted for Trial CAH2006 include analysis of the completed double-blind period (Day 1 to Week 28) and an interim analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label period (Week 28 to Week 52) at the data cutoff (August 9, 2023). Data from the 120-Day Safety Update were incorporated into the review.
L141: We also independently reviewed the literature and the literature review submitted by the Applicant justifying the clinical meaningfulness of the studies' efficacy findings.
L142: The safety review focused on results from the two phase 3 trials in subjects with CAH, with supportive data on any signal identified in the CAH population from a phase 2 study in subjects with major depressive disorder. Two phase 2 dose-finding trials of crinecerfont in adults with CAH (Trial CAH2001) and pediatric subjects with CAH (Trial CAH2008) were used, together with other available information, to select the doses for the phase 3 trials.

L171: ## 11. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical Pharmacology
L172: ## 11.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L173: Cortisol (glucocorticoid) deficiency in patients with CAH causes an increase in corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) hormone from the hypothalamus, which stimulates excessive adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion from the anterior pituitary. Excessive ACTH secretion stimulates the adrenal cortex, which leads to adrenal hyperplasia.
L174: Crinecerfont is a selective first-in-class CRF1 receptor antagonist that reduces the excess ACTH secretion caused by elevated CRF in response to low glucocorticoid levels in patients with CAH. The Applicant provided a series of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies to demonstrate that crinecerfont binds CRF1 receptors and inhibits CRF-induced cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) synthesis and ACTH release. The nonclinical pharmacology data were provided to support the proposed mechanism of action of crinecerfont.
L175: Crinecerfont inhibited the ability of CRF to bind human and rodent CRF1 receptors with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC_{50}) values of 0.6 to 3.99nM and showed no affinity for related receptors human CRF2a or human CRF-binding protein (limited to 11.5% inhibition at 10\muM crinecerfont). The most abundant crinecerfont metabolite (NBI-756179, M6), which represented 6% of human crinecerfont exposure, bound to CRF1 receptors with nanomolar affinity (K_i=1.14nM), but no inhibitor constant (K_i) was provided for crinecerfont. The contribution of this metabolite to CRF1 receptor antagonist activity was considered minor due to its low abundance. In the in vitro functional assays, crinecerfont inhibited CRF-induced cAMP production in Y79 cells with an IC_{50} value of 3.1nM (1.5 ng/mL), and blocked ACTH secretion in AtT-20 mouse pituitary tumor cells, demonstrating that crinecerfont acts as a functional antagonist of CRF1 receptors (Figure 1).
L176: **Figure 1. Crinecerfont Antagonizes CRF-Induced Pituitary ACTH Secretion (AtT-20 Cells)**
L177: Source: Applicant's NDA submission
L178: Abbreviations: ACTH, adrenocorticotropin hormone; CRF, corticotropin-releasing factor
L179: The in vivo primary pharmacodynamic studies reiterated the findings of the in vitro binding and functional studies. The binding of crinecerfont to pituitary and brain CRF1 receptors was evaluated in crude tissue homogenates from rats administered crinecerfont hydrochloride (HCl) orally (PO) or intraperitoneally. The results demonstrated that crinecerfont binds to CRF1 receptors in pituitary and brain, with higher occupancy of CRF1 receptors in pituitary (67 to 81%) than in brain (13 to 29%) at early timepoints (0.5 to 1 hour postdose). The CRF1 receptor binding of crinecerfont was comparable between pituitary and brain at 2 to 24 hours postdose. In vivo, CRF administration caused an increase in plasma ACTH levels. In studies in rats, administration of crinecerfont PO (Figure 2), intravenously (IV), or intraperitoneally showed a dose-dependent inhibition of CRF-stimulated ACTH secretion with 50% inhibitory dose of 1.3 to 4.9 mg/kg crinecerfont HCl, further demonstrating the antagonist action of crinecerfont on CRF1 receptors. The CRF1 receptor antagonist effects of crinecerfont were further investigated in a stressed rat model. Stress was induced by restraining rats for 15 minutes, which caused up to a 6-fold increase in ACTH plasma levels. When crinecerfont HCl was administered PO to male rats 1 hour before inducing stress, crinecerfont significantly antagonized the stress-induced ACTH increase at 10 mg/kg but not at 3 mg/kg crinecerfont HCl. Crinecerfont did not significantly affect basal plasma ACTH level when administered PO daily up to 1000 mg/kg in nonstressed rats, indicating that physiological ACTH levels were not affected by crinecerfont, which likely reflects maintenance of endogenous positive and negative feedback signals within the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis.
L180: Figure 2. Crinecerfont Dose-Dependently Inhibits CRF-Stimulated ACTH Secretion in Rats
L181: Source: Applicant's NDA submission (data source: EVV0033 (Figure (5.2) 2
L182: Note: Data from three to eight rats per group were analyzed by student's t test and are depicted as mean\pmSEM.
L183: *** p&lt;0.001 versus CRF
L184: Abbreviations: ACTH: adrenocorticotropic hormone; CRF, corticotropin-releasing factor; SEM, standard error of the mean; SSR, 30 mg/kg crinecerfont hydrochloride; SSR125543A, crinecerfont hydrochloride
L185: In conclusion, the Applicant's in vitro and in vivo nonclinical studies support the proposed mechanism of action for crinecerfont as a CRF1 receptor antagonist that reduces CRF-induced increases in ACTH.

L201: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L202: Characteristic	Drug Information
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	Population pharmacokinetic analyses indicated that body weight is a significant covariate affecting the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont. Therefore, body weight-banded dosing was used in the pediatric study to ensure comparable exposures to those of adult subjects across pediatric weight groups (i.e., 100 mg bid for subjects weighing \ge 55 kg and 50 mg bid for subjects weighing 20 to <55 kg). For pediatric subjects between 10 to <20 kg, crinecerfont dose of 25 mg bid is recommended based on exposure-matching to pediatric subjects between 20 to <55 kg.
Age	No clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont were observed based on age ranging from 5 to 54 years.
Renal impairment	Mass balance study indicates that renal excretion is unlikely to be a major elimination pathway of crinecerfont. Population PK analysis indicates that the median decreases in AUC24 with mild and moderate renal impairment relative to normal renal function was 2.7% and 8.4%, respectively. Therefore, dosage adjustment is not needed in patients with mild or moderate renal impairment. Considering the potential impact of severe renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont, and the lack of clinical experience in these patients, crinecerfont is not recommended in patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease.
Hepatic impairment	Crinecerfont exposure for subjects with mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment decreased by 9%, 15%, and 17%, respectively, for Cmax and 27%, 34%, and 20%, respectively, for AUC0-\infty, relative to subjects with normal hepatic function. The 90% CI values for GMR for Cmax and AUC for all the hepatic impairment groups included unity as compared to the normal hepatic function group. Therefore, hepatic impairment has no clinically significant effect on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics, and dose adjustment is not needed in patients with hepatic impairment.
Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as a Precipitant)
Inhibition/induction of metabolism	Effect of crinecerfont on the pharmacokinetics of CYP3A substrates:
Concomitant administration of repeated 100-mg daily doses of crinecerfont increased midazolam (sensitive CYP3A substrate) AUC by 23% (90% CI: 9% to 38%) and did not affect the pharmacokinetics of oral contraceptive (nonsensitive CYP3A substrate, 90% CI of GMR for AUC and Cmax within 0.80 to 1.25). Therefore, crinecerfont is considered a weak CYP3A inhibitor and is unlikely to significantly increase the systemic exposures of glucocorticoids, which are generally not sensitive CYP3A substrates.
Crinecerfont is unlikely to induce CYP3A, CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2B6 or inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1 at clinically relevant doses.

Inhibition/induction of transporter systems	Crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter (MATE)1, or MATE2-K.

Effect of CYP3A induction:
Concomitant administration of rifampin, a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and moderate inducer of CYP2B6, led to a decrease in crinecerfont C_{max} and AUC by 23% and 62%, respectively. L207: ## 12. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
L208: ## 12.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential Effectiveness
L209: The Applicant has proposed the following crinecerfont dose regimens:
L210: - Adults and pediatric patients weighing \ge 55 kg: 100 mg twice daily PO with food
- Pediatric patients aged 4 years and older weighing 20 kg to &lt;55 kg: 50 mg twice daily PO with food
- Pediatric patients aged 4 years and older weighing 10 kg to &lt;20 kg: 25 mg twice daily PO with food
L211: The proposed dosing regimens for adult patients and pediatric patients weighing \ge 20 kg are the same as those in Trial CAH3003 (adult trial) and Trial CAH2006 (pediatric trial; see details in Section 12.2). Therefore, the appropriateness of the proposed doses is supported by the safety and efficacy data from these pivotal phase 3 trials. The proposed dosing regimen for pediatric patients weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg is supported by exposure matching to pediatric subjects weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg and is considered acceptable (see Section 12.1.3).
L212: ## 12.1.1. Dose Selection Rationale for Pivotal Trials
L213: ## 12.1.1.1. Adult Phase 3 Trial Dose Selection
L214: The dose selection for the phase 3 adult study, Trial CAH3003, was based on the phase 2 study, Trial CAH2001, an open-label, multiple-dose, sequential dose-escalation study to assess the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, safety, and tolerability of crinecerfont in adult male and female subjects 18 years to 50 years of age with a documented medical diagnosis of classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH. The study assessed four crinecerfont dosing regimens administered for 14 days in a sequential manner. Dose cohorts with sample sizes are listed below:
L215: - Cohort 1 (N=8): 50 mg once daily at bedtime with Ensure Plus® (350 calories, 11 grams total fat, 20 grams sugars, 13 grams protein, and 50 grams carbohydrate)
- Cohort 2 (N=7): 100 mg once daily at bedtime with Ensure Plus
- Cohort 3 (N=8): 100 mg once daily with the evening meal
- Cohort 4 (N=8): 100 mg twice daily at breakfast and dinner
L216: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L217: The doses selected for this phase 2 dose-finding study were based on the following data:
L218: - Crinecerfont 50 mg was well tolerated in single- and repeat-dose safety and pharmacokinetic (PK) studies in healthy volunteers.
- Doses up to 200 mg were well tolerated in single-dose and repeat-dose studies in healthy subjects.
- Crinecerfont 100 mg daily was well tolerated in an 8-week double-blind study in adult male and female subjects with major depressive disorder.
- The anticipated steady-state exposures with the selected crinecerfont doses, using the predicted maximum observed plasma concentration (C_{max}) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC), were within the acceptable safety margins defined by the nonclinical toxicology studies.
L219: Per the Applicant, reductions in ACTH, 17-OHP, and A4 relative to baseline levels were observed in most of the subjects across all dose regimens after receiving 14 days of treatment with crinecerfont. A dose response was observed for androstenedione reduction, with the greatest median reduction observed in the 100 mg twice daily dose group (64%) compared to the other dose groups (21%, 42%, and 51% change from baseline, with 50 mg at bedtime, 100 mg at bedtime, and 100 mg with evening meal, respectively; Table 9).
L220: In addition, the responder rate (i.e., &gt;50% reduction of A4) was greatest in the crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily (bid) group (75%) compared to responder rates between 50% and 63% for the other dose groups. It should be noted that crinecerfont needs to be administered with food due to low bioavailability under fasting conditions. Various meal types (i.e., Ensure Plus versus breakfast and dinner) were used across the cohorts. Similar crinecerfont drug exposures were observed between cohort 2 (100 mg with Ensure Plus) and cohort 3 (100 mg with evening meal). Therefore, the use of different meal types across treatment arms is unlikely to confound the dose-finding results.
L221: Crinecerfont was generally well tolerated in all four dosing cohorts, and there was no dose relationship in the incidence, type, or severity of adverse events. Therefore, 100 mg twice-daily dosing was selected for the phase 3 adult study, CAH3003. It should be noted that interpretation of the dose response for A4 reduction may be confounded by different baselines of A4 among the four dosing cohorts, between-subject variabilities of this pharmacodynamic marker, and relatively small sample sizes across dose groups (refer to Section 20.2.10 for details).
L222: ## 12.1.1.2. Pediatric (Weight &gt;20 kg) Phase 3 Dose Selection
L223: The dose selection for the phase 3 pediatric trial, CAH2006, was based on the following:
L224: - Clinical benefits observed in the phase 2 study, NBI-74788-CAH2008, an open-label multiple-dose study to assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of crinecerfont in eight pediatric subjects (14 to 16 years old with mean body weight of 70 kg) with a documented medical diagnosis of classic CAH.
- An exposure-matching approach to the adult 100 mg twice-daily dose using population pharmacokinetic (popPK) analysis for pediatric subjects with CAH.
L225: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L226: In the phase 2 study, NBI-74788-CAH2008, pediatric subjects with mean body weight of 70 kg received crinecerfont 50-mg capsules twice daily at breakfast and dinner for 14 consecutive days. Study results indicated that on Day 14, compared to baseline, median A4 levels decreased by 58%, and ACTH and 17-OHP as key secondary endpoints decreased by 57% and 69%, respectively (Table 9). It is interesting that the degree of A4 reduction appears to be comparable to that in adult subjects, despite the fact that these adolescents received only half the dose the adults received (50 mg bid versus 100 mg bid). Nonetheless, in the phase 3 pediatric study, the Applicant selected the same dose as adults for pediatric subjects with body weight \ge 55 kg based on the exposure-matching approach rather than relying on the pharmacodynamic (PD) findings.
L227: As body weight is a significant PK covariate, body weight-banded dosing was used in pediatric subjects with varying body weights. Specifically, the population PK model informed the doses selected for the pediatric phase 3 study, Trial CAH2006, (i.e., 100 mg bid for pediatric subjects weighing \ge 55 kg and 50 mg bid for those weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg), as these doses in children provide comparable crinecerfont exposures to those of adult subjects across pediatric weight groups. Refer to Sections 20.2.11 and 20.5 for the in vivo study details and pharmacometrics assessment, respectively.

L233: ## 12.1.1.3. Dose for Pediatric Patients Weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg
L234: The phase 3 pediatric clinical trial (CAH2006) did not enroll any subjects in the 10 to &lt;20 kg weight band; instead, the Applicant relied upon popPK modeling and exposure matching to support the proposed dosing of 25 mg twice daily in the pediatric subgroup of 10 to &lt;20 kg weight band and down to 4 years of age. The dose for the 10 to &lt;20 kg pediatric subgroup was informed by the dose for pediatric subjects weighing 20 kg to &lt;55 kg. The 20 kg to &lt;55 kg subgroup was chosen as the reference population because of similarities between the two groups with respect to disease state, pathophysiology, disease progression, and expected efficacy response. Furthermore, efficacy was demonstrated at the dose administered to the 20 kg to &lt;55 kg pediatric subgroup, which provided additional support to rely on that subgroup for dose determination for the &lt;20 kg weight group (refer to Section 12.3.1).
L235: Utilizing modeling and simulation in virtual pediatric subjects of 10 to &lt;20 kg and at least 4 years of age, 25 mg twice daily is projected to produce similar exposures (i.e., 24-hour area under the concentration-time curve and 24-hour maximum concentration) to those of the 50 mg twice daily regimen in pediatric subjects of 20 to &lt;55 kg. Additionally, a high proportion of virtual pediatric subjects weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg is expected to have crinecerfont exposures within the model-predicted adult exposure (Figure 3). Collectively, the proposed dosage of 25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to &lt;20 kg is expected to have similar safety and efficacy based on comparable exposures observed in pediatric subjects weighing 20 kg to &lt;55 kg and in adults (refer to Section 20.5.5).

L238: ## 12.1.2. Exposure Response
L239: Utilizing the final popPK model and phase 3 clinical data, the Applicant performed exposure-response (E-R) analyses in adults and in pediatric subjects with CAH independently in each population. The efficacy endpoints in the phase 3 clinical trials included the change from baseline in serum A4 prior to morning glucocorticoid dose at Week 4, the percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24 for adults and at Week 28 for pediatric subjects, and the achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels at Week 24 for adults and Week 28 for pediatric subjects while maintaining androgen control. For safety E-R, the most frequent adverse events for adult (i.e., fatigue) and pediatric subjects (i.e., headache) were selected as exploratory safety endpoints for independent analyses in each population.
L240: The E-R efficacy analyses demonstrated that across the studied exposure ranges, for the proposed adult and pediatric dosing regimens (i.e., 100 mg twice daily dose in adults and pediatric subjects weighing \ge 55 kg; 50 mg twice daily in pediatric subjects weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg), the E-R efficacy relationships were relatively flat for change from baseline in serum A4 (prior to morning glucocorticoid dose) at Week 4 and percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose (Figure 4).
L241: The E-R analyses demonstrated an increase in probability of achieving a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels (while maintaining serum A4 control) across studied exposure ranges in the adult and the pediatric E-R models. However, the 95% confidence interval of the slope (i.e., log-odds ratio) for drug exposure contains zero in the pediatric model and is numerically close to zero in the adult model, suggesting that other factors in addition to crinecerfont exposure may be driving the probability of glucocorticoid response.
L242: The following limitations should also be considered when interpreting the E-R findings:
L243: - The exposure ranges in the E-R analysis were relatively narrow. Specifically, the E-R analysis was based on data from the phase 3 trials in adult and pediatric subjects (i.e., Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006). It should be noted that only one dose level was studied in the adult phase 3 trial, data of which was used for the E-R analysis, and pediatric doses were selected to match the adult population.
- An E-R analysis was performed for the most common treatment-emergent adverse event in the adult and pediatric phase 3 trials. There was no apparent relationship between crinecerfont exposure and proportion of adults with fatigue at Week 24 across the studied exposure range. In pediatric subjects, the probability of headache increased across studied exposures at Week 28; however, this finding may have limited interpretation given the small number of pediatric subjects who experienced this adverse event in the crinecerfont arm versus placebo (17 and 2 subjects, respectively).
L244: Overall, the results from the exposure-efficacy and exploratory exposure-safety analyses support the proposed doses for adult and pediatric subjects with CAH (refer to Section 20.5 for details on the E-R analyses).

L254: ## 12.1.4. Switching Between Oral Solution and Capsule Formulation
L255: Crinecerfont is available as an oral solution and as capsules. Study NBI-74788-1716 compared the crinecerfont exposure between the oral solution and the phase 2 capsule formulation. The results show the two formulations were not bioequivalent and crinecerfont exposure (C_{max} and AUC) from the oral solution was ~15% less than the phase 2 capsule formulation6 (refer to Section 20.2.4). In addition, the popPK analysis indicates that the mean exposure for the oral solution is expected to be 26% lower than that for the capsule formulation (Figure 5).
L256: Nonetheless, the Applicant is proposing that the oral solution and the commercial capsule formulation can be switched based on patient preference.
L257: The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposal based on the following considerations:
L258: - This is consistent with the phase 3 pediatric clinical trial (NBI-74788-CAH2006), where subjects were allowed to switch from the oral solution to the capsule formulation in the open-label phase. In clinical practice, we expect the most common scenario to be a switch from oral solution to capsule when pediatric patients become old enough to swallow the capsule. Given that the capsule formulation has slightly higher bioavailability than the oral solution, we do not expect a loss of efficacy when switching to the capsule formulation. In addition, the safety with the capsule formulation has been established in the phase 3 clinical trials.
- Simulation results show that, despite numerically lower exposure (i.e., steady-state AUC) with the oral solution, a large percentage of the simulated exposures in subjects receiving the oral solution fall within those of the capsule formulation.
- The Applicant is proposing the 25 mg bid solution for pediatric patients weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg, and the 50 mg bid solution for pediatric patients weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg. In the randomized, placebo-controlled portion of the pediatric phase 3 trial, about 50% of the subjects were in the 20 to &lt;55 kg weight band (37 crinecerfont, 14 placebo) and received the 50 mg bid (or placebo) solution. The remaining ~50% of subjects were in the \ge 55 kg weight band (32 crinecerfont, 20 placebo) and received the capsule. These subgroups achieved similar reductions in glucocorticoid doses. Although the trial did not enroll pediatric subjects weighing &lt;20 kg, the pharmacokinetic exposure with the 25 mg bid solution in the 10 to &lt;20 kg weight band is expected to match that of the 50 mg bid solution in the 20 to &lt;55 kg weight band (see Section 12.3).
- Exposure-efficacy models based on phase 3 clinical data with both oral solution and capsule formulations demonstrate that the E-R relationships are relatively flat across studied exposure for adult and pediatric subjects, respectively.
L259: Based on these considerations, we conclude that the difference in crinecerfont exposure between the oral solution and capsule is not considered clinically meaningful.
L260: 6 The phase 2 capsule formulation is expected to have a similar crinecerfont exposure to the commercial formulation, as it is nearly identical in composition to the phase 3 capsule formulation, which is bioequivalent to the commercial capsule formulation. The GMRs and 90% CIs for AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} of the commercial capsule compared to the phase 3 capsule at the 100 mg dose were 1.01 (0.94, 1.09), 0.99 (0.91, 1.08), and 1.07 (0.98, 1.16), respectively.

L266: ## 12.2.2. Trial CAH3003
L267: ## 12.2.2.1. Design, Trial CAH3003
L268: ## Overall Design
L269: Trial CAH3003 is titled “A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of crinecerfont in adult subjects with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, followed by open-label treatment.” The study design is appropriate to demonstrate efficacy and is depicted in Figure 6.
L270: This phase 3 trial consisted of a 4-week screening period; a 24-week double-blind, placebo-controlled treatment period; a 6-month open-label treatment period; a 6-month open-label or
L271: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L272: double-blind, active-controlled treatment period; and an open-label extension. The primary objective was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily compared with placebo in reducing daily glucocorticoid dosage while maintaining adrenal androgen control.
L273: ## **24-Week Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period (Day 1 to Week 24)**
L274: A total of 182 adult subjects with classic CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency who required supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids to control androgen excess (i.e., glucocorticoid dose &gt;13 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio (active: placebo) to receive crinecerfont 100 mg taken orally twice daily with breakfast and the evening meal or placebo. The 24-week treatment period consisted of a 4-week glucocorticoid stable dose phase, an 8-week glucocorticoid reduction period, and a 12-week glucocorticoid optimization period.
L275: ## **Week 1 to Week 4**
L276: During the first 4 weeks of the study, subjects were maintained on their baseline glucocorticoid regimen.
L277: ## **Week 4 to Week 12**
L278: Subjects underwent downward dose-titration of their glucocorticoid dosage to a target of 8 to 10 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents by Week 12.
L279: ## **Week 12 to Week 24**
L280: Glucocorticoid dosage was adjusted if needed based on androstenedione (A4) levels, presence of symptoms of glucocorticoid insufficiency, or hyperandrogenism. The treatment goal was to maintain A4 levels at \le 120\% of the subject's baseline or upper limit of normal (ULN) for age and sex.
L281: ## **Open-Label Treatment Period (Week 24 to Month 12)**
L282: At Week 24 (Month 6), subjects transitioned to a 6-month open-label period during which all subjects received crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily until Month 12. During Months 7 through 10, glucocorticoid dosage was reduced as tolerated if androstenedione levels were controlled (i.e., \le 120\% of the subject's baseline or \le \text{ULN} for age and sex) to a goal of 8 to 10 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents by Month 10.
L283: In all parts of the study that allowed for glucocorticoid dose reduction, dose was reduced at a rate of approximately 10% to 20% per month.
L284: ## **Open-Label or Double-Blind Active-Controlled Treatment Period (Month 12 to Month 18)**
L285: At Month 12, subjects whose glucocorticoid dosage remained greater than 11 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents were rerandomized (2:1 ratio) to receive crinecerfont 100 mg every morning and 200 mg every evening, or to continue 100 mg twice daily, in a blinded fashion. Glucocorticoid reduction could be reattempted after the first month of blinded treatment, as
L286: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L287: tolerated, with the goal of achieving a glucocorticoid dose of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day by Month 18 while maintaining control of A4.
L288: Subjects who had been successfully able to reduce their glucocorticoid dosage to \le 11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents continued to receive crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily in an open-label fashion.
L289: ## Open-Label Extension Period (Month 18 Onward)
L290: After Month 18, subjects could enter an open-label extension period during which they initially received crinecerfont 100 mg bid with adjustment as needed to a maximum crinecerfont dose of 100 mg every morning (qAM) and 200 mg every evening (qPM). Glucocorticoid dose was adjusted as needed to achieve the lowest dose required to maintain adequate disease control. After the Month 24 visit, subjects could consider transitioning to crinecerfont 200 mg qPM.
L291: A final posttreatment visit occurred approximately 1 month after the subject's final dose of study drug.

L300: ## Efficacy Endpoints
L301: The primary efficacy endpoint was the percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid (GC) daily dose (in hydrocortisone equivalents adjusted for body surface area [BSA] in mg/m2/day) at
L302: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L303: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L304: Week 24 while also achieving Week 24 androstenedione levels in the controlled range (i.e., \le 120\% of baseline or \le \text{ULN} for age and sex).
L305: Glucocorticoid daily dose was calculated at baseline and at Week 24. If glucocorticoid dosing alternated over the course of 2 consecutive days, then the average of the glucocorticoid dose on those days was used to calculate the glucocorticoid daily dose. If glucocorticoid dosing alternated between weekdays and weekends (or another weekly regimen that varied by day of the week), then the average daily dose was calculated as the sum of the glucocorticoid doses over the 7-day period divided by 7.
L306: According to the statistical analysis plan, the androstenedione level prior to morning glucocorticoid dose served as the baseline and Week 24 level. If androstenedione levels prior to morning glucocorticoid were not available, then androstenedione levels after morning glucocorticoid dose were used.
L307: Subjects who had a decrease in glucocorticoid daily dose but did not meet the definition of androstenedione control at Week 24 were considered to have a zero percent change from baseline in the glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24.
L308: Key secondary efficacy endpoints were the following:
L309: - Change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4 (while glucocorticoid dose was stable)
- Achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to \le 11 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents at Week 24 (while Week 24 androstenedione was adequately controlled)
- Change from baseline in homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR; in fasting subjects not on insulin, at Week 24)
- Percent change from baseline in weight at Week 24
- Change from baseline in percent total fat mass at Week 24
L310: The study design was adequate to meet its stated objectives. The data from Trial CAH3003 that were submitted with the NDA are results from the 24-week (i.e., Weeks 0 to 24) randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled treatment period and the open-label treatment period, which capture treatment Week 24 through Month 12 (data cutoff of July 19, 2023). The 120-day Safety Update included new data obtained in the open-label extension treatment period from Month 12 through the data cutoff of January 16, 2024. The trial is ongoing.
L311: The efficacy analysis is based primarily on data obtained during the initial 24-week placebo-controlled treatment phase.
L312: ## 12.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial CAH3003
L313: The eligibility criteria are reflective of the patient population who would benefit from a reduction in glucocorticoid dose. Study subjects were required to be taking supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses (total daily dosage &gt; 13 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} in hydrocortisone dose equivalents).
L314: The study enrolled adult male and nonpregnant, nonlactating female subjects aged 18 years and older with a diagnosis of classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH (accepted diagnostic criteria were an elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level, confirmed cytochrome P450 (CYP) 21A2
L315: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L316: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L317: genotype, positive newborn screening with confirmatory second-tier testing, or cosyntropin stimulation testing). Individuals with other forms of classic CAH were excluded.
L318: Subjects were also required to be on a stable supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dose regimen (defined as &gt;13 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} in hydrocortisone dose equivalents; prior to protocol Amendment 5, the threshold was &gt;14 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day}) and consisting of one or more of the following orally administered glucocorticoids: hydrocortisone, prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, or dexamethasone.
L319: If treated with fludrocortisone for salt wasting, the dosage was stable for at least 1 month prior to screening, with an upright plasma renin activity (PRA) during screening that was not greater than ULN while maintaining a usual sodium intake. If PRA was &gt;ULN, the subject must have systolic blood pressure &gt;100 \text{ mm Hg}, without orthostatic hypotension, and with serum sodium and potassium in the normal range.
L320: Additional exclusions were conditions requiring chronic glucocorticoid therapy at systemic exposures that may interfere with study endpoints; increased risk of adrenal crisis; history of malignancy; laboratory findings consistent with impaired hepatic or renal function; anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] &lt;1.0 \times 10^3/\text{mm}^3), or impaired coagulation; and active suicidal ideation in the 6 months prior to screening or any history of suicidal behavior within the past year based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale collected at screening.
L321: Contraception was required in female subjects of childbearing potential with fertile male partners from screening until the final study visit or 30 days after the last dose of study drug, whichever was longer.
L322: Medications prohibited during the trial were:
L323: - Orally administered glucocorticoids for indications other than CAH
- Strong inducers of CYP3A4 or CYP2B6 except topically administered medications
- Medications that affect cortisol or glucocorticoid metabolism (e.g., phenytoin, mitotane, phenobarbital, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) except topically administered medications
- Aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole, testolactone)
L324: ## 12.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial CAH3003
L325: The full analysis set (FAS), defined as all randomized subjects regardless of adherence to study treatment administration, was used for all efficacy analyses. Continuous efficacy endpoints were analyzed using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model assuming equal variance between the placebo and the treatment group. The ANCOVA model included respective baseline measurement as a covariate and stratification factors and treatment group (crinecerfont 100 mg bid or placebo) as factors. Categorical efficacy endpoints were analyzed using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test. The CMH test compared treatment groups (crinecerfont 100 mg bid versus placebo) and included the stratification factors used in the randomization.
L326: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L327: The protocol prespecified testing procedure described below was used to control the familywise Type I error rate for the primary and key secondary endpoints (Figure 7). All significance levels noted below were two-sided.
L328: - The primary endpoint was tested using a significance level of 0.05.
- If the primary endpoint was statistically significant, then the first two key secondary endpoints were tested using an unequal allocation of significance levels. The change from baseline at Week 4 in androstenedione was tested using a significance level of 0.02. The achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels (\le 11 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalent adjusted for BSA) with androstenedione control (as defined for the primary endpoint) was tested using a significance level of 0.03.
- The significance level for the family of the remaining three key secondary endpoints was dependent on whether the first two key secondary endpoints were statistically significant. If both were statistically significant, then the significance level for this family of endpoints was 0.05. If only one was statistically significant, then the significance level for that endpoint was used for this family of endpoints. If neither was significant, then this family of endpoints will not be tested for statistical significance.
L329: ## **Missing Data Handling**
L330: The primary efficacy endpoint requires the availability of both the glucocorticoid dose at Week 24 as well as androstenedione values used in the assessment of androstenedione control. The missing data corresponding to the subjects with a missing glucocorticoid dose, androstenedione, or both at Week 24 were multiply imputed as follows:
L331: - For subjects who were on study drug at Week 24 and had missing one or both components of the primary endpoint, their missing Week 24 data were imputed from Week 24 Completers (subjects who completed through the time of the endpoint on study drug) within the same treatment group.
- For subjects who were off study drug at Week 24 and had missing one or both components of the primary endpoint, their missing Week 24 data were imputed from subjects who were classified as “retrieved dropouts” (subjects in the FAS who discontinued study drug but remained in the study and had an evaluable measurement). If there were five or fewer retrieved dropouts, the missing endpoint values would be imputed from subjects in the placebo treatment group. For subjects in the placebo treatment group, missing data were imputed using nonmissing data from subjects in the placebo treatment group.

L349: ## **Baseline Demographics and Clinical Characteristics**
L350: Demographics were generally similar between the treatment groups (Table 12). The mean age of randomized subjects was 31.3 years (range: 18 to 54 years) in the crinecerfont group and 29.8 years (range: 18 to 58 years) in the placebo group. All subjects were younger than age 65 years. The percentage of male and female subjects was approximately 50% in both treatment groups. Most subjects were White (90.1%) and not Hispanic or Latino (92.3%). Geographic region was the United States for 37.9% of subjects and outside the United States for 62.1% of subjects.

L370: ## 12.2.2.4.2. Efficacy Results
L371: Efficacy results for Trial CAH3003 include analysis of the completed double-blind period (Day 1 to Week 24) and an interim analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label period (Week 24 to Month 12) at the data cutoff (July 19, 2023).
L372: ## 12.2.2.4.2.1. Primary Analysis
L373: For the primary efficacy endpoint, the least-squares (LS) mean percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24, while Week 24 androstenedione was controlled at \le 120\% of baseline or \le \text{ULN} for age and sex, was -27.3% (standard deviation [SD] 2.4) for the crinecerfont group and -10.3% (SD 3.2) for the placebo group, with an LS mean difference (crinecerfont - placebo) of -17.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -23.8, -10.2; p&lt;0.0001) (Table 14). For the primary analysis of the primary endpoint, subjects who did not achieve androstenedione control were assigned a change in glucocorticoid dose of 0%.

L386: A sensitivity analysis was performed to test the equality of variances between the placebo and treatment group. Based on the Bartlett's \chi^2 statistic=0.34517 with p-value=0.56, there was not enough evidence (at 0.05 significance level) found against the equal variance assumption. Also, the least squares mean treatment difference (95% CI) obtained from the ANCOVA model adjusted for unequal variances was -17.0 (-23.7, -10.4) is almost identical to what was observed in the primary analysis in Table 14.
L387: A two-way tipping point sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the primary efficacy analysis. The significance at p&lt;0.05 was maintained for the primary endpoint when the delta shift for the multiply imputed values was up to 25 \text{mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} for crinecerfont or up to -25 \text{mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} for placebo. Table 16 contains all combinations of delta values that tipped the result from statistically significant to not statistically significant. The tipping point (p\ge 0.05) was reached when the combined delta shift was 43 \text{mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} or greater (for example 23 \text{mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} for crinecerfont and -20 \text{mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} for placebo). These very extreme values for the tipping point are supportive of the primary results.

L403: Given the mean baseline glucocorticoid daily dose of 17.6 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents (absolute dose of 32.3 mg hydrocortisone equivalents) in all study subjects, a mean decrease of 17% (placebo-subtracted difference in the primary analysis of the primary endpoint) would correspond to a mean dose of 14.6 mg/m2/day (absolute mean dose of 26.8 mg/day), for an absolute mean decrease of 3 mg/m2/day (mean decrease of 5.5 mg) hydrocortisone equivalents.
L404: A decrease of 2 to 3 mg/m2/day (about 3.5 to 5.5 mg/day) hydrocortisone equivalents in subjects with CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages is clinically meaningful. Published studies show a high prevalence of adverse effects on body weight and bone health in individuals with classic CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages. Studies in individuals requiring replacement glucocorticoid therapy show improvements in body mass index, metabolic parameters, and quality of life when supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is decreased to more physiologic levels. In adults, a daily absolute hydrocortisone dose of 15 to 25 mg is widely accepted clinically as physiologic replacement (Bornstein et al. 2016; Husebye et al. 2021). For a typical adult with a body surface area of 1.8 m2, this absolute dose translates to 8 to 14 mg/m2/day.
L405: In published cohort studies, adults and children with classic CAH have a relatively high prevalence of obesity, and adults also have a high prevalence of low bone density. In a cohort of 139 pediatric patients and 44 adults with classic CAH and mean glucocorticoid daily dose in hydrocortisone equivalents of 17.9 mg/m2/day in adults and 15 mg/m2/day in children (similar to the study populations), the prevalence of obesity was 33% in adults and 35% in children. Furthermore, obesity was associated with higher glucocorticoid dose (Finkielstain et al. 2012).
L406: In a cohort of 165 adults with classic CAH in the United Kingdom, a mean age of 33 years in women and 32 years in men, and median daily dosages of hydrocortisone (25 mg in males, 20 mg in females), prednisone (7.5 mg in males, 6 mg in females), and dexamethasone (0.5 mg
L407: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L408: in males, 0.375 mg in females), the prevalence of obesity was 37% in men and 52% in women. In the same study, prevalence of osteopenia and osteoporosis at the lumbar spine for those with available data was 39.2% and 6.8%, respectively.
L409: In a study of adults with primary adrenal insufficiency caused by Addison's disease, decreasing the absolute glucocorticoid dose by 5 mg/day hydrocortisone equivalents and switching from immediate-release to dual-release glucocorticoids for 6 months led to statistically significant improvements in body mass index, hemoglobin A1c, lipid levels, and quality of life (Delle Cese et al. 2020).
L410: Below we further explore the impact of the changes in glucocorticoid dose on other endpoints in the trial and also assess the proportion of subjects who were able to achieve physiologic-range glucocorticoid doses in the setting of androgen control.
L411: ## **Secondary Efficacy Endpoint Results**
L412: The primary analyses of the five key secondary endpoints are given in Table 17. L447: ## 12.2.3. Trial CAH2006
L448: ## 12.2.3.1. Design, Trial CAH2006
L449: ## Overall Design
L450: Trial CAH2006 is titled “A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of crinecerfont in pediatric subjects with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, followed by open-label treatment.” The study design is appropriate to demonstrate efficacy and is depicted in Figure 12. This phase 3 trial consisted of a 4-week screening period, a 28-week double-blind placebo-controlled treatment period, and a 6-month open-label treatment period through Week 52. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the efficacy of crinecerfont, compared with placebo, in reducing adrenal androgen levels during a glucocorticoid-stable period.
L451: ## **Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period (Day 1 to Week 28)**
L452: A total of 103 pediatric subjects aged 4 to 17 years with classic CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency and who required supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids to control androgen excess (&gt;12 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio (active:placebo) to receive a weight-based dosage of crinecerfont orally twice daily with breakfast and the evening meal (25 mg oral solution twice daily for subjects weighing 10 to less than 20 kg; 50 mg oral solution twice daily for subjects weighing 20 to less than 55 kg; and 100 mg oral capsule for subjects weighing 55 kg or more) or placebo. Randomization was stratified by pubertal stage (Tanner breast or genital stage 1 or 2 versus 3, 4, or 5) and sex.
L453: During the first 4 weeks of the study, subjects maintained their baseline glucocorticoid regimen. Serum androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels were measured at Week 4 to evaluate the change from baseline.
L454: From Week 4 to Week 28, glucocorticoid dosage was adjusted to a target of 8 to 10 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents while maintaining goal androstenedione levels (&lt;\text{ULN} for sex and age or if pubertal, pubertal stage; or \le 120\% of the subject's baseline) as long as there was no evidence of glucocorticoid insufficiency.
L455: ## **Open-Label Treatment Period (Week 28 to Week 52)**
L456: At Week 28, subjects transitioned to a 6-month open-label period during which all subjects received a crinecerfont dosage based on their Week 28 body weight. During Week 32 through Week 52, glucocorticoid dosage was reduced as tolerated if androstenedione levels were controlled (\le 120\% of baseline or \le \text{ULN} for sex, age, or pubertal stage) to a goal of 8 to 10 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalents by Week 52.
L457: In all parts of the study allowing for glucocorticoid dose reduction, the attempted dose reduction was approximately 1 to 4 \text{mg/m}^2/\text{day} per month.
L458: After Week 52, subjects could enter an open-label extension period allowing for crinecerfont dose adjustment with the goal of maintaining adequate disease control at the lowest possible glucocorticoid dosage.

## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
