L469: ## **Efficacy Endpoints**
L470: The primary efficacy endpoint was change from baseline (CFB) in serum androstenedione at Week 4.
L471: Key secondary efficacy endpoints were:
L472: - Change from baseline in serum 17-OHP at Week 4
- Percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose (in hydrocortisone equivalents adjusted for BSA [mg/m2/day]) at Week 28, while Week 28 serum androstenedione was controlled (≤120% of the baseline value or ≤ULN, according to sex and either age [for Tanner stage 1] or pubertal stage [for Tanner stages 2 to 5])
L473: ## **12.2.3.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial CAH2006**
L474: The eligibility criteria are reflective of the patient population with uncontrolled disease who would benefit from a reduction in glucocorticoid dose. Study subjects were required to be taking supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses (i.e., total daily dosage &gt;12 mg/m2/day in hydrocortisone dose equivalents). Androstenedione levels (prior to morning glucocorticoid dose) were required to be greater than the midpoint of the reference range and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels (prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose) were required to be greater than twice the upper limit of normal. Key eligibility criteria are summarized below.
L475: ## **Inclusion Criteria**
L476: - Male and nonpregnant and nonlactating female subjects aged 2 to 17 years of age with minimum body weight of at least 15 kg and medically confirmed diagnosis of classic CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency based on standard medically accepted criteria (i.e., elevated 17-OHP, confirmed CYP21A2 genotype, or diagnostic results after cosyntropin stimulation testing).
- Requiring a supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dose regimen (i.e., &gt;12 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} in hydrocortisone dose equivalents, that had been stable for at least 1 month prior to screening, is intended for chronic use, and consists only of one or more of the following orally administered glucocorticoids: hydrocortisone, prednisone, prednisolone, or methylprednisolone;)
- Receiving a morning dose of glucocorticoid
- Androstenedione level (prior to morning glucocorticoid dose) greater than the midpoint of the reference range, according to sex and either age (for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5)
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone level (prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose) &gt;2 \times \text{ULN} according to sex and either age (for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5)
- If treated with fludrocortisone, dose should be stable for at least 1 month prior to screening
- Upright PRA (in the absence of medications that confound interpretation of PRA) during screening &lt;3 \times \text{ULN} and &gt;lower limit of normal on the subject's usual sodium intake. If PRA &gt;2 \times \text{ULN} and &lt;3 \times \text{ULN}, the subject must have normal age-specific systolic blood pressure and heart rate and serum potassium &lt;\text{ULN}
L477: ## **Exclusion Criteria**
L478: - Forms of CAH other than 21-hydroxylase deficiency
- History of other endocrinologic conditions requiring chronic daily therapy with oral glucocorticoids
- Determined to be an increased risk of adrenal crisis
- Presence of a clinically significant medical condition or chronic disease (including history of neurological, hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, significant malabsorption, hematologic, pulmonary, psychiatric, or endocrine disease [excluding CAH]) that in the investigator's opinion would preclude the subject's participation in the study or confound interpretation of study outcome
- History of malignancy, unless successfully treated and considered to be cured
- History of clinically concerning cardiac arrhythmia (including long QT syndrome) or prolongation of screening (pretreatment) QT interval corrected for heart rate using Fridericia's correction (\text{QTcF}) of &gt;450 \text{ msec} (males) or &gt;470 \text{ msec} (females)
L479: - Evidence of chronic renal or liver disease based on any of these screening laboratory test abnormalities:Estimated glomerular filtration rate &lt;60 \text{ mL/min}/1.73 \text{ m}^2
- Aspartate aminotransferase &gt;2 \times \text{ULN}
- Alanine aminotransferase &gt;2 \times \text{ULN}
- Total bilirubin &gt;1.5 \times \text{ULN} unless due to a documented diagnosis of Gilbert's syndrome
- Any of the following hematologic abnormalities at screening:Hemoglobin &lt;10 \text{ g/dL} (age &lt;6 years) or &lt;11 \text{ g/dL} (age \ge 6 years)
- White blood cell count &lt;4.0 \times 10^3/\text{mm}^3
- Platelet count &lt;100,000/\text{mm}^3
- Absolute neutrophil count &lt;1.0 \times 10^3/\text{mm}^3
- Any of the following coagulation abnormalities at screening:Activated partial thromboplastin time that exceeds ULN by more than 5 seconds
- Prothrombin time expressed as international normalized ratio (INR) &gt;1.4, unless the subject is on anticoagulant treatment that affects INR
- Screening serum sodium &lt;130 \text{ mmol/L}
- History or presence of substance dependence or substance or alcohol abuse
- At significant risk of suicidal or violent behavior; for subjects \ge 6 years of age: presence of any suicidal ideation of type 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan) or type 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) in the past 6 months before screening, or lifetime history of suicidal behavior based on the Columbia-Suicide Risk Scale were excluded
L480: Contraception was required in female subjects of childbearing potential (i.e., past menarche and not surgically sterile) with fertile male partners from screening until the final study visit or 30 days after the last dose of study drug, whichever was longer.
L481: The following medications were prohibited from 30 days before screening until the final study visit (or early termination):
L482: - Any active investigational drug (not to be used within 30 days or five half-lives, whichever was longer)
- Orally administered glucocorticoids for indications other than CAH
- Strong inducers of CYP3A4 or CYP2B6 except topically administered medications
- Medications that affect cortisol or glucocorticoid metabolism (e.g., phenytoin, mitotane, phenobarbital, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) except topically administered medications
- Exogenous testosterone treatment
L483: ## 12.2.3.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial CAH2006
L484: The full analysis set, defined as all randomized subjects regardless of adherence to study treatment administration, was used for all efficacy analyses. Continuous efficacy endpoints were analyzed using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model assuming equal variance between the placebo and treatment groups. The ANCOVA model included the respective baseline measurement as a covariate and stratification factors and treatment group (crinecerfont; placebo) as factors. Categorical efficacy endpoints were analyzed using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test. The CMH test compared treatment groups (crinecerfont versus placebo) and included the stratification factors used in the randomization.
L485: For analysis of the primary and key secondary endpoints, the fixed-sequence testing procedure described below was followed to control for the treatment-group comparisons of multiple endpoints. Each step in the sequential testing procedure used a two-sided 0.05 level of significance for the null hypothesis being tested; testing of hypotheses at each step of the procedure commenced only if all null hypotheses in prior steps were rejected.
L486: - Primary endpoint: change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4.
- Key secondary endpoint: change from baseline in serum 17-OHP at Week 4.
- Key secondary endpoint: percent change from baseline in daily glucocorticoid dose (in hydrocortisone dose equivalents adjusted for BSA) at Week 28, while Week 28 serum androstenedione was \le 120\% of the baseline value or \le \text{ULN}, according to sex and either age (for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5).
L487: Missing data imputation for the primary and key secondary endpoints was handled similar to Trial CAH3003, i.e., for the primary and key secondary endpoints, the following steps were taken:
L488: - For subjects on study drug who were missing the endpoint at the timepoint of interest, their missing Week 4 (or Week 28 for secondary endpoints) data were imputed from Completers (subjects who completed through the time of the endpoint on study drug) within the same treatment group.
- For subjects in the crinecerfont treatment group off study drug prior to the timepoint of interest who were missing the endpoint at the timepoint of interest, their missing endpoint was imputed from subjects who were classified as “retrieved dropouts” (subjects in the FAS who discontinued study drug but remained in the study and had an evaluable measurement). If there were five or fewer retrieved dropouts, the missing endpoint values would be imputed from subjects in the placebo treatment group. For subjects in the placebo treatment group, missing data were imputed using nonmissing data from subjects in the placebo treatment group.
L489: ## 12.2.3.4. Results of Analyses, Trial CAH2006
L490: ## 12.2.3.4.1. Disposition, Baseline Demographics and Baseline Clinical Characteristics
L491: ## Disposition During Double-Blind Treatment Period (Baseline to Week 28)
L492: A total of 103 subjects were randomized (69 crinecerfont; 34 placebo, Table 20). All subjects were included in the full analysis set. Most subjects (95.7% crinecerfont; 91.2% placebo) completed the study treatment. Reasons for study discontinuation (and study treatment discontinuation) before Week 28 were withdrawal by subject (1.4% crinecerfont; 8.8% placebo) and AE (2.9% crinecerfont; 0% placebo; see Section 13.6.3.4). The 3 subjects in the crinecerfont group who were reported to have discontinued study treatment (and the study) by Week 28 discontinued the study after completing the Week 28 visit and thus had study data contributing to the key secondary endpoint of glucocorticoid dose.

L496: ## Disposition During Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to 52)
L497: Of the 103 randomized subjects, 97 (97%) completed the double-blind treatment period. All 97 subjects entered the open-label treatment period (66 crinecerfont; 31 placebo) and were treated with open-label crinecerfont, with dosing recalculated based on the current body weight at Week 28. As of the data cutoff date (August 9, 2023), 45% (48% placebo/crinecerfont; 44% crinecerfont/crinecerfont) completed the study through Week 52 and are included in the efficacy analysis. Data from subjects who had not yet completed the open-label treatment period through Week 52 as of the data cutoff date are not included in the efficacy analyses but are included in the safety analysis. The remainder of subjects who entered the open-label treatment period completed treatment after the data cutoff date.
L498: ## Disposition During Open-Label Extension (Week 52 Onward)
L499: All 97 subjects who started the open-label treatment period completed open-label treatment through Week 52. Of the 97 who completed the open-label treatment period, 93 (97%) continued in the open-label extension.
L500: ## **Baseline Demographics and Clinical Characteristics**
L501: Subjects 2 years to 17 years of age were eligible for the study. Randomization in the study was stratified by pubertal stage (Tanner breast or genital stage 1 or 2 versus 3, 4, or 5) and sex. Demographics were generally similar between the treatment groups (Table 21). The mean age of randomized subjects was 12.1 years (range 4.6 to 17.8 years). Approximately 45% of randomized subjects in each treatment group were &lt;12 years of age. There was an equal distribution of male and female subjects in both treatment groups. Most subjects in the study were White (63.1%) and not Hispanic or Latino (74.8%). Geographic region was the United States for 56.3% of subjects and outside the United States for 43.7% of subjects.
L502: Baseline disease characteristics were generally similar between the treatment group and the placebo group (Table 22). Subjects, on average, were taking supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages and had mean androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels significantly above the clinical guideline-specified goal ranges (i.e., androstenedione within the reference range for age and sex (Speiser et al. 2018)). A target 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of less than approximately 1200 ng/dL for children with CAH has been suggested (Merke 2008).
L503: The mean glucocorticoid total daily dose in hydrocortisone equivalents was 16.4 mg/m2/day. In pediatrics, glucocorticoid dosages of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent are clinically accepted as physiologic replacement (Husebye et al. 2021).
L504: The mean androstenedione level was 431 ng/dL prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose (about 3 to 4 times the goal of less than the upper normal range). The androstenedione reference range for prepubertal males and females is up to about 50 ng/dL. During puberty, the androstenedione reference range varies by pubertal stage but generally ranges from a lower limit of 30 to 65 ng/dL to an upper limit of 65 to 210 ng/dL for males and a lower limit of 40 to 80 ng/dL to an upper limit of 100 to 240 ng/dL for females.
L505: The mean 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was 8682 ng/dL (about 7 times the suggested goal of less than approximately 1200 ng/dL) prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose. The 17-OHP reference range for prepubertal males and females is about 0 to 90 ng/dL. During puberty, the 17-hydroxyprogesterone reference range varies by pubertal stage but generally ranges from a lower limit of 0 to 30 ng/dL to an upper limit of 115 to 180 ng/dL for males and a lower limit of 10 to 20 ng/dL to an upper limit of 100 to 265 ng/dL for females.
L506: There were no enrolled pediatric subjects with body weight &lt;20 kg. Therefore, the 25 mg bid solution was not tested in this trial (see Section 12.3 for further details). There were 51 subjects in the 20 to &lt;55 kg weight band (37 crinecerfont, 14 placebo) and 52 subjects in the ≥55 kg weight band (32 crinecerfont, 20 placebo).

L522: ## 12.2.3.4.2. Efficacy Results
L523: Efficacy results for Trial CAH2006 include analysis of the completed double-blind period (i.e., Day 1 to Week 28) and an interim analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label period (i.e., Week 28 to Week 52) at the data cutoff (August 9, 2023).
L524: ## 12.2.3.4.2.1. Primary Analysis
L525: For the primary efficacy endpoint, the LS mean change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4 following the initial 4-week glucocorticoid stable dose period, was -196.8 (standard error [SE] 39.4) ng/dL for the crinecerfont group compared with 71.0 (SE 56.2) ng/dL for the placebo group. The LS mean treatment difference (crinecerfont - placebo) of -267.8 ng/dL (95% CI: -403.4, -132.1) was statistically significant (p-value=0.0002) (Table 23).

L536: A two-way tipping point sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the primary efficacy analysis. Significance at p&lt;0.05 was maintained for change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4 when the delta shift for the multiply imputed values was up to 2006 ng/dL for crinecerfont or -2006 ng/dL for placebo. **Table 25** contains all combinations of delta values that tip the result from statistically significant to not statistically significant. The tipping point (p\ge 0.05) was reached when the combined delta shift was 3926 ng/dL or greater (1920 ng/dL for crinecerfont and -2006 ng/dL for placebo), which is an extreme value that supports the robustness of the primary results.

L552: Subjects not meeting the androstenedione control criteria will have their glucocorticoid daily dose percent change from baseline value set to zero at each visit where control is not met.
L553: Abbreviations: CFT, crinecerfont 100 mg bid; PBO, placebo
L554: In the primary analysis, if a subject did not meet androstenedione control criteria, the change (and percentage change) in glucocorticoid daily dose from baseline was set to zero at each visit where control was not met. As an exploratory analysis, the primary analysis of this key secondary endpoint was repeated without setting the glucocorticoid daily dose to zero for these subjects. In this analysis, the least square mean difference (-25.9% and 95% CI: [-32.5, -19.2]) at Week 28 was similar to that of the primary analysis.
L555: Given the mean baseline glucocorticoid daily dose of 16.5 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents in the crinecerfont group, a decrease of 18% (decrease observed in the crinecerfont group) would correspond to a dose of 13.5 mg/m2/day, for an absolute decrease of 3 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents. A decrease of 3 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents in pediatric subjects with CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages is clinically meaningful. See Section 12.2.2.4 for a discussion of the clinical meaningfulness of this reduction.
L556: A secondary endpoint of clinical importance, reduction in physiologic glucocorticoid doses while maintaining androstenedione control (defined as serum androstenedione &lt;120% of baseline or \leULN, according to sex and either age for Tanner stage 1 or pubertal stage for Tanner stages 2 to 5) at Week 28, showed a 30% responder rate with crinecerfont versus a 0% responder rate for placebo (Table 27).

L592: ## 12.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
L593: ## 12.3.1. Appropriate Dosage in Pediatric Patients Weighing 10 kg to Less Than 20 kg
L594: ## Issue
L595: No pediatric subjects weighing 10 kg to less than 20 kg were enrolled in the pediatric phase 3 Trial CAH2006. Therefore, the proposed crinecerfont dosage of 25 mg twice daily (oral solution) for this patient population was not evaluated in a phase 3 clinical trial.
L596: ## Background
L597: The Applicant selected a dosing regimen of 25 mg bid for the pediatric 10 to &lt;20 kg weight band based on exposure matching to the adult regimen of 100 mg twice daily using popPK modeling and simulation.
L598: ## Assessment
L599: Leveraging popPK modeling and simulation, an exposure-matching approach was employed by the Applicant to propose dosing regimens for pediatric patients by weight bands (10 to &lt;20 kg, 20 to &lt;55 kg, and \ge55 kg), corresponding to doses of 25 mg solution bid, 50 mg solution bid, and 100 mg capsule bid, respectively. The simulated results demonstrate that the percent of pediatric subjects (10 to &lt;20 kg) falling within the 90% prediction interval of the adult exposure (i.e., 24-hour AUC) was relatively low at 68.4% (as compared to 76.8% and 91.6% for the other pediatric weight bands). As such, approximately 31% of the pediatric subjects of 10 to &lt;20 kg are projected to have exposures lower than the 5th percentile of the reference adult exposure (Figure 3).
L600: In regard to the exposure-matching approach, the Applicant used the adult subjects as the reference exposure; however, the review team considers the 20 to &lt;55 kg pediatric subgroup to be more similar to those weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg based on physiology, disease state, and disease progression. Furthermore, the review team assessed efficacy in these pediatric subgroups in the phase 3 clinical trials and found the pediatric subgroup of 20 to &lt;55 kg to be an acceptable efficacy reference group for exposure matching for the 10 to &lt;20 kg group based on the percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid dose and proportion of subjects achieving a glucocorticoid dose \le11 mg/m2/day at Week 28 (Table 30).
L601: Based on popPK modeling and simulation, the proposed 25 mg bid dosing regimen for the 10 to &lt;20 kg pediatric subgroup is expected to produce similar exposures to those of 50 mg bid for the 20 to &lt;55 kg pediatric subgroup, and therefore, efficacy is expected to be similar between these two pediatric subgroups. Additionally, the relatively higher exposure in adult subjects serves as an appropriate safety exposure coverage. Overall, the exposures of the proposed 25 mg bid dosing regimen in the 10 to &lt;20 kg pediatric subgroup is expected to be safe and effective. Refer to Section 20.5 for details on exposure comparison and matching.

L607: The Applicant's proposed dosage of 25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to less than 20 kg is acceptable.
L608: ## 13. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
L609: ## 13.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L610: The safety of crinecerfont was evaluated in nonclinical safety pharmacology studies, subchronic and chronic toxicology studies in rats and dogs, reproductive and developmental studies in rats and rabbits, genetic toxicology studies, juvenile studies in rats, and 2-year rat and 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity studies. Systemic steady-state crinecerfont exposures increased with dose in a less than dose-proportional manner and approached or reached saturation in the pivotal nonclinical studies. Maximum plasma exposures declined after repeated dosing, likely as a result of induced liver drug-metabolizing enzymes, which contributed to the saturation of exposure observed in the toxicity studies. Thus, clinical exposure multiples at the no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) in the pivotal nonclinical studies were limited to one- to fourfold the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD). Nonclinical data relevant to clinical risk assessment or safety concerns are discussed below (see Section 19 for the detailed nonclinical assessment). Overall, nonclinical data support the safe use of crinecerfont for the indicated patients with CAH ≥4 years old.
L611: ## Safety Pharmacology
L612: Crinecerfont administered as a single oral or IV dose had no significant effects on neurobehavioral function in rats, cardiovascular function in dogs, respiratory function in guinea pigs, renal function in rats, or gastrointestinal function in rats at clinically relevant doses. Crinecerfont showed no potential for clinical arrhythmia risk in vitro in human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) current (&lt;5% inhibition at 10µM) or isolated rabbit Purkinje fiber action
L613: potential. Overall, the safety pharmacology data demonstrated that crinecerfont did not pose acute safety concerns at clinically relevant exposure levels.
L614: ## **General Toxicology**
L615: The toxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in a series of single- and repeat-dose studies in mice, rats, and dogs. The target organs for crinecerfont were liver (mouse, rat, and dog), thyroid gland (rat and dog), gastrointestinal (GI) tract (mouse and rat), and coagulation-associated effects. GI tract findings were not clinically relevant and thyroid gland findings are discussed in the context of carcinogenic potential (below). Clinical trial data identified neutropenia and neuropsychiatric safety as potential clinical risks. Neutropenia was not observed in the pivotal rat or dog toxicity studies and there were no nonclinical signals for immunosuppression or neurobehavioral effects. Mechanistic studies showed crinecerfont is active at the pituitary and can cross the blood-brain barrier, but distribution to the central nervous system was low, with an observed brain to plasma ratio of 0.1. In comparison, crinecerfont was highly distributed to liver (where it is metabolized) as evidenced by a \ge 8.5 liver-to-plasma ratio.
L616: Initial studies with a crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy (prolongation of prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial thromboplastin time [APTT] and/or bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies. Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was replaced with a free base form of crinecerfont for evaluation in the pivotal chronic toxicology, carcinogenicity, prenatal and postnatal and juvenile nonclinical studies, and for the clinical studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or bleeding effects were noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT up to 60%, and APTT up to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD exposure). Similar findings (prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study conducted with crinecerfont free base, without any other coagulopathy up to 1000 mg/kg/day (5-fold MRHD exposure).(b) (4) Drug-related effects on coagulation were routinely monitored in clinical trials with the crinecerfont free base formulation.
L617: Crinecerfont is predominantly metabolized by CYP3A4 in the liver in animals and in humans. In rats and dogs, crinecerfont induces drug-metabolizing enzymes, which resulted in increased liver weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy in both species. Mechanistic studies confirmed that induction of metabolizing enzymes contributed to dose- and duration-dependent signs of liver toxicity. In rodents only, higher crinecerfont doses (approximately seven times MRHD exposures) caused a low incidence of more advanced liver injury, including multinucleated hepatocytes and anisokaryosis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis. There were no liver findings of concern at doses corresponding to one- to fourfold clinical exposures, and induction or inhibition of liver metabolizing enzymes is unlikely to occur at clinically relevant doses. Routine monitoring for biomarkers and signs of drug-induced liver injury was conducted throughout the clinical development program.
L618: ## **Reproductive, Developmental, and Juvenile Toxicology**
L619: The effects of crinecerfont on fertility, reproduction, early embryonic and embryo-fetal development, and juvenile development were evaluated in rat and rabbit toxicology studies. Investigations with the crinecerfont tosylate salt did not identify effects on male or female
L620: fertility or early embryonic development at low clinical exposure margins (two- to fourfold clinical MRHD exposures).
L621: There were also no effects of crinecerfont on rat embryo-fetal development, pre- and postnatal development, or juvenile development that raised concerns about clinical safety. Exposure was limited by tolerability in the rat studies, reaching approximately four times maximum clinical exposure. The toxicity profile of crinecerfont in juvenile rats was comparable to the adult toxicity profile. Juvenile animal findings support the safety of crinecerfont in the indicated pediatric patients \ge 4 years of age.
L622: In the embryo-fetal development study in rabbits, there were multiple craniofacial malformations in a few fetuses, from multiple litters, which were not present in the concurrent control and were outside the historical control range. The malformations included microcephaly, microstomia, acephalostomia, misshapen cerebrum and/or cerebellum, among others. Exposure attained in the rabbit study ranged between 2\times to 3\times MRHD, without a dose dependency, despite a 10-fold increase in nominal dose (100 mg/kg low dose to 1000 mg/kg high dose), indicating saturation of absorption. The absence of a dose-related increase in exposure confounds identification of an exposure/response relationship on embryo-fetal development. We therefore assessed the incidence of malformations across all treatment groups because of the similar crinecerfont exposures—there were 4 fetuses from four litters with craniofacial poly-malformations of interest, for a total fetal incidence of 0.8% (4/525) in 7% (4/59) of litters. These specific findings were not present in the historical control data from the same study site. The overall incidence of fetal malformations was low and there was no clear relationship to drug, but absent similar findings in concurrent control fetuses, and with the incidence being outside the historical control range for individual malformations, we cannot rule out a possible effect of crinecerfont treatment on rabbit embryo-fetal development. Rabbit findings and potential implications for clinical risk of special populations will be addressed in labeling.
L623: Additional details of the developmental, reproductive, and juvenile development toxicity studies can be found in Section 19. A discussion of the developmental and reproductive toxicology data relevant to crinecerfont use in pregnant people can be found in Section 14.4.
L624: ## Carcinogenicity
L625: The oncogenic potential of crinecerfont was evaluated in two-year rat and 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity studies. Crinecerfont did not show oncogenic effects in transgenic mice. In the 2-year rat study, crinecerfont increased the incidence of thyroid gland follicular cell adenoma and carcinoma in females at 100 mg/kg crinecerfont (4-fold MRHD exposure). Thyroid gland follicular cell tumors arise from excessive clearance of thyroid hormone from induction of liver drug-metabolizing enzymes, which results in release of, and continuous stimulation by, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) on the thyroid follicular cells. This mechanism of inducing thyroid gland follicular cell hyperplasia and subsequent tumor development in rats is considered not relevant in humans (Wu and Farrelly 2006; Bartsch et al. 2018). Additional evidence from the chronic 6-month rat toxicity study showed increased thyroid gland weights and follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia, with increased TSH measured in the subchronic rat study further supporting thyroid hormone stimulation leading to thyroid gland hypertrophy. Overall, the data from genotoxicity, 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity, and two-year rat carcinogenicity studies show that the potential human oncogenic risk of crinecerfont is low.
L626: ## 13.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L627: Crinecerfont is a first-in-class drug, so there is no marketing experience. Adrenal insufficiency was identified as a potential safety concern because of the drug's mechanism of action. Crinecerfont decreases pituitary ACTH levels, leading to decreased adrenal androgen levels, and ultimately allowing for reduction in glucocorticoid dosage.
L628: Neuropsychiatric safety was identified as another potential concern because crinecerfont is centrally acting and was previously in development as a treatment for major depression.
L629: Potential risks of hypersensitivity and neutropenia were identified because of observations in earlier clinical studies. A hypersensitivity event of angioedema occurred in a phase 1 study (Study NBI-74788-1724) of two dose regimens of crinecerfont (100 mg qAM/200 mg qPM, or 100 mg qAM/150 mg qPM) in healthy adult volunteers. According to the Applicant, the 41-year-old male with no relevant past medical history developed a moderate-grade generalized rash after 3 days of crinecerfont treatment with 100/150 mg. He subsequently experienced perioral edema and throat tightness. No symptoms of shortness of breath or difficulty swallowing were reported, and vital signs were stable. These signs and symptoms resolved following treatment with dexamethasone, inhaled epinephrine, and an oral corticosteroid taper. The study drug was discontinued because of the hypersensitivity event. The investigator considered the event possibly related to study drug. Hypersensitivity reactions are discussed further in Section 13.7.2.
L630: Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont for major depressive disorder (Study DFI5687). There was a higher incidence of transient low neutrophil counts (&lt;1.5\times 10^3 cells/\muL for non-Black subjects, &lt;1\times 10^3 cells/\muL for Black subjects) in the crinecerfont 100 mg group (12.9%) compared with the placebo and escitalopram groups (3.5% and 6.1%, respectively) in this study. Neutropenia is discussed further in Section 13.7.3.
L631: ## 13.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L632: Not applicable. The drug is not marketed in any country.
L633: ## 13.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L634: The phase 3 trials, CAH3003 (conducted in adults with CAH) and CAH2006 (conducted in children aged 4 years to 17 years with CAH), were used to support the safety review. The Applicant's safety analysis included results of the completed 6-month double-blind treatment period for both studies and the subset of available data from ongoing open-label periods through Month 12 for Trial CAH3003 (data cutoff July 19, 2023) and Week 52 for Trial CAH2006 (data cutoff August 9, 2023). The Applicant subsequently submitted the completed 120-day Safety Update (data cutoff January 16, 2024, for Trial CAH3003 and February 6, 2024, for Trial CAH2006), which was incorporated into the safety review and included data from the open-label extension (post-Month 12). We present the safety data from each distinct period (i.e., 24-week double-blind treatment period, open-label treatment Months 6 to 12, followed by open-label

The Applicant defined the open-label period safety analysis set as all subjects who took at least one dose of crinecerfont during the open-label period.
L638: Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were protocol-defined as AEs not present prior to the initiation of study drug dosing, or already present events that worsened either in intensity or frequency following the initiation of study drug dosing, with an onset on or before the last dose of study drug plus 28 days. Laboratory, electrocardiogram, or physical examination findings that were considered clinically significant in the opinion of the investigator could be considered adverse events. All AEs in the reviewed trials were graded by investigators using a three-category intensity scale, shown in Table 31, with options of mild, moderate, or severe, which was reviewed and found to be acceptable.

L648: ## 13.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database

The majority of subjects in both trials completed the full one-year treatment period. A total of 179 subjects were exposed to crinecerfont for \ge46 weeks in the two trials combined. L664: ## 13.6.2. Safety Results, Trial CAH3003
L665: ## 13.6.2.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events Summary, Trial CAH3003
L666: ## 13.6.2.1.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L667: During the double-blind placebo-controlled treatment period of Trial CAH3003, the overall rates of any adverse event were similar in the crinecerfont (83%) compared to the placebo (81%) group (Table 34). Serious adverse events and adverse events leading to permanent discontinuation of study drug were more common in the crinecerfont group than in placebo. The 95% confidence interval for the risk difference between the crinecerfont and placebo group in these adverse event categories crossed zero, so differences were not significantly different. However, the trial was not designed nor powered to determine a statistically significant difference in adverse event rates.

L676: ## 13.6.2.1.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 24 to 48)
L677: The overall rate of any adverse event decreased from 81% in the placebo double-blind (DB) period to 70% during the open-label period in the placebo/crinecerfont group and decreased from 83% in the crinecerfont DB period to 62% during the open-label period in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group (Table 35). During the open-label treatment phase, the rates of serious AEs did not increase significantly (3% to 4%) in subjects who remained on crinecerfont. Subjects who transitioned from placebo during the DB phase to crinecerfont experienced an increase in serious AE incidence from zero to 5% as shown in Table 35.

L695: ## 13.6.2.2. Deaths, Trial CAH3003
L696: There were no deaths in Trial CAH3003 during the double-blind or open-label treatment periods.
L697: ## 13.6.2.2.1. Open-Label Extension (Month 12 Onward)
L698: One death occurred in a subject on study drug (crinecerfont 100 mg in the morning and 200 mg in the evening) during the open-label extension period. The cause of death was an adrenal crisis. The adrenal crisis was precipitated by an acute infectious illness that was not adequately treated with stress-dose steroids. The death was not likely study-drug-related.
L699: The subject, a 56-year-old male with classic CAH, died during an episode of acute adrenal insufficiency. Approximately 19 months after starting crinecerfont and 15 months after achieving a lower glucocorticoid dose of 9.8 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent, he developed a flu-like illness with nausea, vomiting, and lethargy. He had recently been exposed to visiting family members with similar symptoms. The following day, he vomited 3 times. That evening, he informed his visiting family members that he would start stress dosing of steroids with his next glucocorticoid dose and was going to bed. He was found dead on the floor the next morning. Autopsy findings showed inflammatory infiltrates in his lungs consistent with his reported flu-like syndrome, and cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly thought to be related to his uncontrolled diabetes.
L700: ## 13.6.2.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial CAH3003
L701: ## 13.6.2.3.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L702: The overall rate of serious TEAEs during the 24-week double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH3003 was 3.3% (in four subjects) in the crinecerfont group and none in the placebo group (Table 37).
L703: Four subjects experienced serious TEAEs during the double-blind treatment period. One event was presyncope, the cause of which is unclear, but did not recur despite resuming study drug:
L704: - Presyncope occurred in a 48-year-old female who developed fatigue, general malaise, and myalgias on Study Day 64 (Week 9, during the glucocorticoid reduction period) and was admitted to the hospital for evaluation. Her glucocorticoid dose was decreased from 14.5 mg/m2/day at baseline to 11.6 mg/m2/day at Week 6 and she remained at a dose of 11.6 mg/m2/day at Week 9. The evaluation was unremarkable, without orthostatic hypotension or laboratory signs of adrenal insufficiency. She was successfully treated with intravenous fluids, electrolytes, and hydrocortisone. Study drug was interrupted for 1 day and she continued study drug into the open-label treatment period with no recurrence of presyncope.
L705: The three remaining serious TEAEs occurring during the double-blind treatment period are not likely study-drug-related:
L706: - A serious adverse event (SAE) of acute adrenocortical insufficiency during the double-blind treatment period occurred in a 24-year-old female. Concomitant medications administered within 30 days before the event included fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone. On Day 30, the subject experienced vomiting for which she self-administered emergency hydrocortisone. Her glucocorticoid dose at Week 4 was 16 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents, which had not changed from baseline.
L707: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L708: Symptoms persisted and the subject was admitted to the hospital on Study Day 33 for vomiting and tachycardia. Laboratory evaluation revealed signs of adrenal insufficiency (hyponatremia and an elevated plasma renin activity). After admission, the subject developed a cough with elevated white blood count, was diagnosed with a lower respiratory infection, and treated with doxycycline. Her adrenal insufficiency was successfully treated with intravenous hydrocortisone, fluids, and an antiemetic.
L709: Study drug was interrupted for 11 days during her recovery, after which she resumed crinecerfont, completed the double-blind treatment period, and then continued into the open-label treatment period.
L710: The SAE of acute adrenal insufficiency was considered the result of lower respiratory tract infection and not due to study drug. This reviewer concurs with that assessment.
L711: - An SAE of acute cholecystitis occurred on study treatment Day 166 in a 48-year-old transgender female with obesity who was assigned to crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily. Concomitant medications included estradiol. The subject was hospitalized and treated with intravenous antibiotics with full recovery. No change was made to crinecerfont therapy. The subject's history of obesity and treatment with estradiol increased her risk of developing gallstones and subsequently, cholecystitis.
- An 18-year-old female with a history of acne experienced SAEs of cellulitis and groin abscess on Study Day 142 (Week 20). At the Week 12 study visit, routine laboratory testing showed white blood cell and neutrophil counts within the normal range. The abscess was treated with antibiotics, incision, and drainage, and was not likely study-drug-related. No changes to the study drug treatment were made. The investigator considered the SAEs unlikely to be related to study drug. The subject completed the double-blind period and continued into the open-label treatment phase.

L720: ## 13.6.2.3.2. SAEs During Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 24 to 48)
L721: Table 38 shows the serious TEAEs that began during the open-label treatment period according to treatment received in the double-blind phase (i.e., placebo or crinecerfont). There were nine events in eight subjects. Acute adrenal insufficiency was the only preferred term that occurred in more than one subject.
L722: The events (preferred terms) of tympanic membrane perforation, gastroenteritis viral, coronavirus infection, and Bell's palsy are considered unrelated to study drug due either to identification of an alternate cause, or unlikely relationship to pharmacology of crinecerfont. The event of joint injury was a case of right knee torsion injury sustained during a skateboarding accident.
L723: The two cases of adrenocortical insufficiency were both preceded by acute infection accompanied by vomiting. In one of the two cases, the subject had been unable to take stress-dose steroids due to vomiting. Both events were attributed to infection and not considered related to study drug.
L724: There was a serious AE of suicide attempt, for which a drug effect cannot be excluded:
L725: - The serious adverse event of suicide attempt involved a 29-year-old female with a history of acne who had received crinecerfont 100 mg bid starting in the double-blind treatment period and continuing during the open-label treatment period. Concomitant medications administered within 30 days of the event included hydrocortisone and paracetamol/tramadol.
L726: On Study Day 320 (also Day 320 of study drug administration), she was hospitalized after taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin as well as intentionally injuring her arm. Three days prior to hospital admission she had ended a seven-year romantic relationship and experienced significant deterioration of her mental condition. Computed tomography scanning showed cortical brain atrophy. Study drug was discontinued because of the suicide attempt. The investigator considered the suicide attempt to be unrelated to study treatment.
L727: The remaining SAE described below, was not considered related to study drug following review of the narrative:
L728: - A 46-year-old male had an anaphylactic reaction to tree nuts. He had a history of a tree nut allergy and ate cake containing nuts on Study Day 332 during the open-label treatment period. He was treated with antihistamine and hydrocortisone in the emergency department with resolution the same day. He continued on study drug after the event. This SAE was not drug-related.

L738: ## 13.6.2.3.3. Serious Adverse Events Reported in Open-Label Extension (Month 12 Onward)
L739: Nine subjects experienced serious adverse events in the open-label extension through the data cutoff date of the 120-day safety update submission (Table 39). There were three cases of acute adrenocortical insufficiency, one of which was fatal and is described in Section 13.6.2.2.1 above.
L740: Review of this narrative and the other nonfatal cases of acute adrenocortical insufficiency do not suggest a relationship to crinecerfont treatment. All events except one were preceded by acute illness and associated with inadequate stress dosing of steroids. The remaining event involved a 52-year-old male who was hospitalized for vomiting and hypoxia. He reported an antecedent history of several months of generalized weakness and chronic diarrhea. Hospital evaluation yielded no evidence of underlying infection, and no unifying diagnosis was made. However, the subject's symptoms improved with stress-dose steroids, and he resumed crinecerfont without recurrence of symptoms. The cause of adrenal insufficiency in this subject is unclear but could relate to dehydration from chronic diarrhea, or to a subacute non-bacterial infectious or other inflammatory etiology. Negative rechallenge with study drug suggests the event was not related to crinecerfont.
L741: The remaining narratives for SAEs were reviewed and there is no suggestion that the events were related to study drug, as events resolved while the subjects continued on crinecerfont and/or an alternative etiology was identified.

L751: ## 13.6.2.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment Discontinuation, Trial CAH3003
L752: ## 13.6.2.4.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L753: A total of four subjects (3.3%) in the crinecerfont group and none in the placebo group experienced an adverse event leading to study drug discontinuation during the double-blind treatment period (Table 40). No single preferred term occurred in more than one subject.
L754: During the double-blind treatment period, adverse events of restlessness, apathy, dyspepsia, nausea, and vomiting, involving two subjects described below, are possibly study-drug-related:
L755: - A 28-year-old male developed restlessness on Study Day 3 and apathy on Study Day 54. He also had an increase in his Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale from 0 to 2 (nonspecific active suicidal thoughts). He discontinued crinecerfont on Study Day 380 during the extended open-label period due to restlessness, with resolution of the restlessness 11 days after discontinuation. The adverse event of restlessness is possibly study-drug-related because crinecerfont is centrally acting and the restlessness resolved after drug discontinuation. Drug-relatedness for apathy and suicidal ideation cannot be excluded.
- Dyspepsia, nausea, and vomiting developed in a 39-year-old female without any noted medical history other than CAH on Study Day 167, which resolved on Study Day 169. She then discontinued study drug on Day 184 due to nausea, vomiting, and dyspepsia. Information is not available regarding resolution of symptoms off study drug.
L756: The adverse events of rash, and gastric ulcer leading to study drug discontinuation are not likely study-drug-related:
L757: - Rash occurred in a 26-year-old female on Study Day 166. She was treated with clobetasol and discontinued the study on Day 589 because of the rash. The rash was still present on Day 671. The rash is not likely study-drug-related because the rash did not resolve after study drug discontinuation.
- Gastric ulcer occurred in a 31-year-old female on Study Day 10. Her medical history included headache, hypertension, menstrual disorder, and sleep apnea. Concomitant medications included hydrocortisone and propranolol. The timing of a gastric ulcer occurring after only 10 days of study drug treatment makes it unlikely to have been related to study drug.

L800: ## 13.6.2.5.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 24 to 48)
L801: During the open-label treatment period, the rate of any AE decreased from 83% in the crinecerfont DB group to 62% in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group and decreased from 81% in the placebo DB group to 70% in the placebo/crinecerfont group (Table 43).
L802: Adverse events occurring in ≥4% of subjects in the placebo/crinecerfont group were fatigue, headache, coronavirus infection, nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, dizziness, back pain, and abdominal pain (see Table 43).
L803: Fatigue, dizziness, arthralgia, back pain, increased creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and decreased appetite all decreased in frequency from the crinecerfont DB period to the crinecerfont/crinecerfont open-label period, suggesting drug tolerance. Overall AE incidence also decreased. These data raise no concerns with respect to the longer-term safety of crinecerfont.

L815: ## 13.6.2.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial CAH3003
L816: See the schedule of assessments in Section 21 for the frequency of laboratory monitoring.
L817: Laboratory data for CPK, neutrophil count, and coagulation parameters were examined more closely for the following reasons:
L818: - The adverse event preferred term of blood creatine phosphokinase increased occurred with greater frequency in the crinecerfont versus placebo group (see Section 13.6.2.5).
- A higher incidence of neutropenia was noted in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont in subjects with major depressive disorder (see Section 13.2).
- Nonclinical studies of crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy (prolongation of PT and APTT and/or bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies. Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was replaced with a free base form, which was used for the clinical studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or bleeding effects were noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT
L819: up to 60%, and APTT up to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD exposure). Similar findings (prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study conducted with crinecerfont free base but without any other coagulopathy up to 1000 mg/kg/day [5-fold MRHD exposure].
L820: ## 13.6.2.6.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L821: ## 13.6.2.6.1.1. Chemistry Parameters
L822: Elevated CPK levels occurred more frequently in the placebo group, but CPK levels greater than 5\times ULN occurred more frequently in the crinecerfont group. The mean change in CPK levels from baseline over time was slightly higher in the crinecerfont group compared to placebo (Figure 16).
L823: Although more subjects in the placebo group (12%) had CPK levels &gt;3\times ULN (Level 1 abnormality) compared to the crinecerfont group (9%), more crinecerfont-treated subjects had CPK values &gt;5\times ULN (Level 2 abnormality) and &gt;10\times ULN (Level 3 abnormality) than subjects receiving placebo (Table 44).
L824: Of the five subjects with CPK values &gt;10\times ULN (Level 3) in the crinecerfont group during the double-blind treatment period, all elevated levels were documented on a single blood draw and had resolved by the subsequent blood draw. According to the Applicant, most instances of increased CPK levels were associated with significant physical exertion and improved with cessation of the inciting activity. No cases of increased CPK resulted in study treatment discontinuation. There were no reported cases of rhabdomyolysis.
L825: The elevated CPK levels are not likely drug-related because elevated levels &gt;3\times ULN occurred more frequently in the placebo group, most instances of elevated CPK levels were explained by other factors, and there is no mechanistic evidence of causality.

L843: ## 13.6.2.6.1.2. Hematology Parameters
L844: As noted above, because of the higher incidence of neutropenia noted in the major depression study, we examined laboratory data for neutropenia and those findings are discussed further in Section 13.7.3. There was also a decrease in white blood cell count over time in the crinecerfont group during the double-blind treatment period compared to placebo. This issue is addressed further in Section 13.7.3.
L845: There was no notable difference in mean change or outlier incidence in hemoglobin, hematocrit, or platelets (see Table 198 in Section 23.2.2).
L846: With respect to coagulation parameters, mean PT and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) increased slightly over time in both treatment groups, but the effect was larger in the crinecerfont group (see Figure 17). INR remained stabled in both groups (Figure 17). There was no notable difference in incidence of outliers in coagulation parameters of INR or PTT between crinecerfont and placebo groups (Table 46). For study subjects with adverse events classified under the narrow FDA medical query (FMQ) of hemorrhage (Table 47), all had coagulation study parameters within normal limits, that includes PT, PTT, and INR.

L885: ## 13.6.2.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial CAH3003
L886: In rat and dog studies, increased liver weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy were observed, likely due to crinecerfont's induction of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Laboratory data were screened for evidence of drug-induced liver injury to determine cases meeting Hy's Law criteria, defined as any postbaseline total bilirubin equal to or exceeding two times the upper limit of normal (2× ULN) after a postbaseline alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) equal to or exceeding 3× ULN. There were no potential cases of Hy's Law during the double-blind (Figure 18) or open-label treatment periods.
L887: As shown in Table 49, the incidence of excursions in liver parameters outside the normal range during treatment were similar between the crinecerfont and placebo groups. A single subject receiving crinecerfont experienced increase in total bilirubin to &gt;2× ULN without associated transaminase elevation.

L908: ## 13.6.2.8. Vital-Sign Analyses, Trial CAH3003
L909: Review of the vital-sign data did not reveal any safety concerns. There were no clinically significant changes from baseline over time in mean systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, orthostatic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, or body temperature in the crinecerfont versus placebo group during the 24-week double-blind treatment period. See Section 23 for additional details (Figure 78, Figure 79, Figure 80, Figure 81, Figure 82, and Table 199).

L924: ## 13.6.3. Safety Results, Trial CAH2006
L925: ## 13.6.3.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events Summary, Trial CAH2006
L926: ## 13.6.3.1.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L927: During the 28-week double-blind placebo-controlled period of Trial CAH2006, the overall rates of adverse events were similar in the crinecerfont (84%) and placebo (82%) groups. One subject in the crinecerfont group (1.4%) compared to four subjects in the placebo group (12%) experienced serious adverse events. Adverse events leading to interruption of study drug occurred more frequently in the placebo group (15%) compared to the crinecerfont group (3%) (Table 52).

L937: ## 13.6.3.1.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to 52)
L938: The overall rate of any adverse event decreased from 82% in the placebo DB period to 74% during the open-label period in the placebo/crinecerfont group and decreased from 84% in the crinecerfont DB period to 70% during the open-label period in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group (Table 53), which suggests improved tolerability of crinecerfont for the subjects who remained in the trial and continued treatment with crinecerfont. The rate of serious adverse events decreased from 12% in the placebo DB period to 6.5% during the open-label period in the placebo/crinecerfont group and were similar to the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group (6%). These data do not raise any concerns with longer-term treatment.

L958: ## 13.6.3.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial CAH2006
L959: ## 13.6.3.3.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L960: In Trial CAH2006, the overall rate of serious TEAEs was higher in the placebo group (12%, four subjects) compared to the crinecerfont group (1.4%, one subject) during the 28-week double-blind treatment period (Table 55).
L961: The one serious TEAE of pyrexia occurring in the crinecerfont group during the double-blind treatment period was more likely related to an infectious etiology, given the subject's improvement with treatment in the emergency department and in the setting of continued crinecerfont treatment:
L962: - Pyrexia occurred in a 12-year-old-male who presented to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.2°C, vomiting, and headache on Study Day 61. Attempts at oral stress-dose hydrocortisone at home were unsuccessful due to vomiting. In the emergency department, he was treated with intravenous hydration, fluids, dextrose, and hydrocortisone. His condition improved and he was discharged the same day. No changes were made to his study drug regimen.

L973: ## 13.6.3.3.2. SAEs During Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to 52)
L974: **Table 56** lists the serious TEAEs that began during the open-label treatment period, according to treatment received in the double-blind phase (i.e., placebo or crinecerfont). There were six events in six subjects.
L975: Narratives for the events (preferred terms) of vomiting and gastritis were reviewed and are considered unrelated to study drug, due either to identification of an alternate cause or an unlikely relationship to pharmacology of crinecerfont.
L976: Details of the three remaining SAEs, none of which are likely study-drug-related, follow:
L977: - An SAE of hypotension occurred in a 6-year-old female on amlodipine. Her hypotension resolved when her amlodipine dose was reduced. This event can be attributed to effect of antihypertensive medication.
- A seizure occurred in a 5-year-old female on Study Day 222 that led to hospitalization and study drug interruption for 1 day. Initial laboratory evaluation and brain imaging was normal. Further evaluation included chromosomal microarray testing that was suspicious for 15q duplication syndrome, which may be associated with epilepsy. This case represents initial presentation of epilepsy secondary to a chromosomal abnormality.
- An SAE of acute adrenocortical insufficiency occurred in a 7-year-old female on Study Day 223 that led to interruption of study drug for 2 days. She was admitted to the hospital after presenting with vomiting and diarrhea. She vomited her stress-dose hydrocortisone. Evaluation was consistent with adrenal crisis (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis). A viral gastroenteritis panel was positive for norovirus. She was treated with intravenous fluids, dextrose, stress-dose hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, and ondansetron. Her condition significantly improved after two days. In this case, acute adrenal insufficiency was considered secondary to norovirus gastroenteritis.

L987: ## 13.6.3.3.3. Serious Adverse Events Reported in the Open-Label Extension (Week 52 Onward)
L988: Three subjects experienced serious adverse events in the open-label extension that were newly reported in the 120-day safety update. Narratives for the events (preferred terms) of blood CPK increased, Norovirus infection, and cerebrospinal fluid leakage were reviewed, and these events are considered unrelated to study drug due either to identification of an alternate cause, or unlikely relationship to the pharmacology of crinecerfont. The event of blood CPK increased was temporally related to isotretinoin. The event of cerebrospinal fluid leakage was related to cranio-spinal surgery for Chiari malformation.

L1008: ## 13.6.3.4.3. Open-Label Extension (Week 52 Onward)
L1009: One subject, a 14-year-old male, discontinued study drug during the open-label extension for a suicide attempt (preferred term) as specified per protocol. After the data cutoff, the investigations indicated that the event term should be corrected to “suicidal ideation” because the subject did not have a plan and did not make a suicide attempt. He had a history of anxiety, depression, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Concomitant medications included bupropion, fluoxetine, hydroxyzine, aripiprazole, and isotretinoin. The subject visited his family home construction site and had a thought that if he fell off the roof, he would die.

L1025: ## 13.6.3.5.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to 52)
L1026: During the open-label treatment period, the rate of any AE decreased from 84% in the crinecerfont DB group to 70% in the crinecerfont/crinerfont group and decreased from 82% in the placebo DB group to 74% in the placebo/crinerfont group (Table 59).

It is possible that these events relate to symptoms of glucocorticoid withdrawal rather than crinecerfont itself. Both headache and abdominal pain also decreased in frequency from the crinecerfont DB group to the crinecerfont/crinerfont group, suggesting development of tolerance to reduction in glucocorticoid dose or to crinecerfont treatment.

L1040: ## 13.6.3.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial CAH2006
L1041: See the schedule of assessments in Section 21 for the frequency of laboratory monitoring.
L1042: Laboratory data for CPK, neutrophil count, and coagulation parameters were examined more closely for the following reasons:
L1043: - Elevated CPK levels were noted in the adult study.
- A higher incidence of neutropenia was noted in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont in subjects with major depressive disorder (see Section 13.2).
- Nonclinical studies of crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy (prolongation of PT and APTT and/or bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies. Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was replaced with a free-base form, which was used for the clinical studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or bleeding effects were noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT up to 60%, and APTT up to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD exposure). Similar findings (prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study conducted with crinecerfont free base but without any other coagulopathy up to 1000 mg/kg/day (5-fold MRHD exposure).
- Neutropenia and white blood cell count findings are discussed in detail in Section 13.7.3.
L1044: ## 13.6.3.6.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
L1045: ## 13.6.3.6.1.1. Chemistry Parameters
L1046: The mean change in CPK levels from baseline over time was similar in both the crinecerfont and placebo groups, with a peak at Week 8 in the crinecerfont group (Figure 19). Elevated CPK values occurred in one subject in both the crinecerfont (1.4%) and placebo (3%) groups during the 28-week double-blind treatment period, without significant difference between the two groups (Table 200).
L1047: According to the Applicant, the instances of increased CPK levels were associated with significant physical exertion and an increased isotretinoin dose in one case. The levels improved with cessation of the inciting factor. No cases of increased CPK resulted in study treatment discontinuation. There were no reported cases of rhabdomyolysis. The elevated CPK levels are not likely drug-related because elevated levels were explained by other factors and there is no mechanistic evidence of causality.

L1069: ## 13.6.3.6.1.2. Hematology Parameters
L1070: There was no notable difference in mean change or outlier incidence in hemoglobin, hematocrit, or platelets (see Table 203 in Section 23.4).
L1071: There was no notable difference in mean change in coagulation parameters (Figure 20) over the 28-week treatment period. There was a higher incidence of transitions from normal at baseline to above normal during treatment in elevated PTT for the crinecerfont group (7%) compared to the placebo group (3%) (Table 62). However, all such excursions were Level 1 in severity and are not considered clinically meaningful. None of the five subjects with elevated PTT experienced an adverse event related to hemorrhage.

L1122: ## 13.6.3.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial CAH2006
L1123: In rat and dog studies, increased liver weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy were observed, likely due to crinecerfont's induction of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Laboratory data were screened for evidence of drug-induced liver injury to determine cases meeting Hy's law criteria, defined as any postbaseline total bilirubin equal to or exceeding 2× ULN after a postbaseline ALT or AST equal to or exceeding 3× ULN. There were no potential cases of Hy's Law during the double-blind (see Figure 21) or open-label treatment periods. In addition, outlier analysis showed no increased incidence of abnormal liver function tests for the crinecerfont group compared to placebo (see Figure 21).

L1144: Review of the vital-sign data did not reveal any safety concerns. L1159: ## 13.7. Key Safety Review Issues
L1160: ## 13.7.1. Potential for Adrenal Insufficiency
L1161: ## Issue
L1162: Adrenal insufficiency can occur given crinecerfont's mechanism of action of decreasing pituitary ACTH levels, leading to reduced adrenal androgen levels, and ultimately allowing for a reduction in glucocorticoid dose. Acute adrenal insufficiency as a serious adverse event was observed in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006.
L1163: ## Background
L1164: Glucocorticoid deficiency is a clinical feature of CAH and requires replacement glucocorticoid therapy. Additional glucocorticoid is often needed to lower adrenal androgen levels into the recommended goal range. By reducing elevated adrenal androgen levels, crinecerfont may allow for a reduction in glucocorticoid dose to more physiologic levels. Adrenal insufficiency could occur if the glucocorticoid dose is reduced too much or if an inadequate glucocorticoid dose is given at times of stress.
L1165: ## Assessment
L1166: We devised and performed a customized grouped query of preferred terms that could potentially signal acute adrenocortical insufficiency for the double-blind treatment periods of both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006. Results are shown in Table 69 and Table 70 below.
L1167: In Trial CAH3003, adverse events in the adrenal insufficiency grouped query occurred at a greater frequency in the crinecerfont group (43%) compared to the placebo group (27%) (see Table 69). In contrast, in Trial CAH2006, adverse events in the grouped query occurred at a greater frequency in the placebo group (42%) compared to the crinecerfont group (36%). (see Table 70).
L1168: Time of onset of events in the adrenal insufficiency grouped query is shown in the figures below (Figure 22 and Figure 23). The pattern of time to onset is similar between crinecerfont and placebo groups in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006.
L1169: This grouped query search has important limitations. First, most of the preferred terms are nonspecific and may not necessarily reflect adrenal insufficiency. Second, it is possible some of these symptoms could be related to a reduction in the glucocorticoid dose in subjects who are not adrenally insufficient. Third, these symptoms could occur noncontemporaneously, and therefore could reflect different clinical entities at different timepoints. Given these limitations, we next focus on an analysis of specific preferred terms of adrenal insufficiency.

L1199: The Applicant provided narratives for all treatment-emergent adverse events with the preferred terms adrenocortical insufficiency acute and adrenal insufficiency. None were likely drug-related. In almost all cases, the adrenal crisis was precipitated by an acute illness and was not adequately treated with stress-dose steroids.
L1200: The only case of an adrenal crisis not precipitated by an acute illness was one subject in the placebo group of Trial CAH3003, who experienced an adrenal crisis during the double-blind period after stopping her maintenance hydrocortisone upon advice of her endocrinologist (not a study investigator) because she was thought to be on study drug. This endocrinologist erroneously assumed that crinecerfont treated all aspects of CAH, including the adrenal insufficiency. This case illustrates the importance of ensuring patients and healthcare professionals know to continue at least replacement doses of glucocorticoid therapy while taking crinecerfont as adjunct therapy to reduce residual androgen excess.
L1201: Of the eight subjects experiencing an adrenal crisis in Trial CAH3003 while taking crinecerfont, all episodes were secondary to an acute illness coupled with lack of adequate stress-dose steroid. Two episodes of adrenal crisis occurred during the double-blind treatment period, two in the open-label treatment period, and four in the open-label extension beyond Month 12. One subject died from his adrenal crisis in the open-label extension period.
L1202: Similarly, the two subjects with narratives related to adrenal crisis while taking crinecerfont in Trial CAH2006 had episodes secondary to acute illness coupled with lack of adequate stress-
L1203: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L1204: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1205: dose steroid. One episode of adrenal crisis occurred during the open-label treatment period, and one occurred during the open-label extension beyond Month 12. One subject in Trial CAH3003 experienced a serious TEAE of presyncope during the glucocorticoid reduction period, which is potentially related to glucocorticoid withdrawal (see Section 13.6.2.3).
L1206: ## Conclusion
L1207: In conclusion, adrenal insufficiency does not appear to be drug-related but rather related to the underlying disease process of CAH, for which glucocorticoid deficiency is a prominent clinical feature. The adrenal insufficiency case narratives highlight the importance of continuing physiologic replacement glucocorticoid, not decreasing the glucocorticoid below physiologic replacement levels, and taking appropriate stress-dose steroids during times of illness. One case illustrates the importance of ensuring that healthcare professionals know that crinecerfont is adjunctive therapy to at least replacement doses of glucocorticoid therapy.
L1208: ## Action Taken
L1209: - Added the description of crinecerfont as adjunctive therapy to physiologic glucocorticoid replacement in the indication statement
- Ensured directions in the Prescribing Information state not to decrease the glucocorticoid dose below physiologic replacement levels
- Ensured directions in the Prescribing Information state that stress-dose glucocorticoid continues to be necessary during acute illnesses and other situations of increased need
- Added directions for timing of monitoring of androstenedione levels after initiation of crinecerfont so the glucocorticoid dose can be evaluated at appropriate time periods
L1210: ## 13.7.2. Potential for Hypersensitivity
L1211: ## Background
L1212: Throat tightness, perioral edema, and generalized rash (coded as angioedema) occurred in one subject in a phase 1 study (NBI-74788-1724) of crinecerfont in healthy subjects, prompting closer evaluation of potential hypersensitivity events in the phase 3 studies of crinecerfont for the treatment of CAH. The event of angioedema occurred after 3 days of crinecerfont treatment with 100 mg qAM plus 150 mg qPM.
L1213: ## Assessment
L1214: To capture potential hypersensitivity events, we examined narrow FMQs within the “immune system disorders” and “skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders” system organ class (SOC). The narrow FMQs (and also the preferred terms) “anaphylactic reaction” and “hypersensitivity” fall under the “immune system disorders” SOC.
L1215: During the double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH3003, narrow FMQs within the “skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders” SOC occurred more frequently (and with similar frequency) in the placebo group (12%) compared to the crinecerfont group (11%) during the double-blind period (Table 71). There were no reported AEs within the narrow FMQs in the “immune system disorders” SOC in either group during the double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH3003.

L1245: ## 13.7.3. Potential for Neutropenia and Reduction in Total White Blood Cell Count
L1246: ## Background
L1247: Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study (Study DFI5687) of crinecerfont for major depressive disorder. The pathophysiology of this observation is unclear.
L1248: ## Issue
L1249: Decreased neutrophil counts occurred more frequently in study subjects treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006. Decrease in mean white blood count over time was also observed in Trial CAH3003 and was more pronounced in the pediatric study.
L1250: ## Assessment
L1251: In the adult trial (CAH3003), the mean change in neutrophil count was slightly decreased compared to baseline at Week 24 in the crinecerfont group, but the decrease was not notably different from placebo Figure 24.

L1329: As shown in Table 80, over the 36-month treatment period, the median white blood count ranged from 7.6\times 10^3 cells/\muL at baseline to 7.1\times 10^3 cells/\muL at Month 36. L1367: To further examine the potential signal of reduction in white blood cells (WBCs) with treatment, laboratory data from the major depression study (Study DFI5687) were reviewed. Adults with major depressive disorder (N=580) were randomized to receive one of three doses of crinecerfont (20 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg daily), placebo daily, or escitalopram 10 mg daily, for 8 weeks. Median white blood cell count was stable over 8 weeks of treatment in each crinecerfont dose group—median values of 5.8 to 6.0 \times 10^3 cells/\muL for the 100 mg group, 6.1 to 6.2 \times 10^3 cells/\muL for the 50 mg group and 5.7 to 6.0 \times 10^3 cells/\muL for the 20 mg group. In this study, however, subjects received once-daily dosing compared to twice-daily dosing in the CAH studies.
L1368: ## Conclusion
L1369: Decreased neutrophil counts (&lt;2 \times 10^3 cells/\muL) occurred more frequently in study subjects treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo during the double-blind treatment periods of both Trials CAH3003 (14% versus 5%) and CAH2006 (37% versus 16%). The frequency increased from 5% in the placebo DB group to 19% in the placebo/crinecerfont group in Trial CAH3003
L1370: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L1371: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1372: and from 15.6% in the placebo DB group to 26% in the placebo/crinecerfont group in Trial CAH2006. The clinical significance of these decreased neutrophil counts is unclear, but adverse event data do not suggest an association with increased bacterial infections occurring in children in Trial CAH2006
L1373: The reduction in WBCs is more pronounced in children, but in both populations the absolute changes were small, and the absolute values remained within the normal range. Reduced glucocorticoid dose is a possible explanatory factor for the decreased WBCs observed with crinecerfont. The change does not appear to be of clinical significance to treated subjects. Additional postmarketing investigation to evaluate these minor changes in absolute WBC count is unlikely to yield meaningful data that will change the benefit-risk evaluation of crinecerfont. Given that the absolute WBC values stayed in the normal range, we are not requesting the Applicant to include the WBC data in prescribing information.
