L1376: ## **Laboratory Findings**
L1377: - Adults with CAH: Neutrophil count less than 2\times 10^3 cells/\muL occurred in 14% (17 of 120) of CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to 5% (3 of 58) of subjects in the placebo group. Neutrophil count less than 1\times 10^3 cells/\muL occurred in 0.8% (1 of 120) of CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to 1.7% subjects (1 of 58) in the placebo group.
- Pediatric subjects with CAH: Neutrophil count less than 2\times 10^3 cells/\muL occurred in 37% (25 of 68) of CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to 16% (5 of 32) of subjects in the placebo group. Neutrophil count less than 1\times 10^3 cells/\muL occurred in 4% (3 of 68) of CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to no subjects (0 of 32) in the placebo group.
- We will also request that the Applicant conduct enhanced pharmacovigilance of postmarketing safety data for serious adverse events of bacterial infection and concurrent neutropenia.
L1378: ## **13.7.4. Neuropsychiatric Safety Concerns**
L1379: ## **Issue**
L1380: A suicide attempt occurred in a Trial CAH3003 subject taking crinecerfont, and more study subjects taking crinecerfont in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006 increased their score on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale compared to placebo.
L1381: ## **Background**
L1382: The Applicant prospectively identified neuropsychiatric safety as a potential concern because crinecerfont was previously in development as a treatment for depression. The rationale for studying crinecerfont in major depressive disorder was that evidence suggests that CRF1 receptors in the brain mediate CRF-induced anxiety and depression-like behaviors. According to
L1383: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1384: the Applicant's submission, probes to CRF1 receptors decreased anxiety-like behavior in stressed rats and CRF1 knockout mice showed less anxiety-like behaviors when stressed.
L1385: Despite the drug's lack of efficacy in the phase 2 major depressive disorder trial, and limited brain distribution of crinecerfont, the Applicant prospectively monitored for development of suicidality in Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006 using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS).
L1386: The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), a validated instrument to assess suicidal ideation and behavior, was administered at screening and at regular intervals during treatment. The C-SSRS consists of a series of six yes/no questions pertaining to suicidal ideation with each question indicating progressively more severe suicidality. The score ranges from 0 (no thoughts of suicide) to 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent). See Section 21.3 for the C-SSRS questionnaire and scoring.
L1387: In Trial CAH3003, the C-SSRS was administered at the following intervals (screening; baseline; Weeks 4, 9, 12, 16, 20, and 24; Months 7, 8, 9, 10, and 12). Subjects with any suicidal behavior within the past year or suicidal ideation of type 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan) or type 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) in the 6 months before screening based on the C-SSRS were excluded from the study. These were also study drug discontinuation criteria.
L1388: In Trial CAH2006, the C-SSRS was administered at the following intervals to individuals aged \ge 6 years (screening; baseline; Weeks 4, 16, 28, 40, 52, and 56). Subjects aged \ge 6 years with a lifetime history of suicidal behavior or suicidal ideation of type 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan) or type 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) in the 6 months before screening based on the C-SSRS were excluded from the study. These were also study drug discontinuation criteria.
L1389: ## Assessment
L1390: To examine a possible relationship between crinecerfont and neuropsychiatric adverse events including suicidality, we searched the safety databases of both trials for events coding to the psychiatric SOC. We also evaluated for subjects who experienced an increase in C-SSRS score (indicating increased suicidality) while on treatment.
L1391: ## **Neuropsychiatric Adverse Events**
L1392: A subject in Trial CAH3003 attempted suicide by taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin while on crinecerfont:
L1393: - The serious adverse event of suicide attempt involved a 29-year-old female with a history of acne who had received crinecerfont 100 mg bid starting in the double-blind treatment period and continuing during the open-label treatment period. Concomitant medications administered within 30 days of the event included hydrocortisone and paracetamol/tramadol.
L1394: On Study Day 320 (also Day 320 of study drug administration), she was hospitalized after taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin and intentionally injuring her arm. L1460: ## Conclusion
L1461: A serious AE of suicide attempt occurred in a study subject taking study drug. Suicidal ideation, measured by a score above 0 on the C-SSRS, occurred in very few subjects, some of whom had a history of suicidality. The very low event rates significantly limit conclusions, but a suicidality risk cannot be definitively excluded.

L1464: ## **Suicidal Ideation and Behavior**
L1465: - Adults with CAH: Study 1 excluded subjects with active suicidal ideation with intent or plan within the six months prior to screening and those with a history of suicidal behavior within the past year, based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) administered at screening. The C-SSRS was administered to subjects at regular intervals during the study. Three of 122 (2.5%) CRENESSITY-treated subjects reported suicidal ideation without method, intent, or plan on the C-SSRS during the 24-week double-blind treatment period compared to 1 of 59 (1.7%) placebo-treated subjects. One of the three subjects receiving CRENESSITY and the placebo treated subject reported a lifetime history of suicidal ideation. One CRENESSITY-treated subject without a history of suicidal ideation or behavior attempted suicide during the open-label period after 320 days of treatment.
- Pediatric subjects with CAH: Study 2 excluded subjects with active suicidal ideation with intent or plan within six months prior to screening or those with a lifetime history of suicidal behavior within the past year, based on the C-SSRS administered at screening. Four of 67 (6%) CRENESSITY-treated subjects and 0 of the 31 (0%) placebo-treated subjects reported suicidal ideation without method, intent, or plan on the C-SSRS during the 28-week double blind treatment period. Two of the four CRENESSITY-treated subjects reported a lifetime history of suicidal ideation. There were no completed suicides or suicide attempts.
- We will also request that the Applicant conduct enhanced pharmacovigilance of postmarketing safety data for serious and non-serious adverse events of suicidal behavior and/or ideation.
L1466: ## 14. Therapeutic Individualization
L1467: ## 14.1. Intrinsic Factors
L1468: ## Hepatic Impairment
L1469: Study NBI-74788-1717 was a phase 1, single-dose, open-label study comparing the PK of crinecerfont in subjects with normal hepatic function (n=6) and mild (n=6), moderate (n=6), and severe hepatic impairment (n=7). All subjects received 100 mg (two 50-mg capsules) crinecerfont with Ensure Plus (350 calories, 11 grams total fat, 20 grams sugars, 13 grams protein, and 50 grams carbohydrate). PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points from predose to 504 hours postdose. Based on the study results, the mean AUC_{0-\infty} was 27%, 34%, and 20% lower in the mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment groups, respectively, as compared to the normal hepatic function group. The 90% CI values for the geometric mean ratios (GMRs) for C_{max}, AUC_{0-last}, and AUC_{0-\infty} for all the hepatic impairment groups as compared to the normal hepatic function group included unity (Table 90, see details in Section 20.2.5). Therefore, we conclude that hepatic impairment does not have a clinically significant impact on crinecerfont PK and agree with the Applicant's proposed labeling that no dose adjustment of crinecerfont is necessary in patients with mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment.

L1474: ## Renal Impairment
L1475: The Applicant did not conduct a dedicated renal impairment study. Per the Applicant, the mass balance study (BEX5094) suggested limited renal elimination. In Study BEX5094, a single dose of 100-mg crinecerfont capsule with 2.59 MBq (70 \muCi) [^{14}C]-crinecerfont was administered with a high-fat breakfast. PK samples were collected at prespecified times from 1- to 3-day intervals through Day 37 postdose. The recovery of radioactivity was not complete by Day 37, and only 49.4% of the administered dose was recovered on average. Of the total amount of radioactivity recovered, 47.3% of the administered dose was recovered in the feces and less than 2% (mainly as metabolites with undetectable crinecerfont) was recovered in the urine (see Section 20.2.14). Despite the limitations of the mass balance study, considering the negligible amount of crinecerfont in the urine, the review team agrees that renal excretion is unlikely to significantly contribute to the elimination of crinecerfont.
L1476: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1477: The popPK analysis included estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR; Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration 2009 formula for adult subjects and bedside Schwartz formula for pediatric subjects) as a covariate for crinecerfont clearance. The range of eGFR (indexed to BSA) was evaluated against random effect of crinecerfont apparent clearance (in the base popPK model), and no obvious trend was observed. Additionally, the 95% CI of the eGFR effect on crinecerfont clearance included the null effect of zero, indicating minimal effect of eGFR on crinecerfont PK (refer to Section 20.5). Based on covariate effect assessment shown in Figure 28, the median AUC24 for crinecerfont in subjects with mild and moderate renal impairment were 0.973 and 0.916, respectively of the median crinecerfont AUC24 in subjects with normal renal function. The 95% confidence intervals included 1, indicating no statistically significant impact on crinecerfont AUC24 due to mild to moderate renal impairment. Of note, only a limited number of subjects with moderate renal impairment (n=2, based on BSA-indexed eGFR) in the popPK analysis contributed to a relatively wide 95% CI for the estimated moderate renal impairment impact on crinecerfont AUC (Figure 28).
L1478: Overall, mild to moderate renal impairment is unlikely to have clinically meaningful impact on crinecerfont exposure. Therefore, the review team agrees with the proposed labeling that no dose adjustment for crinecerfont is needed in patients with mild or moderate renal impairment. Crinecerfont was not studied in patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease. According to the FDA's guidance for industry *Pharmacokinetics in Patients With Impaired Renal Function* (March 2024), impaired renal function can be associated with changes in absorption, plasma protein binding, or alterations in some drug metabolism and transport pathways in the liver and gut. These changes can be particularly prominent in patients with severely impaired renal function and those with kidney failure. Considering the potential impact of severe renal impairment on the PK of crinecerfont, and the lack of experience in these patients, the review team recommends avoiding the use of crinecerfont in patients with severe renal impairment and end-stage renal disease.

L1482: ## **Other Intrinsic Factors**
L1483: Based on popPK analysis, no clinically significant differences in the PK of crinecerfont were observed based on age (range: 5 to 54 years), sex (58.7% male), and race (4.8% Asian, 9.7% Black, 77.5% White).
L1484: Body weight is a significant PK covariate of crinecerfont. Therefore, weight-band dosing in pediatric patients is proposed to account for the weight impact on crinecerfont PK (refer to Sections 12.1.1, 12.1.3, and 20.5).
L1485: ## **14.2. Extrinsic Factors**
L1486: ## **Food Effect**
L1487: Food has a significant impact on crinecerfont absorption. In Study NBI-74788-1736 (n=19), a single dose of crinecerfont 100-mg commercial capsule was administered with a high-fat, high-calorie meal or under fasted conditions. The GMRs for AUC_{0-\text{last}}, AUC_{0-\infty}, and C_{\text{max}} were 3.78, 3.27, and 4.95, respectively, in the fed state compared to the fasted state (Table 91). A similar magnitude of food effect was observed with earlier capsule formulations (Studies NBI-74788-1712 and NBI-7478-1601, see Sections 20.2.3 and 20.2.1).

L1497: Based on significantly enhanced bioavailability of crinecerfont for both oral solution and capsule formulations, pediatric and adult subjects with CAH were instructed to take crinecerfont with breakfast and dinner in the pivotal clinical trials, CAH2006 and CAH3003. Overall, the review team agrees with the proposed labeling that crinecerfont should be administered with food.
L1498: ## Drug Interactions
L1499: ## **Crinecerfont as a Victim**
L1500: Based on in vitro studies, crinecerfont is metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 (fraction metabolized [fm] ~68 to 74%) and to a lesser extent by CYP2B6 (fm~11 to 25%). Crinecerfont is not a substrate for transporters including P-glycoprotein (P-gp), breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), bile salt export pump (BSEP), organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, or OATP1B3. Metabolism studies in vitro identified a single active metabolite, M6, with a similar affinity for the CRF1 receptor compared to the parent drug. However, due to limited systemic exposure (i.e., approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to significantly contribute to the pharmacological activity of crinecerfont.
L1501: ## **Effect of Strong CYP3A Inhibition on Crinecerfont PK**
L1502: Study INT5449 evaluated the effect of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (ketoconazole) on crinecerfont PK in 16 healthy subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 50 mg crinecerfont was administered with a moderate fat breakfast. Following a 22-day washout period, in treatment period 2, ketoconazole 400 mg once daily was administered for 5 days with standardized breakfast, and on Day 6 subjects received ketoconazole 400 mg and 50 mg crinecerfont with a moderate-fat breakfast. Ketoconazole dosing continued from Day 7 to Day 14 of treatment period 2. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours postdose. The study results show that coadministration with ketoconazole increased crinecerfont AUC and Cmax by ~45% and ~25% respectively (Table 94, see details in Section 20.2.15). According to the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guideline *M12 Drug Interaction Studies* (May 2024), “Sensitive index substrates are index drugs that demonstrate an increase in area under the concentration versus time curve (AUC) of greater than or equal to 5-fold with strong index inhibitors of a given metabolic pathway in clinical DDI [drug-drug interaction] studies.” Therefore, crinecerfont is not considered a sensitive CYP3A substrate.
L1503: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1504: In terms of clinical relevance of the DDI, crinecerfont has been studied at daily doses of 300 mg for 28 days, and no major safety concerns were identified. Additionally, in the open-label extension of Trial CAH3003, subjects with CAH who did not have adequate treatment response to crinecerfont were allowed to have a 50% dose increase (e.g., increase from 100 mg bid to 100 mg in the morning and 200 mg in the evening). Therefore, the 45% exposure increase when coadministered with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is not expected to fall outside the safety margin seen in the subjects studied and does not necessitate dose adjustment.

L1509: ## **Effect of Strong CYP3A Induction on Crinecerfont PK**
L1510: Study NBI-74788-1718 investigated the effect of a strong CYP3A4 inducer (rifampin) on crinecerfont PK in 16 healthy subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 100 mg crinecerfont was administered with Ensure Plus. Following a 21-day washout period in treatment period 2, subjects received 600 mg rifampin once daily for 29 days in the fasted state. On Day 9 of period 2, subjects received 100 mg crinecerfont 2 hours after rifampin dosing with Ensure Plus. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours postdose. The study results show that coadministration with rifampin decreased crinecerfont AUC by ~62% and Cmax by ~23% (Table 94).
L1511: From a clinical perspective, coadministration of crinecerfont with a strong CYP3A4 inducer (rifampin) has a significant impact on the exposure of crinecerfont. Based on the magnitude of exposure reduction, a 2-fold dose increase is necessary to maintain crinecerfont exposure at levels high enough to be effective. The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposed labeling language that crinecerfont dosage should be increased 2-fold (e.g., 200 mg bid in adults) in subjects on concomitant strong CYP3A4 inducers.

L1517: ## Effect of Moderate CYP3A Induction on Crinecerfont PK
L1518: The Applicant did not conduct any clinical DDI studies with moderate CYP3A4 inducers. In Trial CAH3003, 17 adult subjects were on dexamethasone with or without other glucocorticoids at the time of enrollment. The Applicant considered dexamethasone as a moderate CYP3A inducer(b) (4)
L1519: The review team did not agree with the Applicant's approach based on the following considerations.
L1520: Despite no observed data to support the dose adjustment for crinecerfont when taken with moderate CYP3A inducers, the review team expects a reduction of less than 50% in crinecerfont exposure due to moderate CYP3A induction, considering that (1) crinecerfont is not a sensitive CYP3A substrate and (2) per the DDI guideline (May 2024), a moderate CYP3A inducer is defined as decreasing exposure of sensitive CYP3A substrates by 50 to 80%. Thus, the review team recommends that crinecerfont dosage needs to be adjusted in patients taking moderate CYP3A4 inducers. For example, the current dosage of 100 mg twice daily with morning and evening meals should be changed to 100 mg with the morning meal and 200 mg with the evening meal. Increasing the crinecerfont dose by 50% will ensure clinical benefit in this patient population.
L1521: ## **Crinecerfont as a Perpetrator**
L1522: ## Effect of Crinecerfont on PK of CYP3A Substrates
L1523: Study INT6752 investigated the effect of crinecerfont on the PK of midazolam (CYP3A4 probe substrate) in 15 healthy subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 2 mg midazolam solution was administered under fasting conditions. Following a 48-hour washout period, crinecerfont 100 mg phase 2 formulation ((b) (4) capsule) was administered once daily with a moderate fat breakfast for 8 days as part of period 2. On Day 8, midazolam was administered 2 hours after crinecerfont. The DDI study shows a 1.23-fold (90% CI: 1.09 to 1.38) increase in midazolam AUC, indicating that crinecerfont is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4 (Table 95, see Section 20.2.17). It should be noted that the maximal proposed dose of crinecerfont is 100 mg twice daily, whereas a 100-mg daily dose was used in the DDI study. Based on PK data from Trial NBI-74788-CAH2001, crinecerfont exposure in this DDI study may be about 50% lower than that under the maximal clinical dose. Nonetheless, a more than 2-fold increase in midazolam exposure (a minimal effect to be classified as a moderate CYP3A inhibitor) is not

L1530: Study INT11387 investigated the effect of crinecerfont on PK of combined oral contraceptives (COCs, nonsensitive CYP3A substrate per FDA guidance for industry *Clinical Drug Interaction Studies With Combined Oral Contraceptives* (June 2023)) containing ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel in 25 healthy subjects. For Study INT6752, the review team concluded that crinecerfont is a weak CYP3A inhibitor at clinically relevant doses. Based on FDA guidance on drug interactions with COC (June 2023), weak CYP3A inhibitors are unlikely to cause a clinically significant increase in COC exposures. Therefore, the review team concludes that crinecerfont at clinically relevant doses is not expected to affect the PK of COCs containing ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel.

L1536: ## Effect of Crinecerfont on PK of Glucocorticoids
L1537: Glucocorticoids, which are the current standard of care for the treatment of CAH and will be coadministered with crinecerfont in the target patient population, are generally not sensitive CYP3A4 substrates. Based on the study results from the midazolam study (sensitive CYP3A4 substrate) and the oral contraceptive study (nonsensitive CYP3A4 substrate), coadministration with crinecerfont is unlikely to have clinically significant impact on glucocorticoid exposure.
L1538: ## Effect of Crinecerfont on Other CYP Enzymes and Transporters
L1539: Crinecerfont is unlikely to induce CYP3A, CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2B6 or inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1 at clinically relevant doses. Crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter (MATE) 1, or MATE2-K.

L1542: ## 14.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of Reproductive Potential
L1543: The Division of General Endocrinology consulted the Division of Pediatrics and Maternal Health (DPMH) for review of the nonclinical and clinical pregnancy and lactation data, and for recommendations on appropriate language for Section 8 (Use in Special Populations) of the prescribing information based on those data. DPMH also commented on the necessity for postmarketing studies to further evaluate the safety of crinecerfont in the setting of pregnancy and lactation.
L1544: Their findings regarding each subsection of Section 8 of the label are discussed below.
L1545: ## Pregnancy
L1546: ## Animal Data
L1547: Distribution studies in animals indicated that crinecerfont crosses the placenta and is detected at low levels in fetuses of pregnant rats and rabbits.
L1548: Crinecerfont administered during the period of organogenesis in pregnant rats did not result in embryotoxicity or fetal structural malformations at approximately 4 times MRHD exposures. A low incidence of malformations (primarily craniofacial defects) was observed in rabbits at clinically relevant exposures. The incidence of findings in rabbit fetuses was low but exceeded concurrent and historical controls and, therefore, a relationship to crinecerfont cannot be excluded. In a pre- and postnatal developmental toxicity study, no developmental toxicity was observed in rats at 4-fold the MRHD based on exposure.
L1549: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1550: ## Human Data
L1551: There were three reported pregnancies during the drug development program. One resulted in a spontaneous abortion, one had an unknown outcome, and one was a normal pregnancy.
L1552: Details of the three pregnancies are as follows:
L1553: - Two pregnancies occurred in the phase 1 study of QT/QTc (corrected QT) evaluations in healthy volunteers, involving single oral doses of 300 mg or 800 mg of crinecerfont, as follows:A 22-year-old female (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) was administered a single dose of crinecerfont 300 mg and a single dose of moxifloxacin. She was confirmed to be pregnant during the study based on urine and serum pregnancy tests. The estimated date of conception was approximately 10 days after receiving the single dose of crinecerfont and approximately 1 month after receiving moxifloxacin. Study treatment was discontinued. The subject was subsequently lost to follow-up and no additional information, including additional laboratory assessments or the outcome of the pregnancy, is known.
- A female of unreported age (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) was reported to be pregnant based on positive urine and serum pregnancy tests; however, ultrasound showed no evidence of pregnancy. The subject subsequently had decreasing beta human chorionic gonadotropin levels, consistent with a spontaneous abortion.
- One subject in Trial CAH3003 had a reported pregnancy as follows:A 32-year-old female (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) was found to be pregnant (approximately 5 to 6 weeks of gestation) during the open-label period and discontinued crinecerfont on the day that the pregnancy was diagnosed. The subject remained in the study until her Month 18 visit. Subsequently, she underwent an uncomplicated C-section and delivered a healthy infant at 38 weeks of gestation.

L1555: ## Animal Data

Fetuses were exposed to crinecerfont in utero and through lactation until weaning. Crinecerfont was secreted in the milk of lactating rats, with a milk-to-plasma ratio of 1.5 to 12.

L1568: - In Subsection 8.1 of the label, include a statement that data related to crinecerfont use during pregnancy are insufficient to inform the risks.
- A postmarketing requirement (PMR) for a descriptive pregnancy safety study (DPSS) is warranted.
- In Subsection 8.2 of the label, include that there are no data regarding the presence of crinecerfont in human milk but that because nonclinical data demonstrated that crinecerfont was excreted in animal milk, the drug is likely be present in human milk.
- Include text in labeling about monitoring infants exposed to crinecerfont through breast milk for signs and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency.
- A PMR for a clinical lactation study to determine the extent to which crinecerfont is present in human milk is warranted.

L1594: ## III. Additional Analyses and Information
L1595: ## 18. Summary of Regulatory History
L1596: Crinecerfont (NBI-74788) is a small molecule, selective antagonist of the corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor. Sanofi (formerly Sanofi-Synthelabo, Inc., and then Sanofi Aventis US Inc.) originally developed NBI-74788 (then known as SSR125543) and initiated its clinical development for the treatment of major depressive disorder in May 2005 under IND [REDACTED] (b) (4) regulated by the Division of Psychiatry Products. Sanofi withdrew the IND [REDACTED] (b) (4). Neurocrine Biosciences, Inc. (Neurocrine) licensed the compound from Sanofi in 2015.
L1597: The IND application 132849 was submitted by the Sponsor, Neurocrine, on December 23, 2016, to investigate crinecerfont (NBI-74788) for the treatment for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) [REDACTED] (b) (4). On March 16, 2017, following review of the initial IND, FDA issued nonhold comments and requests for additional information regarding quality, nonclinical, and clinical topics.
L1598: On April 16, 2018, a preliminary breakthrough therapy designation (BTD) request teleconference was held. FDA determined it was premature to submit a BTD request and the drug/indication did not meet breakthrough criteria at that stage of development. Three reasons were provided for discouraging the Sponsor from submitting a BTD request at this stage of development:
L1599: - CAH is a serious and life-threatening condition because it is associated with adrenal insufficiency; however, the Sponsor's study drug has the potential to decrease androgen levels but does not treat adrenal insufficiency.
- Approved therapies for treatment of CAH exist and are considered standard of care for this disease (e.g., glucocorticoid [GC] and mineralocorticoid replacement drugs).
- There is no evidence to date that the Sponsor's study drug provides a significant clinical benefit over existing therapies. This drug has been shown to decrease levels of a surrogate biomarker, 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), in adults with classic CAH in a phase 1b proof-of-concept study. More clinical evidence is needed to demonstrate effects of this drug on a clinically significant endpoint (for example, reduction in GC requirements that will be associated with reduction in frequency or severity of adverse events related to GC overreplacement, or improvement in symptoms related to CAH).
L1600: On November 7, 2018, the Sponsor requested a Type C written responses only meeting, to address the Division of General Endocrinology's (DGE's) nonclinical comment regarding new excipients in drug formulations used in the IND-opening study and to obtain agreement on the appropriateness of the drug product formulation proposed for use in the long-duration phase 3 clinical studies and in a commercial setting in adult and pediatric subjects. FDA agreed that the amount of medium-chain triglycerides, lauroyl polyoxylglycerides, and [REDACTED] (b) (4) excipients in the proposed formulation present no specific safety concerns for chronic oral use. Also, the Sponsor's proposed excipient propylene glycol dicaprylocaprate [REDACTED] (b) (4) and its daily
L1601: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1602: doses in the formulation appeared to have sufficient scientific nonclinical information available within the publicly available and manufacturer-supplied literature to support safety.
L1603: On March 15, 2019, Orphan Drug designation was granted to crinecerfont for the treatment of classic CAH.
L1604: On April 24, 2019, the Sponsor submitted a Fast Track designation request. They identified CAH as a serious condition and hypothesized that treatment with crinecerfont may potentially decrease the need for supraphysiologic glucocorticoid regimen to suppress hyperandrogenism in patients with CAH. The request was denied due to the limited data provided from the ongoing phase 2 trial, NBI-74788-CAH2001 (hereafter Trial CAH2001), regarding the potential of crinecerfont to provide a clinically meaningful benefit, or to address an unmet medical need in the patients with CAH population, or to address a serious aspect of CAH. The denial letter was issued on June 20, 2019.
L1605: On May 29, 2019, the Sponsor requested a Type C meeting, to discuss and obtain agreement on the nonclinical and clinical development plan to support an NDA for the treatment of CAH. A written response letter was issued, August 12, 2019, to address the Sponsor's questions regarding the proposed product development plans. In brief, DGE communicated agreement that glucocorticoid dose reduction may be clinically beneficial in patients with CAH and that assessment of glucocorticoid dose reduction and control of adrenal steroid hormone levels was an acceptable approach for the planned phase 3 registration study. Also, DGE agreed that the nonclinical program as described in the meeting briefing materials, as well as the number of subjects and duration of exposures in the clinical safety database, were sufficient to support an NDA submission, provided no new safety signals were identified that would require further evaluation.

L1631: ## 19. Pharmacology Toxicology
L1632: ## 19.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application
L1633: Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of CRF1 receptors. Crinecerfont blocks the binding of CRF to CRF1 receptors in the pituitary but not to CRF2 receptors. Studies in the nonclinical program to support crinecerfont clinical studies were conducted with different salt forms of crinecerfont. The primary pharmacology studies were mainly conducted with crinecerfont hydrochloride
L1634: (HCl). The initial pharmacokinetic (PK) and toxicology studies were conducted with the tosylate salt form. Because of the low absorption and a large food effect in clinical studies, different formulations of crinecerfont tosylate salt and free base forms were evaluated in absorption studies. The free base [REDACTED] (b) (4) formulation was selected for later nonclinical and clinical studies (b) (4)
L1635: Nonclinical studies adequately bridged the data from studies conducted with tosylate salt to those conducted with the free base, and both sets of studies contributed to characterizing the toxicity profile of crinecerfont.
L1636: ## 19.1.1. ADME/PK
L1637: Crinecerfont absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) and PK parameters were characterized in a series of in vitro and in vivo studies. In vivo studies were conducted in rat, dog, mouse, rabbit, and monkeys. The nonclinical PK studies are summarized below.
L1638: ## Absorption
L1639: Crinecerfont absorption and pharmacokinetics were evaluated in vitro and in nonclinical species using intravenous (IV) and oral administration of crinecerfont. An in vitro study in colorectal adenocarcinoma (Caco)-2-TC7 cells with [^{14}C]-crinecerfont tosylate showed that crinecerfont membrane permeability was low and that crinecerfont was not a substrate for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporter. Single-dose in vivo PK studies were conducted with tosylate salt and free-base crinecerfont following oral (PO) or IV administration. Bioavailability from oral dosing was 53% in rats, 14% in rabbits, and 19% in dogs for tosylate salt, and 49% in monkey for free base. Absorption was higher for free-base crinecerfont in [REDACTED] (b) (4) formulation and when administered with food. The half-life (t_{1/2}) of crinecerfont following single oral or IV administration was 8 hours in mice, 13 to 24 hours in rat, 8 hours in rabbits, 24 to 90 hours in dogs, and 5 to 13 hours in monkeys. The time to reach maximum observed plasma concentration (T_{max}) following a single oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate ranged from 2 to 6 hours. In general, exposure of crinecerfont increased less than dose-proportionally and approached saturation or plateaued as dose increased. In repeated-dose toxicokinetic (TK) analyses in toxicity studies, no accumulation was observed in rats when crinecerfont was administered as the tosylate salt. Modest accumulation was observed for free base administered as [REDACTED] (b) (4) at 5, 15, and 50 mg/kg/day doses (less than 3-fold accumulation), with a decrease in exposure observed at the high dose after repeat doses. Exposure was not sex-dependent in rats, but exposure was slightly higher in female dogs compared to males (&lt;2-fold).
L1640: ## Distribution
L1641: Crinecerfont distribution was evaluated in vitro and in vivo studies, including by whole-body imaging, tissue distribution and placenta transfer studies. In in vitro binding assays, crinecerfont exhibited high plasma protein binding with \ge 99.9\% bound in mouse, rat, rabbit, and human plasma independent of drug concentration. Distribution to blood cellular components was low, with blood cell-to-plasma ratios of 0.18 in mouse, 0.17 in rat, 0.14 in dog and 0.08 in human. In vivo studies in rat and dog demonstrated that there was no significant binding of crinecerfont to erythrocytes. Crinecerfont was widely distributed in liver, adrenal gland, lung, spleen, myocardium, fat, and the lymphatic system in tissue distribution studies after oral or IV
L1642: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1643: administration. Crinecerfont crossed the placenta and distributed to the fetal liver (at low levels) in pregnant rats and rabbits. Low crinecerfont exposure was observed in brain, skin, and testis. The brain-to-plasma exposure ratio in rat was 0.1 compared to the liver-to-plasma exposure ratio of \ge 8.5.
L1644: ## Metabolism
L1645: The metabolism of crinecerfont was evaluated in vitro using liver microsomes and hepatocytes and in vivo in mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, and monkey. The metabolism of crinecerfont was similar among species, with no unique or disproportionate human metabolites (Figure 29). Crinecerfont was primarily biotransformed by phase 1 metabolism (hydroxylation of the fluorophenyl moiety and N-depropargylation) by cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4, and to a lesser extent by CYP2B6. The most abundant metabolite, M6 (NBI-756179), was formed by hydroxylation of the fluorophenyl moiety and represented 6% of human crinecerfont exposure. M6 bound to CRF1 receptors with nanomolar affinity (K_i=1.14nM), which, coupled with a relatively slow dissociation rate of 0.01 min^{-1}, resulted in a relatively longer receptor residence time (t_{1/2} of ~63 minutes). Due to its low abundance, the contribution of M6 to CRF1 receptor antagonist activity was considered minor. In vitro studies showed crinecerfont exhibited low potential for drug-drug interaction (DDI) based on limited evidence of inhibition or induction of CYP enzymes or drug transporters.

L1649: ## Excretion
L1650: Crinecerfont excretion studies were conducted in mouse, rat, and dog using [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont tosylate. Crinecerfont was mainly excreted through feces in mouse, rat, and dog, indicating clearance mainly through hepatobiliary system. Renal excretion was negligible (&lt;2%). The elimination rate of crinecerfont was slow. The recovery of an orally administered dose of [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont was not complete at 1 week in rats, with about 10% of radioactivity remaining in the tissues in males and 25% in females. In a dog study, 80% of [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont administered orally was recovered at 2 weeks. Crinecerfont was excreted in the milk of rats with a milk-to-plasma ratio of 1.5 to 12.
L1651: ## 19.1.2. Toxicokinetic Data
L1652: The TK data from pivotal toxicology studies are summarized under the respective toxicological study review in Section 19.1.7. TK results from pivotal 6-month rat and 12-month dog studies are presented in Table 97 and Table 98 below. In general, crinecerfont exposure increases with dose but in a less than dose-proportional manner following oral administration of crinecerfont free base both in rats and dogs. In rats, a 25-fold increase in dose resulted in less than a 4-fold increase in exposure, reaching saturation at doses \ge 250 mg/kg/day. No significant accumulation was observed after repeated oral administration of crinecerfont free base in 6-month rat study. In dogs, a 10-fold increase in dose resulted in up to a 2-fold increase in exposure and approached saturation at doses \ge 300 mg/kg/day. Accumulation of up to 2-fold was observed in the 12-month dog study.

L1664: ## 19.1.3. Primary Pharmacology
L1665: Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of CRF1 receptors. Crinecerfont blocks the binding of CRF to CRF1 receptors in the pituitary but not to CRF2 receptors. Data from a series of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies of crinecerfont were provided by the Applicant to demonstrate the pharmacological effects of crinecerfont. Primary pharmacological studies were conducted with crinecerfont HCl. These studies demonstrated that crinecerfont inhibits CRF1 receptors and antagonizes CRF-induced cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) synthesis and ACTH secretion from pituitary, and blocks stress-induced increases in ACTH in rats (Table 99). In the absence of stress or exogenous ACTH stimulation, crinecerfont had no effect on basal ACTH or adrenal hormones, suggesting low potential for adrenal insufficiency based on mechanism of action of crinecerfont. No signs of adrenal insufficiency were observed in pharmacology (or toxicology) studies in vivo.

L1689: ## 19.1.4. Secondary Pharmacology
L1690: The off-target activity of crinecerfont was evaluated by in vitro binding and enzyme activity assays for 10 receptors and 12 enzymes, and by binding assays against more than 100 receptors, transporters, enzymes, and ion channels. Crinecerfont (10\mu\text{M}) inhibited acetylcholinesterase activity (88% inhibition), the sigma-1 receptor (54% inhibition), and the serotonin transporter (half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC_{50}] of 3.0\mu\text{M}). Crinecerfont did not show any effect on contractility of isolated pig vas deferens up to 10\mu\text{M}, indicating lack of notable functional effects on the sigma-1 receptor. The potential off-target effects of crinecerfont on acetylcholinesterase and serotonin transporter were considered negligible when the micromolar affinity of crinecerfont to the nonspecific targets was compared with nanomolar affinity to CRF1 receptors. Therefore, clinically relevant off-target activities of crinecerfont were not identified.
L1691: ## 19.1.5. Safety Pharmacology
L1692: Crinecerfont's effects on cardiovascular, autonomic nervous system, central nervous system (CNS), respiratory, renal, and gastrointestinal (GI) systems were assessed using in vitro and in vivo safety pharmacology studies (Table 100). Crinecerfont tosylate salt was used in safety pharmacology studies. No significant acute effects were observed on neurobehavioral function in rats, cardiovascular function in dogs, respiratory function in guinea pigs, renal function in rats, or gastrointestinal function in rats at clinically relevant doses. Crinecerfont showed no potential for clinical arrhythmia risk based on human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) current (&lt;5% inhibition) or isolated rabbit Purkinje fiber action potential assays at up to 10µM crinecerfont concentrations. Respiratory depression (increased inspiratory, expiratory, and relaxation times, accompanied by airway obstruction indicated by increased pause and enhanced pause) was observed in anesthetized guinea pigs at a 1000 mg/kg oral dose. No effects on respiratory parameters were observed at doses ≤100 mg/kg (0.2-fold maximum recommended human dose [MRHD]). Anesthetized guinea pigs may have been more sensitive to crinecerfont than other species, as all animals had tonal loss in hind paws under sedation. There were no significant effects of crinecerfont on the respiratory system in repeat-dose toxicity studies in mice, rats, and dogs, indicating the respiratory safety risk of crinecerfont is low. Overall, the safety pharmacology data supported crinecerfont clinical investigations and no remarkable acute safety concerns were identified at clinically relevant exposure levels.

L1702: ## 19.1.7. Toxicology
L1703: ## 19.1.7.1. General Toxicology
L1704: The toxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in a series of single- and repeat-dose studies in mice, rats, and dogs. The target organs for crinecerfont were liver (mouse, rat, and dog), thyroid gland (rat and dog), and GI tract (mouse and rat). In early toxicology studies in rats with the tosylate salt, crinecerfont was associated with mortality due to hemorrhage and changes in coagulation parameters (increase in fibrinogen and prolonged prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial thromboplastin time [APTT]), in addition to the findings in liver, thyroid gland, and GI tract. The bleeding adverse effects were not observed in the pivotal nonclinical studies conducted with free-base crinecerfont, the form of crinecerfont proposed for the commercial drug product. The assessment of the pivotal chronic 6-month rat and 12-month dog studies are summarized in Sections 19.1.7.1.1 and 19.1.7.1.3, respectively.
L1705: ## 19.1.7.1.1. 6-Month Oral Toxicity Study in Rats With a 6-Week Recovery Period, Study TXC1269
L1706: ## Key Findings
L1707: The 6-month rat study was conducted with a once-daily oral gavage dose of 0, 50, 250 or 1250 mg/kg crinecerfont free base. No crinecerfont-related mortality or clinical signs were observed. Crinecerfont was associated with partially reversible mild hematological changes (decreased red blood cell parameters and increased lymphocytes at \ge 250 mg/kg/day, at exposure \ge 7-fold MRHD). Marked increases in PT (+52 to 60%) and APTT (+80 to 90%) were noted in
L1708: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
L1709: CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L1710: males at \ge 250 mg/kg/day (total exposure \ge 7-fold MRHD) without any signs of hemorrhage, which were likely associated with changes in liver function.
L1711: Crinecerfont was associated with partially reversible minimal to moderate liver lesions (centrilobular hypertrophy, vacuolation, multinucleated hepatocytes, hepatocyte anisokaryosis, and minimal hepatocyte necrosis) that correlated with liver enlargement and change in clinical chemistry (such as increased \gamma-glutamyl transferase, cholesterol, and decreased triglycerides) in all dose groups (\ge 50 mg/kg/day, 4-fold MRHD). The liver findings were mainly related to the induction of hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes, which was consistent with the finding of the decrease in exposure following repeated dosing in rats.
L1712: Reversible minimal to mild thyroid follicular cell hyperplasia was observed in males at 1250 mg/kg/day (7-fold MRHD) and in females at \ge 50 mg/kg/day (4-fold MRHD) with dose-related increase in incidence and severity, and may be secondary to liver enzyme induction (Wu and Farrelly 2006).
L1713: Crinecerfont was associated with forestomach lesions which included epithelial hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and/or dyskeratosis to erosion, ulceration, and epithelial necrosis. The forestomach lesions were observed in all groups (\ge 50 mg/kg/day, 4-fold MRHD), and in the vehicle control group, with increasing incidence and severity with increasing dose of crinecerfont. One control female found dead on Day 116 had stomach perforations possibly related to the irritant action of the vehicle or to trauma. The lesion in rat forestomach was considered species-specific and may not be clinically relevant based on the absence of a nonglandular stomach in humans and the tolerability of the final clinical oral formulations.
L1714: Crinecerfont exposure saturation was observed in both sexes at doses \ge 250 mg/kg. The NOAEL was not determined (\le 50 mg/kg/day) for this study, and the exposure multiple for this study was \le 4-fold at MRHD. In a complementary 6-month rat study, the NOAEL was 15 mg/kg/day with exposure comparable to the MRHD (see below, Section 19.1.7.1.2).

L1733: ## 19.1.7.1.2. Complementary 6-Month Oral Toxicity Study in Rats With a 6-Week Recovery Period, Study TXC1412
L1734: ## Key Findings
L1735: This study was conducted as a complementary study to the previous 6-month study (TXC1269) to determine the no-observed-effect level or no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) by using lower doses (NOAEL was not established in study TXC1269). In this study, no remarkable treatment-related mortality, clinical signs, change in body weight gain, food consumption or clinical pathology findings were observed. Microscopic findings were limited to reversible mild multinucleated hepatocytes and minimal anisokaryosis (1/15 female) and minimal centrilobular hepatocyte hypertrophy in males at 15 mg/kg/day. These liver findings were not considered adverse effects because of low incidence and minimum to mild severity. Mild to moderate ulceration, epithelial hyperplasia, submucosal edema and/or subacute inflammation of nonglandular stomach were observed in control and treated groups, which were associated with vehicle and incidence was exacerbated by crinecerfont.

L1748: ## 19.1.7.1.3. 12-Month Oral Toxicity Study in Dogs With an 8-Week Recovery Period, Study TXC1204
L1749: ## **Key Findings**
L1750: The 12-month dog study was conducted with once-daily oral gavage doses of 100, 300 or 1000 mg/kg crinecerfont. Crinecerfont caused reversible minimal to moderate liver lesions (centrilobular hypertrophy, eosinophilic droplets, and pigmented hepatocytes) that correlated with liver enlargement and change in clinical chemistry (such as increased alkaline phosphatase and decreased albumin) at \ge 100 mg/kg/day. Mild decreases in red cell parameters and increases in platelets were noted at \ge 100 mg/kg/day. All the findings observed were not considered adverse effects based on their low magnitude, low incidence, reversibility, and/or lack of dose response. The NOAEL for this study was 1000 mg/kg/day. The AUC24 values at the NOAEL were 399,000 ng·hr/mL for males and 804,000 ng·hr/mL for females. The safety margin based on exposure was ~4-fold, which was calculated using the AUC24=399,000 ng·hr/mL (males) at NOAEL and human PK AUC24=88,802 ng·hr/mg.9

L1772: ## 19.1.7.3. Carcinogenicity
L1773: The Applicant evaluated the oncogenic potential of crinecerfont by conducting 2-year rat and 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity studies. Crinecerfont did not increase the incidence of tumors in Tg.rasH2 mice treated for 26 weeks at oral doses of 5, 50, 500 or 1500 mg/kg/day. In the 2-year rat study, crinecerfont increased the incidence of combined thyroid gland follicular cell adenoma and carcinoma in females at 100 mg/kg/day crinecerfont, the highest dose tested (4-fold MRHD). Crinecerfont did not increase the incidence of tumors in rats at 15 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 2 times the MRHD based on AUC. There were no statistically significant crinecerfont-related increases in the incidence of any other tumors. The thyroid gland follicular cell tumors were likely due to continuous stimulation of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) secondary to liver enzyme induction that causes increased clearance of thyroid hormones. This mechanism of inducing thyroid gland follicular cell hyperplasia and subsequent adenoma and carcinoma development is rodent-specific and is not considered relevant to humans (Wu and Farrelly 2006; Bartsch et al. 2018).
L1774: ## 19.1.7.3.1. A 104-Week Oral Oncogenicity Study in Sprague Dawley Rats
L1775: ## Key Findings
L1776: The 2-year rat carcinogenicity study was conducted by administering once-daily oral gavage 0, 5, 15 or 100 mg/kg/day crinecerfont. The incidence of combined thyroid follicular cell adenomas and carcinomas increased significantly (in both trend and pairwise analyses) in female rats at the highest dose tested, 100 mg/kg/day (4-fold MRHD based on AUC). No evidence of increased tumorigenicity was seen in male rats up to approximately 4 times MRHD or in females rats up to approximately 2 times MRHD based on AUC.

Food consumption	No remarkable crinecerfont-related changes in food consumption were observed. The increase in mean food consumption values in both sexes in the positive control group compared with water and vehicle controls correlated with the increased body weight in the positive control group.
Gross pathology	Crinecerfont-related gross findings were limited to liver diffuse tan discoloration (2 males at 500 mg/kg/day and 1 male and female at HD) that correlated with crinecerfont-related hepatocellular vacuolation. The incidence was low and was not considered toxicologically relevant.
Organ weights	Crinecerfont-related dose-dependent increase in liver weight was observed in all dose levels in males (up to 80%) and at ≥50 mg/kg/day females (up to 54%). These changes correlated with hepatocellular vacuolation noted in males at all dose levels and females at ≥500 mg/kg.

L1803: ## 19.1.7.4. Reproductive Toxicology
L1804: ## 19.1.7.4.1. Oral Male and Female Fertility Study in Rats
L1805: ## **Key Findings**
L1806: In a fertility study conducted by daily oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate to mature male and female rats at dose of 0, 150, 300 or 1000 mg/kg/day, no remarkable toxicities on fertility were observed in male and female rats up to the dose of 1000 mg/kg/day (2-fold MRHD based on AUC). However, crinecerfont tosylate was related with deaths or preterminal euthanasia in mid- and high-dose males, which were associated with hemorrhage and changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT and APTT, and low platelet counts). The NOAEL for fertility in males and females was 1000 mg/kg/day which corresponded to exposures 2 times the MRHD. The NOAEL for paternal toxicity was the low dose (150 mg/kg/day).

L1818: ## 19.1.7.4.2. Oral Embryo-Fetal Development in Rat
L1819: ## Key Findings
L1820: An embryo-fetal development study was conducted with daily oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate to pregnant female rats during the period of organogenesis from gestation day (GD) 6 to 17 at 0, 150, 500 or 2000 mg/kg/day. No remarkable toxicological effects on maternal reproductive performance and fetal development were observed up to 2000 mg/kg/day except for a slight decrease in food consumption (up to -14%) in dams in treatment groups. The decrease in food consumption was not associated with decreased body weight gain and was not considered an adverse effect. The NOAEL for rat maternal and developmental toxicity was 2000 mg/kg/day (exposure 4-fold MRHD based on AUC). The plasma exposure of crinecerfont reached near saturation at the low dose of 150 mg/kg/day (AUC24=296,000 ng·hr/mL), which was comparable to exposure at the NOAEL of 2000 mg/kg/day (AUC24=328000 ng·hr/mL).

L1839: ## 19.1.7.4.3. Embryo-Fetal Development Study in the Rabbit (TER0384)
L1840: ## Key Findings
L1841: An embryo-fetal development study was conducted with daily oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate to pregnant female rabbits during the period of organogenesis from GD6 to GD19 at 0, 100, 500, or 1000 mg/kg/day. The plasma exposures of crinecerfont were not dose-dependent between 100 mg/kg/day (low dose) and 1000 mg/kg/day (high dose), with approximately 2-fold exposure variation across doses, and similar mean systemic exposures were observed in the low and high dose groups. Crinecerfont was associated with slightly lower maternal body weight gain in all treatment groups compared to controls, corresponding with a slight reduction in mean fetal body weight in the high dose group (37.5 g versus 40.4 g in control group). There were a few fetuses that exhibited external, visceral, and/or skeletal skull malformations. The skull malformations included microcephaly, microstomia, acephalostomia, misshapen cerebrum and/or cerebellum, among others (details shown in Table 123).
L1842: There were four fetuses (all females) exhibiting one or more of these malformations, three in the 100 mg/kg/day group and one in the 1000 mg/kg/day group (total incidence of 0.8% fetuses and 7% litters across all dose groups combined). The observed malformations are rare and occurred at incidences above the historical range reported by the conducting laboratory. The observed malformations did not correlate with maternal toxicity. The NOAEL for fetal toxicity was not determined due to the increase in incidence of craniofacial malformations. The potential clinical relevance of the observed fetal malformations is discussed in Section 13 and the fetal craniofacial defects will be described in the labeling.

L1867: Abbreviations: EFD, embryo-fetal development
L1868: The craniofacial malformations described are rarely observed in NZ white rabbit based on the conducting laboratory's historical control data. While the craniofacial malformations were only observed in female fetuses, any relationship to sex is unclear. The Applicant concluded that the observed malformations were not related to crinecerfont treatment because of the low incidence and the absence of a dose-related increase in malformations. However, given the apparent exposure saturation and the absence of dose-related increases in plasma drug exposure, we concluded that malformation incidence should not be delineated between different dose groups. To assess the overall incidence rate of craniofacial malformations, we combined all the crinecerfont-treated animals in the study to compare to concurrent and historical control incidence. The overall incidence of craniofacial malformations was 4 fetuses (4/525, 0.8%) from 4 different litters (4/59, 7%). We included the 1000 mg/kg/day fetus with polymalformations in our grouped analysis, but it was likely a unique case because it was significantly smaller than other fetuses (~50% lower body weight than the study mean) and had a different spectrum of malformations than the three 100 mg/kg/day fetuses with craniofacial malformations. Compared to malformations previously observed in the conducting lab, the craniofacial malformations in this crinecerfont study were different. Historical control data from the conducting laboratory included a single craniofacial malformation of anencephaly (1/1098, 0.09% incidence across 11 studies, ranging 0-0.6% in individual studies). Therefore, it was unclear whether crinecerfont was associated with the low incidence of malformations observed in this study. The malformation finding will be described in the labeling.

No dose-specific NOAEL could be established because crinecerfont exposure was saturated across the dose range (C_{max}=8470-15,200 ng/mL, AUC_{24}=138,000-260,000 ng·hr/mL). There was no maternal toxicity identified in the study, up to approximately 3-times the MRHD exposure.
L1870: Potential crinecerfont-related effects on embryo-fetal development observed in the study at 2 to 3 times MRHD exposures included slightly lower mean fetal body weight and a low incidence of craniofacial malformations.

L1896: ## 19.1.7.4.5. Juvenile Toxicity Study in Rats on Postnatal Day 21 Through 49
L1897: ## **Key Findings**
L1898: In a juvenile rat study conducted with oral daily administration of crinecerfont free base on postnatal day (PND) 21 to PND49 at 0, 15, 100 or 1000 mg/kg/day, the toxicological findings in juvenile rats were largely comparable to the findings observed in adult rats (liver and thyroid gland toxicity, and changes in coagulation parameters). Increased liver weight associated with hypertrophy in females (partially reversed), and increased thyroid/parathyroid weight associated with thyroid follicular cell hypertrophy, minimal to moderate increase in coagulation times and decreased triglycerides in males (nonreversible) were observed at ≥100 mg/kg/day. Hepatocellular hypertrophy in liver and follicular cell hypertrophy of thyroid gland were possibly related to enzyme induction and were also seen in adult rats. Slightly delayed sexual maturation in 1000 mg/kg/day males was noted. In females mated with untreated males after a 7-week recovery period, a higher mean number of pre- and postimplantation losses at 1000 mg/kg/day was observed. Crinecerfont was not associated with CNS effects. The NOAEL was the mid dose of 100 mg/kg/day, with exposure of ~2-fold MRHD based on AUC.

L1911: ## 19.1.7.4.6. Juvenile Toxicity Study in Rats on PND4
## Through PND21, With Developmental Observations
## From PND22 Through PND70
L1912: ## Key Findings
L1913: For this study, juvenile rats were administered crinecerfont orally once daily at 0, 15, 100, 300 or 1000 mg/kg/day on PND4 to PND21 followed by a treatment-free period PND22 to PND70 before euthanasia on PND71. The recovery phase animals were euthanized on PND119 to PND121 (males) or GD21 (females).
L1914: The juvenile rats did not tolerate 1000 mg/kg/day dose (13-fold MRHD based on AUC), which resulted in early termination of the dose group. Crinecerfont-related findings in decedent animals included hepatocellular necrosis and vacuolation, increased hepatocellular mitosis, and thyroid gland follicular cell hypertrophy.
L1915: Crinecerfont was associated with significant decreases in body weight gain (up to -30%) and absolute body weights in all doses (\le 0.5-fold MRHD based AUC) during dosing (PND4 to PND21) and during the treatment-free period (PND22 to PND70), but these resolved after PND70. Sexual maturation parameters in both sexes were not affected by decrements in body weights (delayed growth). The decrease in learning and memory on PND24 (shortly after weaning) in 300 mg/kg/day males and females (at exposure 3-fold MRHD based on AUC) and the decrease in femur length in 300 mg/kg/day females on PND71 were considered related to low body weight gains (delayed growth), which were resolved during recovery period PND71 to PND121.
L1916: Decreases in lymphocytes and total white blood cell count at 300 mg/kg/day (at exposure 3-fold MRHD based on AUC) were observed on PND71, which were resolved at the end of recovery period. Increases in triglycerides were noted in 300 mg/kg/day males at the end of recovery period.
L1917: Crinecerfont was associated with thyroid gland follicular cell hypertrophy at all doses. This finding was not resolved at the end of the recovery period in 300 mg/kg/day males and all doses in females.
L1918: The reproductive and developmental NOAEL was 300 mg/kg/day with exposure approximately 4-fold the MRHD.

L1931: The plasma exposures (Cmax and AUC0-t) of crinecerfont increased in a less than dose-proportional manner from 15 to 300/1000 mg/kg/day. A 20-fold increase in dose from 15 to 300 mg/kg led to an increase in about 8-fold Cmax and AUC0-t. The exposures for 1000 mg/kg were for a single dose on PND4. Tmax and Tlast were 4-6 and 24 hours postdose, respectively. Exposures were comparable between males and females, with no accumulation after multiple doses. Exposures for 15 and 300 mg/kg/day doses trended low after multiple doses.
L1932: All metabolites (NBI-756179, NBI-742939 (M4), NBI-1084059 (M9) and 1084060 (M11)) increased in less than dose-proportional manner. Plasma levels of metabolites were &lt;1% for M11, &lt;5% for NBI-756179, &lt;8% for M9, and &lt;14% for M4. M11 accumulation was noted in all doses in both sex at PND21. The other metabolite accumulations were noted at 100 mg/kg/day dose in both sexes.

Mortality	Treatment-related mortalities occurred at 1000 mg/kg/day, which led to early termination of this dose group and the addition of another high-dose group at 300 mg/kg/day. L1940: ## 19.1.7.4.7. Other Toxicology Studies
L1941: ## Comments on Inactive Ingredients
L1942: Crinecerfont is presented in two oral dosage forms: soft gel capsules of 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg (NDA 218808); and 50 mg/mL oral solution (NDA 218820). The two proposed clinical oral dosage formulations contain different excipients. Table 133 and Table 134 show the components and quantities of the crinecerfont 100 mg soft gel capsule and the 50 mg/mL oral solution, respectively. All the excipients, except for the propylene glycol (PG) dicaprylocaprate in soft gel capsules and the orange flavor in 50 mg/mL oral solution, are present in the FDA IID for oral formulations, and thus are not a safety concern. The safety of the two excipients (PG dicaprylocaprate and orange flavor) that are not in the IID database is assessed below.

L1972: ## **NDA 218808—Propylene Glycol Dicaprylocaprate** (b) (4)
L1973: Propylene glycol dicaprylocaprate is used in the manufacturing of crinecerfont soft gel capsules (NDA 218808). The levels of PG dicaprylocaprate in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg soft gel capsule drug products are (b) (4) mg, (b) (4) mg, and (b) (4) mg, respectively. The maximum daily intake of PG dicaprylocaprate in the maximum 400-mg oral human dose (in patients concomitantly using a strong CYP3A4 inducer) is approximately (b) (4) mg. The Applicant used publicly available data and data from the manufacturer of the excipient to support its safe use.
L1974: The Applicant provided publicly available data from GLP-compliant oral acute, subchronic (90-day), and embryo-fetal developmental toxicity studies of PG dicaprylocaprate (Table 135). These studies demonstrated that there were no remarkable PG-dicaprylocaprate-related adverse effects. The maximum tolerated dose for acute toxicity study was &gt;2000 mg/kg/day. The NOAEL for the 90-day rat study was the maximum dose tested (1000 mg/kg/day). No maternal or fetal toxicities were observed in a rat embryo-fetal developmental toxicity study up to 1000 mg/kg/day (the highest dose tested). In addition, safety assessment data generated by a read-across approach for PG esters with similar structure, properties, and functions were used to support the safety of PG dicaprylocaprate. The findings from read-across assessment of PG esters were negative for genotoxicity both in an in vitro and in an in vivo genotoxicity assay and did not show adverse effects on development or reproductive performance in rats (Table 136).

L1984: PG esters also have been used as food additives and nutraceutical products/dietary supplements. The mono- and diesters of propylene glycol are permitted as direct and secondary food additives [21 CFR 172.856, 21 CFR 173.340]. The estimated human acceptable daily intake of PG esters of fatty acids (determined by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives) is 25 mg/kg/day in terms of PG (Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives 1974), equivalent to ~80 mg/kg/day PG esters (EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings et al. 2018).
L1985: Since the maximum daily dose of PG dicaprylocaprate in the drug product (mg, mg/kg/day) is lower than human recommended limit of 25 mg/kg/day in food additives and no adverse effects were observed in toxicological studies (NOAEL of 1000 mg/kg/day in rats, equivalent to multiple ~10-fold human exposure), the amount of PG dicaprylocaprate in crinecerfont soft gel capsule is not a safety concern for the target patient population of ≥4 years of age.
L1986: ## NDA 218820—Orange Flavor
L1987: Orange Flavor is a noncompendial excipient used in the manufacturing of crinecerfont oral solution 50 mg/mL drug product (NDA 218820). The maximum daily intake of orange flavor is mg in a 400-mg dose of crinecerfont.

L2010: ## Immunotoxicity
L2011: The potential immunotoxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated by oral dosing of rats at 0, 15, 50 or 250 mg/kg/day for 28 days. Animals were immunized with keyhole limpet hemocyanin on Days 15 and 24 to assess the primary and secondary immune responses. Crinecerfont was associated with slight to moderate increase in lymphocytes, slight increase in B-cell count and slight increases in absolute CD3/CD4 T-cell count in females, and a slight decrease in T-cell-dependent antibody response in males. The changes in leukocytic parameters and lymphocyte subpopulation and T-cell-dependent antibody responses were small in magnitude and occurred in one sex (males) and showed no remarkable evidence of immunotoxicity in rats. Cyclophosphamide (positive control) induced marked immunotoxic effects, indicating the sensitivity of the assay.
L2012: ## Phototoxicity
L2013: A potential risk for phototoxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in vitro using 3T3 cells at crinecerfont concentrations up to 20 \mug/mL. No cytotoxicity was observed with or without ultraviolet A irradiation, indicating no phototoxic potential of crinecerfont. Chlorpromazine (positive control) induced a positive phototoxic effect, indicating the sensitivity of the assay.
L2014: ## Abuse Liability
L2015: Crinecerfont acts by inhibiting ACTH release from anterior pituitary, which is outside the blood-brain barrier. Tissue distribution studies following IV or PO administration in rats showed crinecerfont brain:plasma ratios of 0.1. The ex vivo binding studies following PO or IV dosing showed that crinecerfont was bound to CRF1 receptors both in pituitary and brain, with higher
L2016: percentage of CRF1 receptor occupancy in pituitary at early timepoints (0.5 to 1 hour postdose) than in brain and with similar levels of occupancy in later timepoints (2 to 24 hours postdose). Crinecerfont was not associated with clinical signs related to CNS effects in single- or repeat-dose toxicity studies in mice, rats, rabbits, and dogs dosed up to maximum tolerated doses. There was no evidence of a withdrawal syndrome during recovery periods of chronic toxicology studies in rats or dogs. Although the binding and tissue distribution studies were indicative of the potential for CNS effects, the series of single- and repeat-dose studies in multiple species indicated crinecerfont risk for potential for physical dependency is low.

L2021: ## 20.1.1. Plasma Protein Binding in Rat, Mouse, Rabbit, Dog, and Human Plasma, Study LPR0879
L2022: The objective of this study was to assess plasma protein binding of crinecerfont tosylate in mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, and human plasma. Plasma samples from various species were spiked with [^{14}C]-crinecerfont tosylate at 50, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, and 30000 ng/mL and allowed to equilibrate for 1 hour. Specific binding of crinecerfont tosylate at 500 and 5000 ng/mL to human serum albumin and human serum \alpha1-acid glycoprotein was also determined. All studies were done in triplicate and radioactivity was determined by liquid scintillation counting. Results indicate that plasma protein binding was \ge 99.9\% at concentrations above 50 ng/mL in all species evaluated. The mean percentage of binding of [^{14}C]-crinecerfont tosylate to human serum albumin and \alpha1-acid glycoprotein for both concentrations tested was &gt;99.9\% and 96.6%, respectively. Thus, the in vitro studies indicate that crinecerfont is highly plasma protein bound and specifically binds albumin and \alpha1-acid glycoprotein.11

L2028: ## 20.1.3. In Vitro Hepatic Clearance From Rat, Rabbit, Dog, and Human Hepatocytes, Study MIV0370
L2029: The objective of this study was to determine metabolic clearance of crinecerfont free base from fresh hepatocyte cultures obtained from rat, rabbit, dog, and humans. Crinecerfont free base was incubated for 24 hours at 1\mu\text{M} in animal hepatocytes and 0.1 and 1\mu\text{M} in human hepatocytes. The \text{CL}_{\text{int}} at 0.1\mu\text{M} in human hepatocytes was 0.029\text{ mL/hr}/10^6\text{ cells}. Results indicate that the human hepatocytes were not saturable over the concentrations tested, and the \text{CL}_{\text{int}} from the hepatocytes of all the species tested was low and not concentration-dependent in human hepatocytes.13
L2030: ## 20.1.4. In Vitro Metabolism in Mouse, Rat, Guinea Pig, Rabbit, Dog, Monkey, and Human Liver Microsomes, Study MIV0341
L2031: The objective of this study was to characterize the in vitro metabolism of [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont in mouse, rat, guinea pig, dog, monkey, and human liver microsomes. [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont tosylate at 5\mu\text{M} and 25\mu\text{M} was incubated up to 60 minutes in microsomes. All studies were done in triplicate and metabolite profiles were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography with an online radio-detection and metabolite structures were elucidated by LC-MS/MS. In vitro metabolism of [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont tosylate was characterized at 5\mu\text{M} (9.25 kBq/mL; 0.25\ \mu\text{Ci/mL}), while the samples at 25\mu\text{M} (18.5 kBq/mL; 0.50\ \mu\text{Ci/mL}) were used for metabolite elucidation. Crinecerfont metabolism percentages were 5% in human, 12% in mouse, 14% in dog, 17% in rabbit, 26% in monkey, 56% in rat, and 61% in guinea pig. Excluding the rat and the guinea pig, metabolism of crinecerfont was slow. The rank order of liver metabolism in microsomes, from slowest to fastest, shows the following order: human &lt; mouse \approx dog \approx rabbit &lt; monkey &lt;&lt; rat \approx guinea pig. The primary metabolic pathways in humans were hydroxylation of the fluorophenyl moiety (M6) and N-dealkylation of the propargyl moiety (M4). Metabolites M6 and M4 constituted 4% and 3% of recovered drug material, respectively. Metabolites M6 and M4 were present in all the species tested.14

L2035: ## 20.1.5. In Vitro Metabolic Profile in Rabbit, Dog and Human Fresh Hepatocytes, Study MIV0358
L2036: The objective of this study was to assess the in vitro metabolism of [^{14}\text{C}]-crinecerfont in different animal species (rat, rabbit, dog) and human hepatocytes. Crinecerfont was assessed at 5\mu\text{M} and 25\mu\text{M} in hepatocytes for 24 hours at 37^\circ\text{C}. Samples were assessed by high-performance liquid chromatography with an online radioactivity detector. Metabolites were elucidated using LC/MS. Crinecerfont was stable, with unchanged crinecerfont accounting for 82% of the recover drug-related material. The major metabolic pathways and metabolites identified from three human donors were named HH followed by number. These included hydroxylation on methyl of fluorophenyl moiety (HH7; M6 from study MIV0341), N-depropargylation (HH8) followed by hydroxylation (HH6; M4 from study MIV0341) and/or glucuronidation (HH3), hydroxylation on methyl-cyclopropane moiety followed by glucuronidation (HH5), and O-demethylation followed by glucuronidation (HH4) or followed by both hydroxylation and glucuronidation (HH2). Metabolites HH7, HH8, HH3, HH5, and HH4 were found in all the species tested. Metabolite HH6 was not detected in rabbits, metabolite HH4 was not detected in rats, and metabolite HH2 was not detected in dog. No interindividual variability was detected in the three tested human donors.15
L2037: ## 20.1.6. In Vitro Metabolism in Human Liver Microsomes and Hepatocytes, Study MIH0179
L2038: The objective of this study was to assess the role of CYP450 enzymes on the metabolism of crinecerfont metabolism in human microsomes or from insect cells transfected with human CYP cDNA (SupersomesTM) or cryopreserved human hepatocytes. In human microsomes, crinecerfont (0.1 and 1\mu\text{M}) was incubated with or without a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)-generating system for up to 60 min. In Supersomes, crinecerfont (0.1 and 1\mu\text{M}) was incubated with or without an NADPH-generating system for 30 min. In human hepatocytes, crinecerfont (0.1 and 1\mu\text{M}) was incubated with or without selective inhibitors of CYP2D6 (quinidine) or CYP3A (ketoconazole) for up to 6 hours. In human hepatocytes, bufuralol and midazolam metabolism were used as positive controls to confirm CYP2D6 and CYP3A activity. All samples were quantified using LC-MS/MS. In human liver microsomes, crinecerfont did not exhibit NADPH-dependent metabolism at 0.1 and 1\mu\text{M}. In Supersomes, crinecerfont exhibited metabolism via CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C19 at both 0.1 and 1\mu\text{M} concentrations. Additionally, crinecerfont at 0.1\mu\text{M} concentration in Supersomes exhibited metabolism (to a lesser extent) by CYP2A6, and flavin-containing monooxygenases 1 and 2. In human hepatocytes, metabolism of crinecerfont was not inhibited by either quinidine (selective for CYP2D6) or ketoconazole (selective for CYP3A). Per the Applicant, the lack of metabolism by CYP2D6 and CYP3A is possibly because of the insolubility of crinecerfont in the heat-inactivated hepatocyte studies, given that the positive controls established activity for both enzyme isoforms. The Applicant concluded further investigation was necessary to determine the in vitro metabolism of crinecerfont.16

L2041: ## 20.1.7. In Vitro Clearance and Fraction Metabolized by CYP3A in Human Hepatocytes Using Recombinant Human Enzymes, Study MIH0659

L2060: ## 20.1.12. CYP2C8 Time-Dependent Inhibition in Human Liver Microsomes, Study XT195084

L2069: ## 20.1.15. Permeability Assessment in Caco-2-TC7 Cells Expressing P-gp, Study AIV0071
L2070: The objective of this study was to assess the apparent permeability coefficient (P_{app}) of crinecerfont in Caco-2-TC7 cells and evaluate the role of P-gp in the absorption of crinecerfont. Caco-2-TC7 cells were seeded in 12-well plates, incubated at 37°C with 10% CO2 and 95% relative humidity under a continuous gentle orbital agitation. The transport of [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate from apical to basal chamber was tested at 1\muM (0.046 \mu Ci/mL), 5\muM (0.23 \mu Ci/mL) and 20\muM (0.92 \mu Ci/mL) in the absence and in the presence of cells. Incubation time was 2 hours and at the end of the incubation time, samples were withdrawn from the apical and basolateral side and radioactivity was determined by liquid scintillation counting to determine P_{app}. Bidirectional transport (apical to basolateral and basolateral to apical) of 1, 5, and 20\muM [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate across Caco-2-TC7 monolayers was performed to determine the role of P-gp in crinecerfont absorption. Controls for the P_{app} studies included [3H]-mannitol and high [14C]-testosterone, and the positive control for P-gp studies was [3H]-vinblastine. All studies were done in triplicate. The P_{app} of crinecerfont was 2.2 \times 10^{-7} cm/s at 20\muM and was similar to the low-permeability compound [3H]-mannitol, indicating the crinecerfont has a low permeability. Results for the P-gp studies indicate that the efflux ratio of crinecerfont was 0.9 at 20 \muM and it is not considered a substrate for P-gp.25
