L2074: ## 20.1.16. Crinecerfont Transporter Substrate Potential for BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, and OATP1B3, Study XT198097
L2075: The objective of this study was to assess the potential of crinecerfont (0.2, 1, 5, and 10\muM) to be a substrate of transporters breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), bile salt export pump (BSEP), organic anion transport polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, and OATP1B3. Substrate potential was defined as uptake or efflux ratio \ge 2 that is reduced &gt;50% in the presence of an inhibitor.
L2076: Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for BCRP was assessed using bidirectional permeability of in Madin-Darby canine kidney type II (MDCKII) cells with and without inhibitors (Ko143 and lopinavir). Samples were drawn from the receiver chamber over 120 minutes and concentrations were assessed by LC-MS/MS. In BCRP-expressing cells, the crinecerfont uptake could not be measured, due to poor permeability across these cells. Thus, crinecerfont potential as a substrate for BCRP could not be evaluated.
L2077: Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for BSEP was assessed by determining accumulation of crinecerfont in transporter-expressing vesicles with and without inhibitors (cyclosporine and glyburide) and with either ATP or AMP (negative control). At 1, 3, and 10 minutes crinecerfont accumulation in vesicles was assessed by LC-MS/MS. In BSEP vesicles, the crinecerfont uptake ratio was &lt;2 compared to control at both 5 and 10 \muM concentrations, thus indicating that crinecerfont is not a substrate for BSEP.
L2078: Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 was assessed by determining accumulation of crinecerfont in transporter-expressing human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells with and without inhibitors (rifampin and cyclosporine). At 1, 3, and 10 minutes crinecerfont accumulation in vesicles was assessed by LC-MS/MS. In OATP1B3 cells, the crinecerfont uptake ratio was &lt;2 compared to control at both 5 and 10 \muM concentrations, thus indicating that crinecerfont is not a substrate for OATP1B3. In OATP1B1 cells, the crinecerfont uptake ratio was &gt;2 (range: 1.36 to 3.70). However, crinecerfont uptake was decreased by &lt;50% in the presence of inhibitors of OATP1B1. Thus, overall, crinecerfont is not a substrate of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3.26
L2079: ## 20.1.17. P-gp Inhibition in Caco-2 Cells Expressing P-gp, Study AIV0107
L2080: The objective of this study was to assess if crinecerfont can inhibit P-gp transport of [^3H]-vinblastine in Caco-2-TC7 cells. Basal-to-apical transport and apical-to-basal transport of 5\muM [^3H]-vinblastine in the absence (control) and in the presence of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30 and 100\muM crinecerfont was assessed over a 2-hour incubation period. Crinecerfont was added to both the apical and basal chambers. Verapamil (200\muM) was used as the positive control for P-gp inhibition. Radioactivity in the samples was quantified by liquid scintillation. At 100\muM crinecerfont precipitated and P-gp inhibition could not be quantified at this concentration. At
L2081: 26 Source: Report XT198097
L2082: crinecerfont concentrations up to 30\mu\text{M}, crinecerfont did not inhibit the net efflux of [^3\text{H}]-vinblastine indicating the crinecerfont is not a P-gp inhibitor at the concentrations tested.27
L2083: ## 20.1.18. Crinecerfont Inhibition Potential for Transporters P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2-K, Study XT188068
L2084: The objective of this study was to assess the potential of crinecerfont (10\mu\text{M}) to inhibit transporters P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter (MATE) 1, and MATE2-K.
L2085: P-gp inhibition was evaluated in Caco-2 cells and in MDCKII cells. Digoxin (10\mu\text{M}) was used as substrate for P-gp. The bidirectional permeability of the digoxin was assessed and quantified by LC-MS/MS. At 10\mu\text{M} crinecerfont, digoxin efflux ratio in Caco-2 cells decreased from 16.3 to 10.6, indicating a 37% inhibition in P-gp transport. At 10\mu\text{M} crinecerfont, digoxin efflux ratio in MDCKII-P-gp cells was not affected, indicating that in this system crinecerfont does not inhibit P-gp transport.
L2086: BCRP inhibition was evaluated in MDCKII cells. Prazosin (1\mu\text{M}) was used as substrate for BCRP. The bidirectional permeability of the prazosin was assessed and quantified by LC-MS/MS. At 10\mu\text{M} crinecerfont, the corrected prazosin efflux ratio in MDCKII-BCRP was not affected, indicating that crinecerfont does not inhibit BCRP.
L2087: Crinecerfont potential as an inhibitor of BSEP was assessed by determining accumulation of [^3\text{H}]-taurocholic acid (0.4\mu\text{M}) by LC-MS/MS in transporter-expressing vesicles. At 10\mu\text{M} crinecerfont, the ATP-dependent uptake of [^3\text{H}]-taurocholic acid (0.4\mu\text{M}) in BSEP vesicles did not decrease, indicating that crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of BSEP.
L2088: Crinecerfont potential as an inhibitor of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2-K was assessed in HEK293 cells. OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MATE1, MATE2-K, and control cells were incubated with butyric acid (10\text{mM}) for 24 hours prior to the experiment to induce transporter gene expression. Crinecerfont 10\mu\text{M}, positive control, or negative control were preincubated for 15 minutes or 30 minutes before adding the probe substrate and incubating for 1 to 5 minutes. Probe substrates used for OATP1B1/B3, OAT 1, OAT 3, OCT2/MATE1/MATE2-K were [^3\text{H}]-Estradiol- 17\beta-glucuronide (50\text{nM}), [^3\text{H}]-p-aminohippurate (1\mu\text{M}), [^3\text{H}]-estrone-3-sulfate (50\text{nM}), and [^{14}\text{C}]-metformin (10\mu\text{M}), respectively. Positive controls used in this study were rifampin (10\mu\text{M}) and cyclosporine (1\mu\text{M}) for OATP1B1/B3; probenecid (100\mu\text{M}) and novobiocin (300\mu\text{M}) for OAT 1; probenecid (100\mu\text{M}) and ibuprofen (100\mu\text{M}) for OAT 3; quinidine (300\mu\text{M}) and cimetidine (2500\mu\text{M}) for OCT2; cimetidine (20\mu\text{M}) and pyrimethamine (0.5\mu\text{M}) for MATE1; and cimetidine (300\mu\text{M}) and pyrimethamine (3\mu\text{M}) for MATE2-K. Samples were quantified by liquid scintillation.

L2093: ## 20.2. In Vivo Studies
L2094: ## 20.2.1. Single Ascending Dose Study of Crinecerfont Between 20 mg to 800 mg, Study TDU10479
L2095: ## Study Design
L2096: This is a phase 1 single oral ascending dose, safety, tolerability, and PK study of crinecerfont in healthy young male subjects. The primary objectives of this study were to assess safety and tolerability, and PK of single ascending doses of crinecerfont under fasted conditions or 30 minutes post moderate-fat breakfast. Subjects (n=6 per group) received oral doses of 20, 50, 100, 200, 400 or 800 mg crinecerfont or placebo and PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. A total of 64 subjects were randomized with 48 subjects in the crinecerfont groups. Dropouts included three from the placebo group, one each from the 50 mg fasted and fed groups, and two each from the 100 mg fed and 800 mg fed groups primarily due to personal reasons. Crinecerfont PK parameters were calculated and 90% confidence intervals (CIs) for the geometric mean of fed versus fasted ratio for Cmax, AUC, and AUC0-tlast were provided for each dose level. The food effect was determined at the 20 mg and 50 mg dose levels under fed and fasted conditions. Dose proportionality was assessed by regression analysis under fed conditions for Cmax, AUC0-tlast, and AUC.
L2097: 28 Source: Report XT188068
L2098: ## **Results**
L2099: The plasma time profile and PK parameters are presented in Figure 34 and Table 138, respectively. The median time to reach maximum observed plasma concentration (T_{max}) value was between 3 and 6 hours after a single dose of the drug between 20 to 800 mg. The apparent terminal elimination half-life was observed with mean values ranging from 188 to 464 hours (7.83 to 19.3 days) in fed condition.

L2117: ## **20.2.2. Crinecerfont Capsule Dose Linearity 20 mg to 200 mg, Study TDR10671**
L2118: ## **Study Design**
L2119: This is a phase 1, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the tolerability and pharmacokinetics of 14-day repeated ascending oral doses of crinecerfont in 48 healthy young male subjects. The primary objectives of this study were to assess the tolerability, safety, and pharmacokinetics after repeated oral ascending doses of crinecerfont. Crinecerfont was administered at 20, 50, 100, and 200 mg under fed-conditions (moderate-fat breakfast) every day for 14 days. A total of 48 subjects were enrolled, with 32 subjects in the treatment group (all subjects in the treatment group completed the study). Dropouts included 4 in the placebo group. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. PK parameters were calculated from plasma concentrations of crinecerfont and time to steady state, dose proportionality, and accumulation ratio were calculated.

L2166: Abbreviations: AUC, area under the concentration-time curve; CSR, clinical study report; LOD, limit of detection; M(X), metabolite (X = 4, 6, 7, 9, 11); nd, below the LOD; SSR125543, crinecerfont
L2167: ## Conclusions
L2168: - Following a single dose of 100 mg crinecerfont, with 2.59 MBq (70 µCi) [14C]-crinecerfont, only 49.4% of the administered dose was recovered.
- The total mean amount of radioactivity recovered in the feces over 37 days was 47.3% of the administered dose. Approximately 2.7% of the parent compound was recovered in the feces indicating that the parent compound is extensively metabolized.
- The total amount of radioactivity recovered in the urine over 37 days was &lt;2% of the administered dose.
- An abundant metabolite, M6, constituting 14.4% of the parent AUC was identified. All other metabolites represented &lt;6% of the parent compound.
- The M6 metabolite has a high affinity for CRF1 with Ki of 1.14nM, similar to crinecerfont affinity (0.6 to 3.99nM). However, in vivo, due to its limited exposure at steady state in humans (approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to significantly contribute to the clinical CRF1 inhibition profile.

L2190: ## 20.2.5. Hepatic Impairment Study, Study NBI-74788-1717
L2191: ## Study Design
L2192: This is a phase 1, single-dose, open-label study designed to assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont and its metabolites in subjects with mild, moderate, or severe stable chronic hepatic impairment relative to subjects with normal hepatic function. The primary objective of this study was to assess the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont (NBI-74788) and its metabolite (NBI-7456179; M6) in subjects with normal, mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment. Hepatic impairment was defined using the Child-Pugh scale. A total of 25 adult subjects between the ages of 18–75 years were enrolled. The normal, mild, and moderate groups had six subjects each while the severe hepatic impairment group had seven subjects. The group
L2193: of subjects with normal hepatic function were similar in age (\pm 5 years), sex, race, and weight (\pm 10\%) to the subjects with hepatic impairment. An overnight fast of 10 hours was followed by the administration of two 50 mg crinecerfont capsules with 237 mL of Ensure Plus and 120 mL of water. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. GMRs with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC_{0-\infty}, AUC_{0-t_{last}}, and C_{max} in the mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment groups to the reference normal group. All subjects completed the study.
L2194: ## Results
L2195: The mean plasma crinecerfont concentrations versus time in subjects with normal, mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment are presented in Figure 37. The mean apparent terminal half-life (\pm standard deviation [SD]) of crinecerfont in normal mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment were 136 h (96.0), 87.2 h (71.3), 119 h (34.9), and 221 h (87.1), respectively. In subjects with severe hepatic impairment, apparent terminal half-life did increase, however, the increase is not significant due to the large standard deviation associated with this parameter.
L2196: The effective half-life of crinecerfont is ~14 hours and a PK sampling time of 504 hours is appropriate as it covers more than five half-lives. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for AUC_{0-t_{last}}, AUC_{0-\infty}, and C_{max} for 100 mg crinecerfont and its metabolite M6 in the different hepatic impairment groups are presented in Table 146.

L2205: ## Conclusions
L2206: - Overall, the mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment groups had lower AUC_{0-t_{last}}, AUC_{0-\infty}, and C_{max} compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The magnitude of impact on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics seems to be comparable between mild and severe hepatic impairment. The mechanism of decreased crinecerfont exposures due to hepatic impairment is not known. However, the 90% CI values for the GMRs all included unity indicating that while the PK exposure is lower it does not appear to be clinically significant.
- There were no deaths, severe adverse events (AEs), or discontinuations from the study due to AEs reported in this study. No safety concerns related to routine clinical laboratory results, vital signs, or electrocardiogram results were identified.
L2207: Metabolite M6 has a similar affinity for the CRF1 compared to the parent drug. However, due to limited systemic exposure (i.e., approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to significantly contribute to the pharmacological activity of crinecerfont.
L2208: ## 20.2.6. Extrinsic Factors: Rifampin Study, Study NBI-74788-1718
L2209: ## Study Design
L2210: This is a phase 1, open-label, one-sequence crossover study to assess the effect of rifampin on the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont (NBI-74788) in healthy subjects. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate and compare the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont when crinecerfont is administered alone and concomitantly with rifampin. A total of 16 adult subjects between the ages of 18–55 years were enrolled. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 100 mg crinecerfont was administered with 237 mL Ensure Plus following a 10 hour overnight fast. Following a 21-day washout period, treatment period 2 commenced with subjects receiving 600 mg rifampin once daily for 29 days in the fasted state. On Day 9 of period two subjects received crinecerfont 2 hours after rifampin dosing with 237 mL Ensure Plus. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont and its major metabolite NBI-756169. GMRs with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC_{0-t_{last}}, AUC_{0-\infty}, and C_{max} for crinecerfont with rifampin versus reference (crinecerfont alone). All subjects completed the study.

L2235: ## 20.2.8. Extrinsic Factors: Midazolam Study, Study INT6752
L2236: ## Study Design
L2237: This is a phase 1, open-label, two-treatment, single-sequence PK interaction study of 8-day repeated oral 100 mg doses of crinecerfont on single oral doses of midazolam in 15 healthy male subjects.
L2238: The primary objective of this study is to assess the impact of 8-day repeated oral 100 mg doses of crinecerfont on the pharmacokinetics of midazolam, as a probe substrate for CYP3A activity, and the reversibility of the inhibition of CYP3A activity by crinecerfont 1 and 2 weeks after crinecerfont last administration.
L2239: In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 2 mg midazolam solution was administered under fasting conditions. Following a 48-hour washout period, crinecerfont 100 mg was administered daily with a moderate fat breakfast for 8 days as part of period 2. On Day 8, 15, and 22 of period 2, midazolam 2 mg oral solution was administered. On Day 8 midazolam was administered 2 hours after crinecerfont. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont. Midazolam plasma concentrations were obtained for 24 hours postadministration on Day 1 of Period 1, and Days 8, 15, and 22 of Period 2. GMRs with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC_{0-\infty}, AUC_{0-t_{last}}, and C_{max} for midazolam with or post crinecerfont 100 mg dosing versus reference (midazolam alone). All subjects completed the study.

L2248: ## Conclusions
L2249: - Coadministration of midazolam with steady-state concentrations of crinecerfont (8 days) results in a 1.23-fold increase in midazolam AUC, indicating that crinecerfont is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4.
- Midazolam AUC and C_{max} levels at 7 days post crinecerfont administration were 1.04- and 1.02-fold, respectively, compared to midazolam treatment alone, thus, indicating reversibility of the CYP3A4 inhibition by crinecerfont.
- While this study was conducted with an earlier formulation of crinecerfont, it is anticipated that the commercial formulation will have a similar impact on the CYP3A enzyme. This is because both formulations are (b) (4) The only difference (b) (4) in each phase of the study.
- The dose of crinecerfont tested was 100 mg once daily for 8 days prior to midazolam administration. This is not the maximum dose studied in the pivotal phase 3 clinical trial in adults (Trial CAH3003), which was 100 mg twice daily. The study results can still assess the impact of crinecerfont inhibition of CYP3A4. Based on PK data from Trial NBI-74788-CAH2001, crinecerfont exposure in this DDI study may be about 50% lower than that under the maximal clinical dose. Nonetheless, a more than 2-fold increase in midazolam exposure (a minimal effect to be classified as a moderate CYP3A inhibitor) is not expected even if the DDI study had been conducted with 100 mg bid. Overall, crinecerfont is expected to be a weak CYP3A inhibitor at the maximal proposed dose of 100 mg twice daily.
L2250: ## 20.2.9. Extrinsic Factors: Oral Contraceptive Steroids Study, Study INT11387

Based on FDA Guidance on drug interactions with combined oral contraceptives (COCs) (June 2023), weak CYP3A inhibitors are unlikely to have a clinically significant increase in COC exposures.
L2268: ## 20.2.10. QTc Study, Study NBI-74788-1719
L2269: ## Study Design
L2270: This is a phase 1 single-dose, randomized, placebo- and active-controlled, four-way, cross-over study that evaluated the effect of crinecerfont on the QT/QTc (corrected QT) interval in adult healthy subjects. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the effect of a single therapeutic (300 mg) and supratherapeutic (800 mg) dose of crinecerfont on the heart rate- QTc. A total of 48 adult subjects were enrolled and 41 completed the study. Each subject received single doses of crinecerfont 300 mg, crinecerfont 800 mg, placebo, or moxifloxacin 400 mg (positive control).
L2271: All treatments were administered with 240 mL water after 30 minutes following the start of a high-fat, high-calorie breakfast. There was a washout period of 21 days between each treatment group. Electrocardiogram samples were collected at specified times for 24 hours postdose. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont and placebo groups, while samples were collected at prespecified times for 24 hours for the moxifloxacin group. Crinecerfont and four of its metabolites (NBI-756179, M4, M9, and M11) were analyzed by LC-MS/MS. GMRs were calculated at 300 mg and 800 mg for crinecerfont and its major metabolite NBI-756179.
L2272: ## Results
L2273: ## PK Analysis
L2274: The 800 mg dose of crinecerfont had 2.4-fold high GMRs for AUC_{0-\text{last}} and AUC_{0-\infty} compared to the 300 mg dose. The 800 mg dose of crinecerfont had a 2.3-fold higher value for C_{\text{max}} compared to the 300 mg dose. A similar trend was noted with the major metabolite NBI-756179.
L2275: ## QTc Analysis
L2276: The mean-placebo-corrected change in baseline in QT interval corrected for heart rate using Fridericia's correction (\Delta\Delta\text{QTcF}) and 90% CI following 300 mg crinecerfont, 800 mg

## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L2278: crinecerfont, and 400 mg moxifloxacin are presented in Figure 42. At a 1 hour the \Delta\Delta\text{QTc} for the 800 mg crinecerfont dose was +1.61 msec. At 2 hours post-300 mg and 800 mg doses of crinecerfont until 24 hours postdose, the \Delta\Delta\text{QTc} values were negative. For further details please see the review by the QTc-IRT (interdisciplinary review team) dated August 21, 2024.29

L2281: ## **Conclusions**
L2282: Per review from the Interdisciplinary Review Team for Cardiac Safety Studies:30
L2283: - Crinecerfont did not prolong the QTc interval in this thorough QT study. Instead, crinecerfont shortened the QTc interval in a dose-dependent manner. The highest dose in the thorough QT study provides 3.3-fold the high clinical C_{\text{max}}.
- The small magnitude of QTc shortening at high clinical exposure (-5 msec) in the thorough QT study is unlikely to be clinically important.

L2286: ## 20.2.11. Pilot Ensure Plus Study, Study NBI-74788-1601
L2287: ## Study Design
L2288: This is a phase 1, randomized, open-label, two-period crossover study to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics, and safety of crinecerfont (NBI-74788) in healthy adult subjects. A total of 16 subjects were randomized to receive NBI-74788 (crinecerfont) under fasted or fed conditions. Following a washout period of 21 days, subjects crossed over into the alternate group. Subjects in the fasted group, fasted overnight for at least 10 hours and continued to fast an additional 4 hours postdrug administration. Subjects in the fed group also fasted for at least 10 hours overnight and had liquid supplement breakfast with the study drug. Study intervention was an oral 50 mg crinecerfont formulation that was consumed with 240 mL water (fasted state) or Ensure Plus (350 calories; fed state). PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours and GMRs with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC_{0-\infty}, AUC_{0-\text{tlast}}, and C_{\text{max}} under fed and fasted conditions.

L2386: ## Conclusions
L2387: - Bioequivalence was demonstrated between the phase 3 capsule (hard gel) and the commercial capsule, at the 100 mg dose level, as the 90% CI values for GMR for AUC and Cmax were within the specified criteria of 0.8–1.25.
- Following a high-fat, high-calorie meal, crinecerfont 100 mg oral soft gel capsule dose exposure increased between 3 to 4-fold compared to the same dose under fasted conditions.
L2388: ## **20.2.17. Phase 2 Dose-Finding Study, Trial NBI-74788-CAH2001**
L2389: ## Study Design
L2390: This is a phase 2, open-label, multiple-dose, dose-escalation study to assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of crinecerfont in adult female and male subjects (18 to 50 years of age) with a documented medical diagnosis of classic CAH with a serum 17-OHP level of \ge 1,000 ng/dL at screening. The primary objectives of this study are to assess different dosing regimens of crinecerfont in adults with CAH, evaluate the effect of repeated doses of crinecerfont and different dosing regimens on endogenous levels of pharmacodynamic (PD) biomarkers in adults with CAH, and evaluate the plasma exposures following repeated doses of crinecerfont.
L2391: Crinecerfont doses evaluated were:
L2392: - Cohort 1: 50 mg once daily at bedtime (2200 hours) (n=8 enrolled/8 completed)
- Cohort 2: 100 mg once daily at bedtime (2200 hours) (n=7 enrolled/6 completed)
- Cohort 3: 100 mg once daily with evening meal (1900 hours) (n=8 enrolled/7 completed)
- Cohort 4: 100 mg twice daily with breakfast (0700 hours) and evening meal (1900 hours) (n=8 enrolled/8 completed)
L2393: Each dosing regimen was administered over 14 consecutive days. A total of 18 subjects were enrolled in the study, of which 13 subjects were re-enrolled in cohorts 3 and 4. Cohorts 1 and 2 received the crinecerfont dose with 237 mL of vanilla-flavored Ensure Plus while subjects in cohorts 3 and 4 were in outpatient settings for most of the study duration and ate meals at home. On the last day of dosing, subjects took the drug in cohorts 3 and 4 following a moderate fat, moderate calorie evening meal. All subjects took their usual morning dose of concurrent steroidal treatments at approximately 1000 hours.

L2429: ## Conclusions
L2430: - The mean crinecerfont plasma concentrations increased with increasing doses.
- The AUC_{24} 100 mg twice daily cohort (cohort 4) was approximately 2-fold higher than the AUC_{24} 100 mg once daily cohort (cohorts 2 and 3).
- A dose-response for A4 was observed with approximately 20% median reduction from baseline with the 50 mg once-daily cohort, approximately 40% with each of the 100 mg once-daily cohorts, and approximately 60% with the 100 mg bid cohort. It should be noted that interpretation of the study results may be confounded by different baselines of clinical endpoints (e.g., serum A4), between-subject variabilities of observed clinical endpoints during study, and relatively small sample sizes across dose groups.

L2467: ## 20.2.19. Phase 3 Study in Adults With CAH, Trial CAH3003
L2468: This is a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of crinecerfont versus placebo in 182 adult subjects with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CAH). The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily in reducing daily GC dosage while maintaining adrenal androgen control. Subjects were randomized 2:1 in crinecerfont: placebo group (122:60). The study design and the doses for each period are presented in Figure 52.
L2469: PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points during the study duration and plasma concentrations (ng/mL) were calculated for crinecerfont and its metabolites (NBI-756179, NBI-742939 (M4), NBI-1084059 (M9), and NBI-1084060 (M11)). The primary study endpoint was percent change from baseline (CFB) in GC daily dose at Week 24 with A4 levels controlled at \le 120\% of baseline or \le upper limit of normal (ULN) for age and sex. A key secondary endpoint was CFB in A4 levels at Week 4. Data are presented until the end of the open-label period (12 months) where 174 subjects entered the open-label period. Two subjects in the crinecerfont PK subset were not included, one due to an adverse event and another lost to follow-up, while one subject in the placebo group was not included in the analysis as they withdrew from the study.

L2497: ## **Conclusions**

- At Week 4, ~66% reduction in the 24-hour average concentrations from baseline for PD marker A4 at 100 mg twice daily doses was observed.

L2500: ## **20.2.20. Phase 3 Study in Pediatric Subjects With CAH, Trial NBI-74788-CAH2006**

L2521: ## Conclusions
L2522: - Mean plasma concentrations for crinecerfont and its metabolites (data not shown) remained similar for the 12 months of data reported within each weight dosing band.
- Mean predose plasma concentrations of crinecerfont were similar across postbaseline assessments in the double-blind period, with mean (CV [%]) values that ranged from 1094 ng/mL (57.1%) to 1527 ng/mL (40.9%) for subjects receiving crinecerfont 50 mg twice daily (bid) and 1572 ng/mL (60.3%) to 2073 ng/mL (38.2%) for subjects receiving crinecerfont 100 mg bid.
- At Week 4, ~80% reduction in the 24-hour average concentrations from baseline for PD marker A4 and 17-OHP at 50 mg twice daily doses was observed.
L2523: ## 20.3. Bioanalytical Method Validation and Performance

Three LC-MS/MS methods were developed and validated for the quantitative determination of crinecerfont and its metabolite concentrations in human serum in the completed clinical studies. Detailed methods and validation parameters are described below (Table 167, Table 168, and Table 169). The linearity of standard curve, selectivity/specificity, assay accuracy and precision, extraction efficiency and dilution fulfilled the standard acceptance criteria. The established frozen storage stability and run storage stability covered the corresponding study period and sample analysis period. We determined that these method validation and sample analysis are acceptable.

L2558: ## 20.5.1. Review Summary
L2559: (b) (4)
L2560: Crinecerfont is a selective CRF1 antagonist indicated
L2561: To support the proposed marketed dose, (i.e., clinical doses evaluated in phase 3 studies), the Applicant conducted popPK modeling and exposure-response (E-R) efficacy analyses. Additionally, E-R safety analyses were also explored for select safety endpoints.
L2562: In general, the Applicant's popPK analysis is considered acceptable for characterization of crinecerfont pharmacokinetics, evaluation of impact of clinically relevant covariates, and generation of exposure metrics for E-R analyses for safety and efficacy in the target adult and pediatric CAH populations. We verified the Applicant's analyses, and no significant discordance was identified. More specifically, the developed model was used to support the current submission as outlined in Table 172.

Predict exposures at alternative dosing regimen	Steady-state C_{max} and 24-hour AUC for 37.5 mg twice daily and 50 mg twice daily	Using the final popPK model, simulated alternative regimens of 37.5 mg twice daily and 50 mg twice daily (oral solutions) had improved AUC and C_{max} relative to those of the reference population of 20 to <55 kg; however, relatively higher proportions of the simulated subjects (10 to <20 kg) were also projected to have exposures above the 95th percentile of the reference exposures. Therefore, 25 mg bid (for the 10 to <20 kg subgroup) is expected to produce similar exposures to those of the 50 mg bid (for the 20 to <55 kg subgroup).

L2568: ## 20.5.2. Introduction
L2569: The primary objectives of the Applicant's analysis were to:
L2570: - Develop a popPK model to characterize crinecerfont pharmacokinetics in healthy subjects and adult and pediatric subjects with CAH
- Evaluate the covariate effects on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics
- Generate individual crinecerfont PK exposure metrics for E-R analyses for safety and efficacy
L2571: ## 20.5.3. Model Development
L2572: ## Data
L2573: The popPK analysis was based on PK data from four phase 1 studies in healthy subjects, two phase 2 studies, and two phase 3 studies in subjects with CAH. The study design, study population, dose levels, drug formulation, and type of PK samples are summarized in Table 173. For clinical studies that were excluded and the associated rationale, details can be found in Section 3.1 in the Applicant's popPK report.
L2574: The final nonlinear mixed-effects modeling (NONMEM) data file for analysis contained 6647 PK observations from 342 unique subjects (Table 174). Note that nine subjects were included in both phase 2 and phase 3 studies, contributing to 351 subjects in the summary tables. Table 175 provides summary statistics of the baseline demographic covariates in the analysis dataset.

L2600: ## **Base Model**
L2601: The base model was a three-compartment popPK model with transit compartment absorption and linear clearance. Interindividual variability (or random effects) was modeled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient level random effects. Residual variability was described using a log-additive error model during model development and subsequent model runs. Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of goodness-of-fit, diagnostic plots, significant reductions in objective function value, accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model convergence, and diagnostic plots.

L2604: ## **Covariate Analysis**
L2605: Covariate-parameter relationships were investigated and identified using clinical and physiologic relevance, exploratory analysis, prior knowledge, and mechanistic plausibility. Collinearity of covariates was assessed to ensure that no collinear covariates were added to the model. An assessment of any remaining trends was conducted by graphical inspection of covariate effects (plots of maximum a posteriori Bayes estimates of individual random effects and/or normalized prediction distribution error versus covariates). Continuous covariates were evaluated using a power function, and categorical covariates were parameterized as a fractional change.

L2613: ## 20.5.4. Final Model
L2614: The final popPK model included fixed effects of body weight on clearance and volume of distribution-related terms. For pediatric subjects under 18 years of age, time-varying body weight was used. For adult subjects, time-varying body weight was used for adult volume of distribution terms. Allometric scalers were fixed to 0.75 and 1, respectively, for clearance and volume of distribution-related terms. Effects of food and formulation were evaluated on mean transit time, absorption rate constant (K_a), and relative bioavailability (F_{rel}). Effect of baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was evaluated on clearance. Effect of baseline age was evaluated on central volume of distribution.
L2615: The parameter estimates for the final covariate model are listed in Table 177. The diagnostic plots (observed versus predicted, conditional weighted residuals, normalized prediction distribution errors, and Q-Q plots), for the final covariate model for all data are shown in Figure 55. The visual predictive checks (VPCs) for the final covariate model stratified by phase 3 study, formulation, and disease status are shown in Figure 56. Relationships of ETAs (i.e., random effects) for apparent clearance and select covariates are shown in Figure 57. Forest plot for steady-state AUC is shown in Figure 58.

L2645: The reviewer was able to reproduce and verify the Applicant's final popPK model, and no discordance was identified. The model parameters were estimated with reasonable precision based on the relative standard errors (RSEs) and the 95% CIs (as shown above). The highest RSEs for the key PK parameters were 51.2% and 29.4% for K_a and Q_2, respectively, and all other RSEs were below 5%. The shrinkages were generally acceptable in supporting simulation for dose selection in another population (between 20.5% to 33.9% except for K_a at 43.5%). Given the populations studied (adults and pediatric subjects), formulation differences, and food effect (fed and fasted states), the relatively higher variabilities around K_a and associated interindividual variability are expected. Based on the observed versus predicted data scatter plots, the data points are randomly scattered around the line of unity with no significant trend identified. The conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) and normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE) plots also demonstrate no bias or misspecification of the final model.
L2646: Additionally, the VPCs and select ETA plots also support that the popPK model adequately captures the central tendency of crinecerfont pharmacokinetics. For additional model diagnostic plots, such as random effects versus covariates, refer to the Applicant's popPK report. Overall, the popPK model is adequate in describing crinecerfont pharmacokinetics in the target adult and pediatric patient populations, in simulation for dose selection in the 10 to &lt;20 kg pediatric group, and in deriving phase 3 individual PK exposure metrics for E-R safety and efficacy analyses.

L2648: ## 20.5.5. Comparison of Adult and Pediatric Exposures
L2649: Based on clinical benefits achieved with crinecerfont exposures (i.e., AUC_{24}) corresponding to 200 mg once daily (Study TDR10671) or 100 mg bid (Trial NBI-74788-CAH2001), the Applicant selected the 100 mg bid dosing regimen because of the potential to produce sustained CRF antagonist activity over the entire day (refer to Section 12.1.1). For selection of the dosing regimen for pediatric patients by weight bands (10 to &lt;20 kg, 20 to &lt;55 kg, and \ge55 kg, corresponding to regimens of 25 mg solution bid, 50 mg solution bid, and 100 mg capsule bid), the Applicant used exposure matching to the adult subjects. To match to the adult exposures of 100 mg bid, simulations were performed incorporating allometry for pediatric subjects with CAH using the final popPK model.
L2650: A total of 500 virtual subjects were simulated for each dose level and weight band. Ages and weight were sampled from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) dataset, and crinecerfont doses were simulated for the fed state. Simulated exposures of steady-state AUC_{24} were compared between pediatric subjects and adult subjects. For the simulation, PK parameters were fixed to the final popPK model values. Of note, the clinical studies did not include pediatric subjects under 20 kg. Covariates sampled from the NHANES dataset provided virtual pediatric subjects of 10 to &lt;20 kg. Simulated steady-state AUCs are summarized in Table 178 and Table 179 and are illustrated in Figure 59 by dosing groups and formulation.

L2663: The simulation results demonstrated that pediatric subjects weighing \ge 55 kg and 20 to &lt;55 kg have overlapping exposures (i.e., AUC at steady state) when compared to the adult exposures, resulting in 91.6% and 76.8% of pediatric subjects within the 90% prediction interval, respectively. For pediatric subjects weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg, the percentage of simulated subjects falling within the 90% prediction interval of the adult exposure was numerically lower (68.4%) than those of the other two pediatric subgroups. Additionally, the median AUCs of the two lowest pediatric weight bands were lower than the 50th percentile of the adult AUC.
L2664: To further assess the appropriateness of the 25 mg bid dosing in the absence of studying the 10 to &lt;20 kg population (i.e., no PK or clinical outcomes data), the following key points were considered:
L2665: - Based on the disease state, pathophysiology, and current standard of care, pediatric patients down to 4 years of age with CAH are likely to fall under the 20 to &lt;55 kg group (see Section 12.3.1).
- PK data and clinical outcomes data were available from pediatric subjects weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg in the phase 3 clinical trial (Table 175), and this pediatric subgroup is more physiologically similar when compared to pediatric patients weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg regarding physiology, disease state, disease progression, and expected efficacy response for CAH (based on the indicated age cut-off).
- Efficacy outcomes of the pediatric subjects weighing 20 to &lt;55 kg are considered acceptable per the clinical review team assessment (see Section 12.3.1).
- The relatively higher exposure in adult subjects serve as the safety exposure coverage.
L2666: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L2667: Therefore, the pediatric subgroup of 20 to &lt;55 kg is an acceptable efficacy reference group for exposure matching for the 10 to &lt;20 kg group.
L2668: Further simulations of alternative regimens were conducted by the reviewer to support the 25 mg bid regimen. For the virtual population, a total of 9500 subjects were generated using the NHANES database across all 4 groups as shown below. Specifically, 1000 and 3500 subjects were allocated to the 10 to &lt;20 kg group and 20 to &lt;55 kg group, respectively, with 500 virtual pediatric subjects allocated for each subgroup at 5-kg increments. In the reviewer's analysis, two adjustments were made to reflect the indication for crinecerfont in this NDA: (1) the minimum age was raised to 4 years, and (2) the upper bound of the adult body weight was capped at 155 kg, which is approximately one standard deviation (of the body weight distribution of the overall PK population) above the highest body weight studied in the PK population.
L2669: The 25 mg bid, 37.5 mg bid, and 50 mg bid dosages of the solution formulation were simulated for the 10 to &lt;20 kg group. The proposed dosage of 50 mg bid was simulated for the 20 to &lt;55 kg group.
L2670: As shown in Figure 60 and Figure 61, the simulated regimens of 37.5 mg bid and 50 mg bid for the 10 to &lt;20 kg group had improved AUC and C_{max} relative to those of the reference population of 20 to &lt;55 kg; however, relatively higher proportions of the simulated subjects were also projected to have exposures above the 95th percentile of the reference exposures. Therefore, 25 mg bid for the 10 to &lt;20 kg subgroup is expected to produce similar exposures to those of 50 mg bid for the 20 to &lt;55 kg subgroup, and because a high proportion of subjects weighing 10 to &lt;20 kg is expected to have exposures within the adult exposure, the exposures of the proposed 25 mg bid in 10 to &lt;25 kg subgroup is expected to be safe and effective.

L2680: ## 20.5.6. E-R Analysis
L2681: Using data from the phase 3 studies in adult (CAH3003) and pediatric (CAH2006) subjects with CAH, E-R analyses were conducted independently in each population to characterize the relationship between plasma exposure and clinical endpoints and to support evidence of effectiveness of the proposed doses for adult and pediatric patients with CAH. The Applicant's objectives of the E-R analyses were to:
L2682: - Develop an exposure-efficacy model for percent CFB in daily GC dose while maintaining adequate control of androgen levels at Week 24 (CAH3003) and Week 28 (CAH2006) in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH, respectively
- Develop an exposure-efficacy model for the achievement of reduction in GC daily dose to physiologic levels (\le 11 \text{ mg}/\text{m}^2/\text{day} hydrocortisone equivalent adjusted for body surface area [BSA]) while maintaining adequate control of androgen levels at Week 24 (CAH3003) and Week 28 (CAH2006) in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH, respectively
- Develop an exposure-efficacy model for change from baseline in serum A4 (i.e., androstenedione) prior to morning GC dose at Week 4 while subjects were on a stable background GC daily dose in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH
- Develop an exposure-safety model for a safety endpoint in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH, if deemed necessary
- Evaluate the effects of select covariates of interest on E-R relationships
- Compare the E-R relationships between adult and pediatric subjects
L2683: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L2684: Refer to Section 20.2 for primary and secondary endpoints for Trial CAH3003 and Trial CAH2006. Each phase 3 study was used for adult and pediatric E-R analysis, respectively, and the studies are summarized in Table 180. Exposure metrics were generated based on the final popPK model structure using the individual PK parameter, actual dosing record, and covariates for individuals. Base E-R model structures (i.e., maximum drug effect [E_{max}] model and logistic regression) are shown in Equation 1 and Equation 2, respectively, to describe the efficacy endpoints for both the adult and pediatric E-R analyses. Additionally, select covariates were adjusted for in the E-R models as summarized in Table 181. Model evaluation includes model fit adequacy, parameter precision, model stability, significant reductions in objective function value between hierarchical models, and standard goodness-of-fit plots.

L2733: ## NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
## CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L2734: In the Applicant's E-R model for GC response at Week 24 from baseline, the parameter precision of fixed effects appears reasonable based on the 95% CI. Null effect is contained within the 95% CI of age, sex, body weight, and baseline GC dose effect on intercept, indicating minimal impact. Based on the final model predictions, the exposure-response relationship suggests that the probability of achieving a GC response (i.e., GC dose at physiologic levels) increases as crinecerfont exposure increases (within the range of studied exposure); however, the 95% CIs of the beta slope are numerically small (0.0000191 to 0.0000385) and approaching zero, suggesting that the odds ratio is close to 1 and that other factors may also be driving the probability of GC response. Overall, the results of this E-R analysis should be interpreted with caution.
L2735: ## 20.5.6.1.4. Safety
L2736: In the adult study, TEAEs that occurred with at least 5% greater incidence in the crinecerfont arm were fatigue (24.6% crinecerfont; 15.3% placebo), coronavirus infection (13.9%; 8.5%), and arthralgia (7.4%; 0%). Fatigue had the highest reported frequency in the crinecerfont arm and was, therefore, selected as the AE for exploratory E-R analysis.

L2999: ## 21.3. Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale
L3000: The Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale was used to screen for suicidal ideation and behavior during trials CAH3003 and CAH2006. The questionnaire content is shown in Figure 71.
L3001: **Figure 71. Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale Questions**
L3002: Always ask questions 1 and 2.	Past Month
1) Have you wished you were dead or wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?	
2) Have you actually had any thoughts about killing yourself?	
If YES to 2, ask questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.
If NO to 2, skip to question 6.
3) Have you been thinking about how you might do this?	
4) Have you had these thoughts and had some intention of acting on them?	High Risk
5) Have you started to work out or worked out the details of how to kill yourself? Did you intend to carry out this plan?	High Risk
Always Ask Question 6	Life-time	Past 3 Months
6) Have you done anything, started to do anything, or prepared to do anything to end your life?
Examples: Took pills, tried to shoot yourself, cut yourself, tried to hang yourself, or collected pills, obtained a gun, gave away valuables, wrote a will or suicide note, took out pills but didn't swallow any, held a gun but changed your mind or it was grabbed from your hand, went to the roof but didn't jump, etc.
If yes, was this within the past 3 months?	High Risk
L3003: Source: https://cssrs.columbia.edu/the-columbia-scale-c-ssrs/about-the-scale/ Accessed: 26 October 2024.
L3004: ## Scoring Scale
L3005: 0 – No suicidal ideation
L3006: 1 – Wish to be dead
L3007: 2 – Nonspecific active suicidal thoughts
L3008: 3 – Active suicidal ideation with methods without intent to act
L3009: 4 – Active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan
L3010: 5 – Active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent
L3011: ## 22. Efficacy
L3012: The efficacy assessment was based on the two phase 3 trials, CAH3003 in adults and CAH2006 in children. The efficacy findings are discussed in Section 12.2 of this document.
L3013: The two phase 2 dose-finding trials—Trial CAH2001 in adults with CAH and Trial CAH2008 in pediatric subjects with CAH—informed dosing for the phase 3 trials and are discussed in Section 12.1 of this document.
L3014: The review team conducted additional subgroup analyses of the primary efficacy endpoint for trials CAH3003 in adults and CAH2006 in children.
L3015: ## **Subgroup Analysis of Primary Endpoint**
L3016: ## **Trial CAH3003**
L3017: Analyses of the primary endpoint by subgroup showed that the glucocorticoid total daily dose decreased from baseline to Week 24 in the crinecerfont group, compared with the placebo group, in all prespecified subgroups (Figure 72). Interpretation of 95% CIs in some subgroups was limited by their small sample sizes and likely some random highs and random lows in sample estimates of subgroup treatment effects. Therefore, we also derived shrinkage estimates of subgroup treatment effects using a Bayesian hierarchical model based on summary sample estimates.
L3018: The total variability in the sample estimates is the sum of the within-subgroup variability of the sample estimator and the across-subgroups variability in underlying/true parameter values. Shrinkage estimates of the subgroup treatment effect, which borrows information from the other subgroups while estimating the treatment effect for a specific subgroup, is a “weighted” average of the sample estimate and overall estimate. The weights are based on the ratio of the between-subgroup variability to the within-subgroup variability. The greater that ratio, the smaller the weight on the overall estimate (the less the shrinkage).
L3019: For i=1, 2, \dots, n, Y_i represents the observed sample estimate of treatment effect in a subgroup level i, assume Y_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma_i^2) where:
L3020: - \sigma_i^2 are the observed variance for sample estimates,
- \mu_i \sim N(\mu, \tau^2), and
- \mu \sim N(0, 400), 1/\tau^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(0.001, 0.001).
L3021: The variance of 400 for the hyper-prior \mu \sim N(0, \text{variance} = 400), was chosen as 4 \times \text{Residual Variance} of the treatment effect.
L3022: **Figure 72. Forest Plot of LS Mean Differences of Percent Change From Baseline at Week 24 in Glucocorticoid Total Daily Dose in Different Subgroups, Trial NBI-74788-CAH3003, Full Analysis Set**
L3023: Source: Statistical reviewer's analysis
L3024: Subjects not meeting the androstenedione control criteria, had their glucocorticoid daily dose percent change from baseline values set to 0 at each visit where control was not met. Due to small number of participants Black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native and Asian were combined into OTHER category of Race.
L3025: Abbreviations: ETHN, ethnicity; F, female; LS, least squares; M, male; REGI, region; REST, rest of world; US, United States

L3035: ## 23. Clinical Safety
L3036: ## 23.1. Abuse Potential
L3037: The FDA controlled substance staff (CSS) reviewed the drug abuse liability assessment of crinecerfont. In a memorandum to NDA 218808 and finalized in Document Archiving, Reporting, and Regulatory Tracking System (DARRTS) on October 23, 2024, CSS concluded:
L3038: - The receptor binding and activity data indicate that crinecerfont is a CRF1 receptor antagonist. Receptor binding studies demonstrated that crinecerfont did not bind to any receptors, transporters, or ion channels typically associated with drugs having a potential for abuse.
- Additional studies including nonclinical abuse potential assessments and a human abuse potential study were not requested.
- A review of TEAEs in clinical studies did not reveal any evidence to suggest that crinecerfont has a potential for abuse or physical dependence. The most prevalent AEs observed in clinical trials were fatigue, headache, and pyrexia.
L3039: NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
L3040: - The proposed drug product, if approved under this NDA, will not require a Drug Abuse and Dependence section in its label.
L3041: SS concluded that crinecerfont does not appear to have abuse potential and should not be controlled under the Controlled Substances Act. Crinecerfont does not require a Section 9 (Drug Abuse and Dependence section) in its label.
L3042: ## 23.2. Laboratory Analyses, Trial CAH3003
L3043: ## 23.2.1. Chemistry, Trial CAH3003
L3044: There were no meaningful differences between crinecerfont and placebo groups in mean change from baseline in any chemistry parameter during the double-blind treatment period. Renal function remained stable (see Figure 74 and Figure 75) and lipid parameters in both treatment groups declined slightly during the double-blind treatment phase (Figure 76).
L3045: Outlier analysis tables for chemistry and renal function parameters are shown in Table 195 and Table 196. Other than what was discussed in earlier sections of this review, there were no clinically meaningful differences in incidences of laboratory parameters outside the normal range between treatment groups. The higher incidence of low bicarbonate (&lt;20 mEq/L) and low calcium (&lt;8.4 mg/dL) with crinecerfont vs. placebo in this trial was not observed in the pediatric trial; this lack of consistency across trials reduces the likelihood that these findings are drug-related.
L3046: Outlier analysis for lipid parameters is shown in Table 197. The greater frequency of outliers in some of the lipid parameters in the crinecerfont group is not clinically meaningful because the mean change from baseline was not significant and not significantly different from placebo (figures included).

L3230: ## 30. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L3231: The review team is concerned about a serious risk of inhibition of ACTH secretion in the developing fetus, which may lead to fetal growth restriction, preterm delivery, or demise, and to an unexpected serious risk of infant exposure to crinecerfont during lactation. The Division of Pediatrics and Maternal Health (DPMH) in a memorandum of consultation filed to NDA 218808 in DARRTS on September 13, 2024, recommends a postmarketing requirement (PMR) for a descriptive pregnancy safety study (DPSS) for the following reasons:
L3232: - Three pregnancies occurred during the drug development program, indicating that females of reproductive potential with classic CAH may take crinecerfont. Although there were pregnancies that occurred during drug development, there are no data from these pregnancies to inform the use of crinecerfont during pregnancy. Thus, a DPSS would provide necessary pregnancy safety data.
- Given that classic CAH is a rare disease, the number of pregnant patients who use crinecerfont is likely to be small. With a small number of pregnant patients using crinecerfont, a pregnancy exposure registry would be unlikely to adequately enroll patients; therefore, a DPSS is preferred.
- Crinecerfont is systemically absorbed and will cross the placenta. Crinecerfont has the potential to inhibit ACTH secretion in the developing fetus, thereby reducing cortisol levels in the fetus, which may result in fetal growth restriction, preterm delivery, or demise.
L3233: DPMH also recommends a PMR for a clinical lactation study to determine the extent to which crinecerfont is present in human milk. Their rationale is that crinecerfont is present in animal milk, which presents a potential for adrenal insufficiency or crisis in healthy neonates and infants exposed to crinecerfont via breast milk.
L3234: The following are postmarketing requirements to assess the effect of crinecerfont on developing fetuses and lactation:
L3235: - Conduct a worldwide descriptive study that collects prospective and retrospective data in women exposed to crinecerfont during pregnancy and/or lactation to assess risk of pregnancy and maternal complications, adverse effects on the developing fetus and neonate, and adverse effects on the infant. Infant outcomes will be assessed through at least the first year of life. The minimum number of patients will be specified in the protocol.
L3236: - Perform a lactation study (milk only or mother-infant pair study) in lactating women who have received crinecerfont to measure concentrations of crinecerfont and its major metabolites in breast milk using a validated assay and to assess the effects on the breastfed infant, if available, based on study population.
L3237: DGE discussed advice from the Division of Pharmacovigilance in the Office of Surveillance and Epidemiology regarding further assessment of suicidality and neutropenia in the postmarket setting. The Division of Pharmacovigilance recommends the Applicant commit to the following enhanced pharmacovigilance plan:
L3238: - NeutropeniaSubmit all serious and non-serious domestic and/or foreign cases of neutropenia as 15-day “alert reports”) through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval.
- Include narrative summary analyses of events of neutropenia in the required periodic safety reports through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval. Use the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) high-level term (HLT) “neutropenias” to retrieve reports.
- SuicidalitySubmit all serious and non-serious domestic and/or foreign cases of suicidal behavior and/or ideation as 15-day “alert reports” through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval.
- Include narrative summary analyses of suicidal behavior and/or ideation in the required periodic safety reports through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval. Use the MedDRA preferred terms (PTs) of “completed suicide,” “suicide attempt,” “suicidal behavior,” and “suicidal ideation” to retrieve reports.
L3239: Narrative summary analyses of neutropenia and suicidality in the periodic safety reports should include interval and cumulative data relative to the date of approval of CRENESITY (crinecerfont) and should provide an assessment of causality, with documentation of indication, temporal association, duration of therapy, associated signs and symptoms, confounders, underlying risk factors (e.g., psychiatric history), treatment given for the event, outcome, and drug disposition.

L3342: ## 1. Summary
L3343: In this submission the sponsor included reports of two animal carcinogenicity studies, one in CD[Crl:CD(SD)] rats and one in CByB6F1-Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice. These studies were intended to assess the carcinogenic potential of Crinecerfont, when administered via oral gavage at appropriate drug levels for 100 weeks in rats and 26 weeks in mice.
L3344: ## Rat Study:
L3345: ## Survival data analyses:
L3346: - For male rats, the survival analyses didn't show any statistically significant dose response relationship in mortality across the water control group and treated groups. However, p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0152&lt;0.05 but the p-value of log-rank test is 0.0675&gt;0.05. The pairwise comparisons did not show any statistically significant differences in mortality between the water control group and treated groups.
- For male rats, the survival analyses didn't show any statistically significant dose response relationship in mortality across the vehicle control group and treated groups. However, p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0120&lt;0.05 but the p-value of log-rank test is 0.0563&gt;0.05. The pairwise comparisons showed statistically significant differences in mortality between the vehicle control group and the high dose group. The p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0428&lt;0.05 and the p-value of log-rank test is 0.0393&lt;0.05.
- For female rats, the survival analyses didn't show any statistically significant dose response relationship in mortality across the water control group and treated groups or across the vehicle control group and the treated groups. The pairwise comparisons did not show any statistically significant differences in mortality between the water control group and treated groups or between the vehicle control group and the treated groups.

L3356: ## 2. Background
L3357: In this submission the sponsor included reports of two animal carcinogenicity studies, one in CD[Crl:CD(SD)] rats and one in CByB6F1-Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice. These studies were intended to assess the carcinogenic potential of Crinecerfont, when administered via administered by oral gavage at appropriate drug levels for 100 weeks in rats and 26 weeks in mice.
L3358: In this review the phrase "dose response relationship" refers to the linear component of the effect of treatment, and not necessarily to a strictly increasing or decreasing mortality or tumor incidence rate as the dose increases.
L3359: ## 3. Rat Study
L3360: Two separate experiments were conducted, one in males and one in females. In each of these two experiments there were three treated groups, one water group and one vehicle control group. Three hundred and fifty rats of each sex were randomly assigned to the five groups in equal size of 70 rats per group. The dose levels for treated groups were 5, 15 and 100 mg/kg/day. The rats in the water control group received the De-ionized water. The study for the rats was designed to continue for up to 100 weeks.

L3363: ## 3.1. Sponsor's analyses
L3364: ## 3.1.1. Survival analysis
L3365: Intercurrent mortality data was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier product-limit method. An overall test comparing all groups was conducted using a log-rank test (Allison, PD, 1995). If this overall test was significant (p&lt;0.05) and there were more than two groups, then a follow up analysis was done where each treatment group was compared to the control group using a log-rank test.
L3366: Results of all pair-wise comparisons were reported at the 0.05 and 0.01 significance levels. All endpoints were analyzed using two-tailed tests.
L3367: Sponsor's findings: Sponsor's analysis showed the numbers (percents) of survival were 20 (29%), 21 (30%), 20 (29%), 18 (26%), and 15 (21%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high dose groups, respectively in males and 20 (29%), 22 (31%), 17 (24%), 23 (33%), and 23 (33%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high dose groups, respectively in females.
L3368: No NBI-74788-related unscheduled deaths or euthanasias occurred in either sex, and no statistically significant survival differences were noted.
L3369: ## 3.1.2. Tumor data analysis
L3370: Tumor incidence data was analyzed using both survival adjusted and unadjusted tests. The unadjusted tests were based on the incidence and number of sites examined for each tumor type. The Cochran-Armitage test (Agresti, A. 1999) was for trend test and Fisher's exact test (Zar JH, 1999) was used to compare each treatment group with the control group. Trend test was applied for all control and treatment groups that were arranged in a strictly increasing dose level. The survival adjusted test was conducted according to the prevalence/mortality methods described by Peto et al (Peto et al, 1980). The Poly-3 method (Bieler and Williams, 1993) (Bailer and Portier, 1988) was used to assess prevalence of tumors. The survival-adjusted rates based on the risk weights was displayed. The tests of significance included both an overall trend and pair-wise comparisons of each treatment group with the control. All p-values were reported using upper-tailed tests, unless otherwise indicated.
L3371: Sponsor's findings: Test article-related neoplastic microscopic findings were limited to an increased incidence of benign and malignant thyroid follicular cell tumors (adenomas and carcinomas) in females at 100 mg/kg/day.

L3375: ## 3.2.1. Survival analysis
L3376: The survival distributions of animals in four groups were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier product limit method. The dose response relationship and homogeneity of survival distributions were tested for the water control, vehicle control, low, medium and high dose groups using the Likelihood Ratio test and the Log-Rank test. The intercurrent mortality data are given in Tables 11 and 12 in the appendix for males and females, respectively. The Kaplan-Meier curves for survival rate are given in Figures 1 and 2 in the appendix for males and females, respectively. Results of the tests for dose response relationship and homogeneity of survivals, are given in Tables 13 to 16 in the appendix for males and females, respectively.
L3377: Reviewer's findings: This reviewer's analysis showed the numbers (percents) of survival were 20 (29%), 21 (30%), 20 (29%), 18 (26%), and 15 (21%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high dose groups, respectively in males and 20 (29%), 22 (31%), 17 (24%), 23 (33%), and 23 (33%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high dose groups, respectively in females.

However, p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0152 &lt; 0.05 but the p-value of log-rank test is 0.0675 &gt; 0.05. The pairwise comparisons did not show any statistically significant differences in mortality between the water control group and treated groups.

L3381: ## 3.2.2. Tumor data analysis
L3382: The tumor data were analyzed for the positive dose response relationships and the positive pairwise comparison increases between each of the treated groups with control group. Both the dose response relationship tests and pairwise comparisons were performed using the Poly-K method described in the paper of Bailer and Portier (1988) and Bieler and Williams (1993). In this method an animal that lives the full study period (w_{max}) or dies before the terminal sacrifice but develops the tumor type being tested gets a score of s_h = 1. An animal that dies at week w_h without a tumor before the end of the study gets a score of s_h = \left(\frac{w_h}{w_{max}}\right)^k &lt; 1. The adjusted group size is defined as \sum s_h. As an interpretation, an animal with score s_h = 1 can be considered as a whole animal while an animal with score s_h &lt; 1 can be considered as a partial animal. The adjusted group size \sum s_h is equal to N (the original group size) if all animals live up to the end of the study or if each animal that dies before the terminal sacrifice develops at least one tumor, otherwise the adjusted group size is less than N. These adjusted group sizes were then used for the dose response relationship (or the pairwise) tests using the Cochran-Armitage test. One critical point for Poly-k test is the choice of the appropriate value of k, which depends on the tumor incidence pattern with the increased dose. For long term 104 week standard rat and mouse studies, a value of k=3 is suggested in the literature. Hence, this reviewer used k=3 for the analysis of this data. For the calculation of p-values the exact permutation method was used. The tumor rates and the p-values for the positive dose response relationship tests and pairwise comparisons are listed in Tables 17 to 20 in the appendix for male and female rats, respectively.
L3383: **Adjustment for multiple testing:** For the chronic study in rats, the adjustment of multiple testing of the dose response relationship for a submission with one chronic rat study and one transgenic mouse study, the more recently revised draft (January, 2013) FDA guidance for the carcinogenicity studies suggests the use of test levels \alpha = 0.005 for common tumors and \alpha = 0.025 for rare tumors for the chronic rat study. For pairwise comparisons for the chronic rat study in the above type of submission with one chronic rat study and one transgenic mouse study, the same guidance document suggests the use of test levels \alpha = 0.01 for common tumors and \alpha = 0.05 for rare tumors for the chronic rat study.
L3384: It should be noted that the FDA guidance for multiple testing for dose response relationship is based on a publication by Lin and Rahman (1998). In this work the authors investigated the use of this rule for Peto analysis. However, in a later work Rahman and Lin (2008) showed that this rule for multiple testing for dose response relationship is also suitable for Poly-K tests.
L3385: Reviewer's findings: The tumor types in Tables 2 to 5 below showed p-values less than or equal to 0.05 in the tests for pairwise comparisons between vehicle control and treated groups for males.
L3386: Based on the criteria of adjustment for multiple testing discussed in the data analysis section, we make the following statistical conclusions:
L3387: - For female rats, the tumor data analysis showed statistically significant positive dose response relationships across the water control and the treated groups in incidences of adenoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value&lt;0.001), carcinoma follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0032&lt;0.025), and combined adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value&lt;0.001). The pairwise comparisons between the water control and the high dose group showed statistically significant increases in the incidences of adenoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0041&lt;0.05), carcinoma follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0332&lt;0.05), and combined adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value&lt;0.001).
- For female rats, the tumor data analysis showed a statistically significant positive dose response relationships across the vehicle control and the treated groups in the incidences of adenoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value&lt;0.001), carcinoma follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0032&lt;0.025), combined adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value&lt;0.001) and schwannoma, uterus with cervix (P-value=0.0205&lt;0.025). The pairwise comparisons between the vehicle control and the low dose group showed statistically significant increases in incidences of pheochromocytoma, adrenal glands (P-value=0.0065&lt;0.05). The pairwise comparisons between the vehicle control and the high dose group showed statistically significant increases in
L3388: incidences of pheochromocytoma, adrenal glands (P-value=0.015&lt;0.05), carcinoma follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0312&lt;0.05), and combined adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0027&lt;0.01).

L3398: ## 4. Mouse Study
L3399: Two separate experiments were conducted, one in males and one in females. In each of these two experiments there were four treated groups, one water group, one vehicle control group and one positive control group. Two hundred and fifty mice of each sex were randomly assigned to the treated and control groups. There are 25 mice in water control group. There are 35 mice in each of the vehicle control group and treated groups. The dose levels for treated groups were 15, 50, 500 and 1500 mg/kg/day for males and females. There were ten mice in positive control group for each sex. Animals in positive control group were administered once via intraperitoneal (IP) injection once on Day 1. The positive control article was N-Nitroso-N-methylurea (NMU).

L3402: ## 4.1. Sponsor's analyses
L3403: ## 4.1.1. Survival analysis
L3404: Intercurrent mortality data were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier product-limit method. An overall test comparing all groups was conducted using a log-rank test (Allison, 1995). If this overall test was significant (p&lt;0.05), then a follow up analysis was done where each treatment group was compared to the control group using a log-rank test. Results of all pair-wise comparisons were reported at the 0.05 and 0.01 significance levels. All endpoints were analyzed using two-tailed tests.
L3405: Sponsor's findings: The sponsor's analysis showed that the numbers (percents) of survival were 23 (92%), 32 (91%), 32 (91%), 33 (94%), 32 (91%), 33 (94%) and 8 (80%) in male mice, and 25 (100%), 31 (89%), 32 (91%), 32 (91%), 35 (100%), 35 (100%) and 9 (90%) in female
L3406: mice in water control, vehicle control, low, medium, high and high 2 dose groups, respectively.
L3407: The sponsor concluded that, no test article-related mortality occurred and evaluations of survival revealed no statistically significant differences.
L3408: ## 4.1.2. Tumor data analysis
L3409: Tumor incidence data were analyzed using both survival adjusted and unadjusted tests. The unadjusted tests were based on the incidence and number of sites examined for each tumor type. The Cochran-Armitage test (Agresti, 2002) was for trend and Fisher's exact test (Zar, 1999) was used to compare each treatment group with the control group. Trend test was applied for all control and treatment groups that could be arranged in a strictly increasing dose level. The survival adjusted test was conducted according to the prevalence/mortality methods described by Peto et al (Peto R, Pike MC, Day NE et al, 1980).
L3410: The Poly-3 method (Bailer and Portier, 1988) (Bieler and Williams, 1993) was used to assess prevalence of tumors. The survival-adjusted rates based on the risk weights were displayed. The tests of significance included both an overall trend and pair-wise comparisons of each treatment group with the control. All p-values were reported using upper-tailed tests, unless otherwise indicated.
L3411: Sponsor's findings: The sponsor concluded that the occurrence of none of the observed tumors in the NBI-74788-treated groups were statistically significant when compared to the control groups.

L3416: control group were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier product limit method. The dose response relationship in survival was tested using the likelihood ratio test and the homogeneity of survival distributions was tested using the log-rank test. The Kaplan-Meier curves for survival rates are given in Figures 3 and 4 in the appendix for male and female mice, respectively. The intercurrent mortality data are given in Tables 21 and 22 in the appendix for male and female mice, respectively. Results of the tests for dose response relationship and homogeneity of survivals among the water control, vehicle control, positive control and the treated groups are given in Tables 23 to 26 in the appendix for male and female mice, respectively.

L3422: The tumor rates and the p-values for the positive dose response relationship tests and pairwise comparisons between water/vehicle control and the treated groups, and between water/vehicle and positive control are listed in Tables 27 to 34 in the appendix for male and
L3423: female mice, respectively.
L3424: Adjustment for multiple testing: For the adjustment of multiple testing of the dose response relationship for a submission with one 2 year chronic rat study and one 26 week chronic mouse study, the more recently revised draft (January, 2013) FDA guidance for the carcinogenicity studies suggests the use of test levels \alpha = 0.005 for common tumors and \alpha = 0.025 for rare tumors for the chronic mouse study. For pairwise comparisons of submission with one 2 year chronic rat study and one 26 week chronic mouse study, the same guidance document suggests the use of test levels \alpha = 0.01 for common tumors and \alpha = 0.05 for rare tumors for the chronic mouse study.
L3425: It should be noted that the FDA guidance for multiple testing for dose response relationship is based on a publication by Lin and Rahman (1998). In this work the authors investigated the use of this rule for Peto analysis. However, in a later work Rahman and Lin (2008) showed that this rule for multiple testing for dose response relationship is also suitable for Poly-K tests.
L3426: Reviewer's findings: The tumor types in Tables 7 to 10 below showed p-values less than or equal to 0.05 in the tests between vehicle control and treated groups for males.

L3531: Figure 6 is a schematic diagram illustrating the trial schema from Screening to Month 18 (Trial CAH3003). The timeline is divided into Weeks (from -4 to 24) and Months (from 7 to 19).
The trial consists of a Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period followed by an Open-Label Treatment Period.
Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period:
Screening: Subjects are randomized on Day 1 (Week 0).
GC Stable Period (GCS): Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid) or Placebo.
GC Reduction Period: Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid) or Placebo.
GC Optimization Period: Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid) or Placebo.
Assessments during this period include Safety FU (Follow-Up) at Weeks 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12, and GC1 assessments at Weeks 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12.
Open-Label Treatment Period:
GC Stable Period (GCS): Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid).
GC Reduction Period: Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid).
GC Optimize: Subjects receive Crinecerfont (100 mg bid or 100 mg qAM and 200 mg qPM).
Assessments during this period include Safety FU at Weeks 16, 20, and 24, and GC1 assessments at Weeks 16, 20, and 24.
Assessments during the Open Label Treatment Period (GC Optimize) include Safety FU at Months 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, and 18, and GC1 assessments at Months 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, and 18.

First Key Secondary Endpoint (\alpha = 0.02), (unequal allocation)
Second Key Secondary Endpoint (\alpha = 0.03), (unequal allocation)
Both First Key Secondary Endpoint and Second Key Secondary Endpoint lead to:
Other Key Secondary Endpoints (\alpha = 0.02, 0.03, \text{ or } 0.05), (test collectively via Holm)

L3582: Figure 52 is a timeline diagram illustrating the Study Design and Crinecerfont Doses in Each Period for Trial NBI-74788-CAH3003.
The study is divided into two main phases:
Day 1 – Week 24: Blinded/ Randomized PeriodCrinecerfont 100 mg twice daily
Day 1 – week 4: GC stable period (>13 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day})
Week 4 – Week 12: GC reduction period (target dose of 8 to 10 \text{mg/m}^2/\text{day})
Week 12 – Week 24: GC doses adjusted based on A4 levels

Week 24 – 12 months: Open LabelCrinecerfont 100 mg twice daily
Week 24 – Month 7: Stable GC period
Month 7 – Month 10: For subjects who did not achieve target GC dose, GC dose reduction continued to achieve target GC dose of 8 to 10 \text{mg/m}^2/\text{day}
Month 10 – Month 12: GC Maintenance Period

Months 12–18: Open Label or Double BlindedMonth 12 – Month 18 (Open label): Crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily for subjects with GC dose of \le 11 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day}
Month 12 – Month 18 (blinded, randomized): Crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily OR 100 mg qAM & 200 mg qPM for subjects with GC dose > 11 \text{ mg/m}^2/\text{day}; GC reduction protocol was followed to achieve target GC levels of 8 to 10 \text{mg/m}^2/\text{day}

Months 18 – 24: Open-label Extension*Crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily OR 100 mg qAM & 200 mg qPM

Months 24+: Open labelCrinecerfont 100 mg twice daily OR 100 mg qAM & 200 mg qPM OR 200 mg qPM

L3584: Diagram illustrating the Scheme of Base PopPK Model Structure. The model starts with Oral dosing, which enters a Transit compartment (NT) via rate constant k_tr. The Transit compartment releases drug into the Central compartment (Vc/F) via rate constant k_a. The Central compartment (Vc/F) exchanges drug with Peripheral compartment 1 (V2/F) via Q1/F, and with Peripheral compartment 2 (V3/F) via Q2/F. The Central compartment (Vc/F) also has linear clearance (CL/F) leading to elimination.
